Summary statement Heat-dependent conformational change of tomato rhomboid protease 3 facilitates SlNACMTF3 recognition within plasma membrane. The protease-mediated rapid activation leads to stress gene regulation for thermotolerance.
items.authors: Talukdar S, Paul D, Roy S, Harikishore A, Bhunia A, Dastidar SG, Kundu P.

items.title: Functional characterization of flowering-associated PbMADS33 and PbMADS8 in Phoebe bournei.
items.abstract: PbMADS8 and PbMADS33 from Phoebe bournei promote flowering when overexpressed in Arabidopsis and interact in the nucleus; their co-expression enhances PbGA20ox1 and PbFBX promoter activity in transient assays. Phoebe bournei has a prolonged juvenile phase that limits breeding, but the functions of its flowering-associated regulators remain poorly understood. Transcriptome analysis of leaves from trees of different ages and floral samples identified 5,921 differentially expressed genes. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) identified a black module associated with leaves from flowering trees and containing three SUPPRESSOR OF OVEREXPRESSION OF CONSTANS 1 (SOC1)-like genes, PbMADS8, PbMADS33, and PbMADS38. Comparative genomic analysis revealed expanded SOC1-like loci enriched in repetitive sequences. PbMADS8 and PbMADS33 were selected for functional analysis because of their higher transcript abundance relative to PbMADS38. Heterologous overexpression of either gene accelerated flowering in Arabidopsis thaliana under long-day conditions. Yeast two-hybrid (Y2H) and bimolecular fluorescence complementation (BiFC) assays supported an interaction between PbMADS33 and PbMADS8 in the nucleus. DNA affinity purification sequencing (DAP-seq) identified candidate PbMADS33-binding regions, and promoter assays supported regulation of PbGA20ox1 and the putative F-box gene PbFBX. Co-expression of PbMADS8 and PbMADS33 produced the highest reporter activity for both promoters in Nicotiana benthamiana. Together, these results nominate PbMADS8 and PbMADS33 as flowering-associated candidates and PbGA20ox1 and PbFBX as candidate promoter-associated genes in P. bournei. Their effects on endogenous gibberellin levels, protein turnover, and the juvenile phase of P. bournei remain to be established.
items.authors: Sun Q, Zhang Y, Qiu Y, Wang B, Zhou S, Li C, Han X, Yang Q, Tong Z, Zhang J.

items.title: VpsCDPK9 negatively regulates the salt and alkaline tolerance of grapevine by enhancing the reactive oxygen burst of VviRbohs.
items.abstract: The grape industry, critical for rural economic development and farmer income, faces escalating challenges from soil salinization. Calcium-dependent protein kinases (CDPKs) are important calcium signaling components that have been shown to play crucial roles in modulating plant abiotic stress responses. The CDPK-RBOH module has previously been shown to regulate grape cold stress by modulating photosynthesis. However, whether VpsCDPK9 is involved in salt stress response remained unclear. In this study, we found that saline-alkaline stress induced VpsCDPK9 expression. Compared to wild-type plants, VpsCDPK9 overexpression lines exhibited heightened sensitivity to saline-alkaline stress, indicating a negative regulatory role of VpsCDPK9 in grapevine salinity-alkalinity tolerance. Under stress conditions, VpsCDPK9 specifically enriches at the plasma membrane and interacts with VviRbohs. Consistently, VviRbohs gene expression is significantly upregulated, promoting excessive accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS). Transient overexpression of VviRbohs significantly exacerbated stress damage, while transient overexpression of VviRbohD in the VpsCDPK9 overexpression background further amplified ROS accumulation, leading to aggravated leaf phenotypic damage. This study elucidates the molecular mechanism by which the VpsCDPK9-VviRbohs module negatively modulates the grapevine response to saline-alkaline stress through regulating the balance of the ROS family, providing a theoretical foundation for the discovery of stress-resistant genes and the breeding of saline-alkaline-tolerant grapevine varieties.
items.authors: Zhang Q, Tang R, Guo Y, Zhang Y, Han D, Wen Y, Li T.
items.journal: Plant science : an international journal of experimental plant biology

items.title: Silicon Nanoparticle Seed Priming Modulates Germination, Early Seedling Growth, and Biochemical Responses of Soybean Under PEG-Induced Drought Stress.
items.abstract: Drought stress during germination and early seedling growth can impair soybean performance, while silicon nanoparticle (SiNP) seed priming may modulate early stress responses. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of SiNP seed priming on the germination, early seedling growth, and biochemical responses of 11 soybean (Glycine max (L.) Merr.) genotypes under non-stressed conditions and two levels of PEG-induced drought stress (5% and 10% PEG 6000), and to assess how these responses varied with stress intensity and genotype. Seeds were untreated, hydroprimed, or primed with SiO2 nanoparticles at 500 or 1000 mg L-1. Across genotypes and stress levels, priming generally increased germination energy and total germination and reduced non-germinated seeds, with similar improvements observed following hydropriming and SiNP priming, whereas normal seedling development was not consistently improved. Increasing stress strongly inhibited shoot elongation and seedling fresh mass, whereas root growth was comparatively maintained. SiNP priming generally resulted in higher seedling fresh mass, with SiNPs 500 producing higher values than the untreated control in most genotypes under mild stress and all genotypes under severe stress. SiNP priming also increased proline accumulation and total amylolytic activity, with SiNPs 1000 showing the highest values under mild and severe stress. Overall, SiNP seed priming most consistently improved soybean germination under PEG-induced drought stress, whereas its effects on early seedling growth and biochemical responses varied with nanoparticle concentration, genotype, and stress intensity.
items.authors: Šimić N, Agić D, Grljušić S, Zdunić Z, Andrić L, Tomičić I, Lisjak M, Antunović M, Varga I.

items.title: Changes in Biomass and Root Architecture During Axillary Bud Development of Pinus yunnanensis
items.abstract: Abstract Pinus yunnanensis , a member of the genus Pinus , a dominant coniferous species on the Yunnan-Guizhou Plateau, shows great potential for asexual propagation owing to the difficulty of retaining desirable traits in afforestation. Eight month old P. yunnanensis seedlings were used to divide axillary bud development into four stages. Seedling growth traits, biomass allocation and root architecture were investigated from axillary bud dormancy to elongation. The main findings were that seedling height and basal diameter followed a logistic growth pattern throughout axillary bud development, with the rapid growth phase occurring during bud dormancy, and both height and basal diameter were highly correlated with axillary bud number. Seedling roots were dominated by 0–2 mm fine roots. Most root morphological indices peaked at the axillary‑bud elongation stage except average root diameter, which kept increasing. Mantel test revealed a significant correlation between axillary bud elongation and root architecture. With axillary bud development, plant organ biomass increased continuously, and the root-stem ratio first increased and then decreased, reaching the maximum value in the development stage. Biomass was mainly allocated to roots and needles with a low stem proportion. During axillary bud formation, resources are preferentially allocated to roots, while axillary bud elongation shifts growth priority to above ground needles. In summary, axillary bud development is closely linked to seedling growth, root‑architecture formation and biomass allocation strategies. These findings provide a theoretical basis for scion cultivation of elite P. yunnanensis clones.
items.authors: Gu X, Zhou C, Kang X, Cai N, Xu Y, Yang B.

items.title: The xyloglucan endotransglucosylase/hydrolase TaXTH16 enhances wheat drought tolerance and pre-harvest sprouting resistance via ABA-mediated pathways.
items.abstract: Drought and PHS are major constraints on wheat production worldwide. Cell wall remodeling plays a crucial role in plant adaptation to water deficit. Xyloglucan endotransglucosylase/hydrolases (XTHs) are key cell wall-modifying enzymes, yet how they integrate with ABA signaling, the central pathway controlling drought responses and seed dormancy, remains unknown in wheat. The primary objective of this study is to functionally characterize TaXTH16 in drought tolerance and PHS resistance, with a focus on its transcriptional regulation by ABA responsive transcription factors and its natural haplotype variation for breeding applications. We generated TaXTH16 overexpression and CRISPR/Cas9 knockout wheat lines for drought and PHS phenotyping. We performed biochemical assays for XET activity and subcellular localization, physiological measurements of water loss rate, stomatal aperture, ABA content, and ROS levels, transcriptomic analysis, and molecular assays including Y1H, EMSA, ChIP-qPCR, and dual-luciferase. Haplotype analyses were conducted across a wide range of wheat accessions. TaXTH16 encodes a functional XET enzyme localized to the plasma membrane and cell wall. Overexpression of TaXTH16 significantly enhanced drought tolerance, whereas knockout lines were more sensitive. TaXTH16 promoted xyloglucan and cellulose accumulation and enhanced ABA-mediated stomatal closure and ROS scavenging under drought. It also positively regulated PHS resistance, likely via ABA-mediated pathways. TaABF2 was identified as a direct transcriptional activator of TaXTH16. A natural variant, TaXTH16-2B-HapII, showed a higher promoter activity, significant association with greater drought resistance, and enrichment in modern cultivars. This study establishes TaXTH16 as a positive regulator of wheat drought tolerance and PHS resistance, linking ABA signaling and cell wall remodeling. TaXTH16 is directly activated by TaABF2, and TaXTH16-2B-HapII represents a promising allele for breeding. These findings provide mechanistic insights into ABA-cell wall crosstalk and a valuable resource for improving wheat stress resilience.
items.authors: Bi H, Wu P, Wang J, Chen P, Zhang Q, Liu Z, Pang Z, Yang X, Wang Y, Qiao W, Wang D, Zhang K.

items.title: Contrasting water use stability among dominant woody species across hillslope habitats in an alpine catchment of the upper Heihe River Basin.
items.abstract: Topographic position modulates soil moisture distribution and seasonal dynamics in alpine ecosystems, thereby shaping vegetation water-use patterns. However, whether dominant woody species occupying different hillslope habitats differ in the stability of their water-use strategies remains poorly understood at the hillslope scale. We investigated two dominant conifers, Picea crassifolia and Juniperus przewalskii, and a widespread alpine shrub, Dasiphora fruticosa across upslope, midslope, and footslope positions during the pre-rainy, rainy, and late-rainy seasons in an alpine catchment of the upper Heihe River Basin. By integrating δ2H and δ18O of soil and xylem water with a MixSIAR Bayesian mixing model, together with leaf δ13C, we quantified water sources for each species and evaluated water-use stability across hillslope positions and seasonal stages. Despite differences in dominant uptake depth, both conifers maintained relatively stable water-use strategies across slope positions and seasons. J. przewalskii persistently relied on deep soil water, which contributed 47% to 53% of total uptake, whereas P. crassifolia predominantly used shallow soil water, accounting for 44% to 65%. In contrast, D. fruticosa showed strong plasticity, with deep water uptake increasing from 16.2% to 41.0%, although this flexibility was constrained at upslope positions where available water was largely confined to shallow soil layers. Variability in leaf δ13C further indicated stronger physiological stability in the two conifer species within their respective hillslope habitats than in the shrub species, particularly at upper slope positions under greater evaporative demand. These findings suggest that water-use stability was associated with the sustained dominance of reliable soil water sources.
items.authors: Wang Y, Xiao X, Zhang J, Hong Y.

items.title: From loci to mechanisms: wheat autoimmunity as a window into plant immune activation.
items.abstract: Wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) is a major staple crop, and developing broad-spectrum resistance to multiple fungal pathogens is essential for sustainable production. Wheat autoimmunity (WAI) mutants represent genetic resources that spontaneously activate immune responses under non-stress conditions, exhibiting lesion-mimic or leaf-tip necrosis phenotypes and enhanced resistance to multiple foliar diseases, including powdery mildew and rusts. Increasing evidence indicates that WAI arises from dysregulation of immune homeostasis across multiple regulatory levels, involving receptor activation, cellular homeostasis, and membrane transport processes, ultimately converging on evolutionarily conserved defense outputs such as reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation, activation of defense-related genes, ion fluxes, and programmed cell death (PCD). Recent advances have identified key WAI-associated loci, including nucleotide-binding and leucine-rich-repeat receptors (NLRs), membrane proteins, regulatory components, and transporters, revealing mechanistically distinct pathways underlying constitutive immunity and its trade-off with growth. This review summarizes recent progress in the genetics and molecular mechanisms of WAI, critically assesses its roles in broad-spectrum, multi-disease resistance, and discusses strategies to minimize the growth and fitness costs. Furthermore, we propose that structure-guided allele optimization combined with spatiotemporal regulation of gene expression holds promise for the rational engineering of WAI alleles that confer durable disease resistance while minimizing associated fitness costs.
items.authors: Li W, He M, Xiong F, Wu Q, Jia H, Liu Z.
items.journal: Journal of genetics and genomics = Yi chuan xue bao

items.title: The SlLRR-RLK94-SlPti1a Module Enhances Salt Tolerance by Modulating Reactive Oxygen Species and Hormone Homoeostasis in Tomato.
items.abstract: Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) is a globally cultivated crop of high economic and nutritional importance, yet its growth and productivity are severely threatened by soil salinization. Although leucine-rich repeat receptor‑like kinases (LRR-RLKs) are key environmental sensors, the mechanisms governing tomato salt tolerance remain elusive. Here, we demonstrate that the SlLRR‑RLK94 and its downstream interacting protein, the receptor‑like cytoplasmic kinase SlPti1a, form a functional plasma membrane complex that positively regulates salt tolerance in tomato. CRISPR/Cas9‑mediated knockout of SlLRR‑RLK94 or VIGS‑mediated silencing of SlPti1a markedly reduced salt tolerance, resulting in severe leaf chlorosis and restricted root growth under salinity. Disruption of this module severely compromised physiological defence systems, leading to excessive reactive oxygen species accumulation, altered antioxidant enzyme activities, and an elevated Na+/K+ ratio caused by uncontrolled Na+ buildup. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that loss of SlLRR‑RLK94 extensively reprogrammed metabolic networks under salt stress, impairing photosystem homoeostasis and suppressing the diterpenoid biosynthesis pathway. This transcriptional reprogramming led to an endogenous hormonal imbalance characterised by gibberellin deficiency and abscisic acid accumulation. Collectively, our findings elucidate the molecular mechanisms by which the SlLRR‑RLK94‑SlPti1a module coordinates ionic, oxidative, and hormonal homoeostasis, providing promising genetic targets for breeding salt‑tolerant tomato cultivars.
items.authors: Zhu J, Yao Y, Li Y, Lv R, Yang R, Luan Y.

items.title: Real-time monitoring of root dielectric properties for assessing crop plant damage caused by foliar application of glyphosate.
items.abstract: There is a knowledge gap regarding how foliar injury and restricted water uptake can be detected by measuring root dielectric response. This pot study nondestructively evaluated the efficiency of real-time dielectric measurement to monitor the effects of glyphosate spraying. Root dielectric properties were recorded on a minute scale in control and glyphosate-treated maize, cucumber, and pea. Chlorophyll, stomatal conductance, and biomass measurements were taken to interpret the dielectric changes. Electrical capacitance and conductance varied diurnally due to the circadian regulation of water uptake and hydraulic conductance. Glyphosate application reduced capacitance, indicating the impeded root growth and activity caused by impaired amino acid synthesis, foliar damage, and restricted transpiration. The dissipation factor decreased in response to glyphosate due to impeded apoplastic water flow, suppressed root lignification, and hampered water absorption. The enhanced leaf and root hydraulic resistance caused by glyphosate was manifested in sharply reduced electrical conductance. Changes in the species' dielectric response were consistent with physiological symptoms and biomass loss. Real-time dielectric measurement proved suitable for the nondestructive monitoring of plant responses to foliar stress through altered root traits. This method could be employed to evaluate herbicide tolerance in crops and to develop and determine dosage of herbicide ingredients.
items.authors: Cseresnyés I, Füzy A, Takács T.

items.title: SlNF-YC9 coordinates NF-Y trimer assembly and SlWRKY16-mediated antagonism to regulate drought tolerance in tomato.
items.abstract: Drought stress severely constrains tomato productivity, yet the transcriptional circuitry governing drought adaptation remains incompletely understood. Here, we demonstrate that SlNF-YC9 assembles with SlNF-YB3b and SlNF-YA3a into a functional NF-Y heterotrimer that enhances drought tolerance. This complex promotes stomatal closure, limits reactive oxygen species accumulation, and elevates abscisic acid levels. Mechanistically, the NF-Y trimer directly activates the drought-responsive genes SlAREB1 and SlDREB2 by binding the CCAAT motif, with SlNF-YA3a mediating DNA contact and the intact complex conferring maximal transcriptional activation. Notably, this activity is antagonized by SlWRKY16, which physically interacts with SlNF-YC9 and suppresses NF-Y-dependent transcription. Genetic analyses further support the cooperative function of SlNF-YC9 and SlNF-YB3b, as well as the antagonistic role of SlWRKY16, in regulating drought tolerance. Together, our findings define the NF-Y complex as a key regulatory component that coordinates positive and negative transcriptional inputs during the tomato drought response, providing a molecular framework for targeted crop improvement.
items.authors: Liang Y, Ma F, Shi H, Sun H, Chen R, Zhan X.

items.title: Single-cell transcriptome atlas reveals a WRKY33-HSP81 regulatory module that orchestrates phenylpropanoid-mediated defense against Sclerotium rolfsii in Dendrobium officinale.
items.abstract: Plants employ cell-type-specific transcriptional programs to defend against pathogens, yet the cellular heterogeneity of immune responses in the medicinal orchid Dendrobium officinale Kimura et Migo remains largely unexplored. A single-cell transcriptomic atlas of the D. officinale stem base upon Sclerotium rolfsii infection was constructed, profiling over 20 000 cells across 12 and 24 h post-infection. A total of 21 cell clusters were resolved into 6 major cell types-epidermal, ground tissue parenchyma, proliferating, xylem, phloem, and vascular bundle parenchyma cells-with identities validated by fluorescence in situ hybridization. Cell-type-specific analyses revealed that epidermal and phloem cells mounted early defense responses, while xylem cells exhibited the most extensive transcriptional reprogramming at 24 hpi, coinciding with the activation of lignin biosynthesis pathways. WRKY33 was identified as a central transcriptional activator that directly binds W-box motifs in the promoters of lignin biosynthetic genes C4H and HCT, promoting lignin deposition and enhancing disease resistance. Conversely, the nuclear-localized chaperone HSP81 physically interacts with WRKY33 and functions as a broad regulator of multiple transcription factors via co-factor sequestration, thereby compromising defense when overexpressed. These findings uncover a WRKY33-HSP81 regulatory module that orchestrates phenylpropanoid-mediated defense in D. officinale, providing a high-resolution cellular framework for understanding plant immunity and offering potential targets for improving disease resistance in this economically valuable species.
items.authors: Li L, Xu Y, Liu W, Niu Z, Xue Q, Ding X.
items.journal: The Plant journal : for cell and molecular biology

items.title: Genome-Wide Identification and Analysis of Brassica napus Nonexpressor of Pathogenesis-Related Genes Family and Functional Analysis of BnaNPR3.A02 in Clubroot Resistance.
items.abstract: Nonexpressor of pathogenesis-related (NPR) proteins are key regulators of salicylic acid (SA)-mediated plant immunity, functioning as transcriptional co-regulators. In this study, we aimed to comprehensively identify NPR family members in Brassica napus and its diploid progenitors, investigate their evolutionary dynamics and expression profiles, and functionally characterize the role of BnaNPR3.A02 in clubroot resistance. We identified 23, 12, and 12 NPR genes in B. napus, B. rapa, and B. oleracea, respectively, which were phylogenetically divided into six conserved subfamilies (I-VI). Structural characterization showed that these genes possess conserved ankyrin repeats, BTB-POZ domains or the DUF3420 domains, and exhibit diversified exon-intron structures. Spatiotemporal expression profiling uncovered tissue-specific expression patterns of NPRs under normal conditions. Promoter cis-element analysis and transcriptomic profiling in response to phytohormones and abiotic stresses suggested broad involvement of BnaNPRs in environmental adaptation. GO annotation revealed that NPR1-4 members are enriched in jasmonic acid/salicylic acid-mediated defense pathways, whereas NPR5/6 members are associated with floral development. qRT-PCR analysis of 11 expressed BnaNPR1-4 genes was performed in resistant (R) and susceptible (S) rapeseed plants upon P. brassicae infection. BnaNPR3.A02 showed the greatest expression divergence, with significant induction in R plants but consistent suppression in S plants. Because NPR3 is a negative feedback regulator of SA signaling, the induction of BnaNPR3.A02 in R plants likely reflects feedback attenuation after immune activation, whereas its suppression in S plants may indicate a defective SA signaling node. Heterologous overexpression of BnaNPR3.A02 in Arabidopsis significantly increased disease severity and pathogen biomass, whereas Arabidopsis npr3 knockout mutants showed enhanced resistance, supporting a conserved negative regulatory role of NPR3 in this heterologous system. Protein-protein interaction and co-expression analyses further revealed that BnaNPR3.A02 is embedded in a stress- and defense-related network. These findings provide a foundation for understanding the evolutionary and functional divergence of the NPR family and identify BnaNPR3.A02 as a candidate target for future functional validation and breeding of clubroot-resistant B. napus varieties.
items.authors: Zheng L, Zhao F, Li Y, Xu K, Guo Z, Nie J, Ma Y, Chen Z, Sha H, Li R, Li K, Sun W, Huang Z.

items.title: Integrated multi-omics analysis reveals coordinated root and rhizosphere responses underlying AMF-mediated drought tolerance in kiwifruit.
items.abstract: Drought stress substantially restricts kiwifruit (Actinidia spp.) growth and productivity, yet the mechanisms through which arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) promote drought tolerance remain insufficiently understood. To address this gap, root physiological and molecular analyses were integrated with multi-omics profiling of the rhizosphere microbiome to investigate AMF-mediated drought responses under well-watered and drought-stress conditions. Under drought stress, AMF inoculation improved plant growth, root development, cellular ultrastructure, and physiological performance. More importantly, root omics analysis revealed coordinated regulation of drought-responsive pathways involving glutathione metabolism, amino acid biosynthesis, phytohormone regulation, and energy metabolism. Beyond these plant responses, AMF inoculation altered bacterial and fungal community composition, enriched potentially beneficial taxa, and increased rhizosphere network connectivity under drought stress. Within the restructured microbiome, we identified an AMF-specific drought-responsive amplicon sequence variant (ASV) module composed primarily of bacterial taxa and associated with cross-kingdom microbial interactions. Integrated microbial-metabolite network analysis further identified a metabolite feature annotated as 1-piperideine as a candidate associated with selective microbial recruitment in AMF-colonized rhizospheres. Together, these findings suggest that AMF-associated drought tolerance in kiwifruit involves complementary changes in plant physiology, root molecular responses, and rhizosphere microbiome assembly. A mechanistic basis is thereby provided for developing AMF-based strategies to improve kiwifruit production under increasing water limitation.
items.authors: Shah OU, Shuchen F, Jia W, Hongfei S, Luyao C, Wenjie Z, Wenping X.

items.title: Metabolic and transcriptional responses reveal co-option of symbiotic processes during early soybean-soybean cyst nematode interaction
items.abstract: The biochemical mechanisms by which virulent populations of soybean cyst nematode ( Heterodera glycines , SCN) overcome host resistance are critical to understanding this economically important pathogen. Here, we deployed metabolic and transcriptome profiling of soybean roots during the SCN infection and establishment process to investigate the molecular and biochemical mechanisms of pathogen establishment. Across samples from a time series spanning nematode invasion to syncytium maturation, we demonstrate that compatible SCN infection does not bypass host immunity but systematically remodels it. In a compatible interaction between soybean carrying the high-copy Rhg1 resistance locus challenged with HG Type 2.5.7 SCN virulent on this host, we identify a 72-metabolite defense signature spanning isoflavonoids, triterpenoid saponins, and phenylpropanoids that persist across all infection stages. Despite activation of this metabolic defense signature by the pathogen on infection, defense transcription is near silence by 3 days post-infection, while defense metabolites persist, revealing a critical decoupling of transcriptional and metabolic defense programs at the precise window of syncytium initiation. Suppression of phenylpropanoid accumulation occurs downstream of PAL transcription, indicating a block at the metabolic level invisible to transcriptomics alone. By 5 days post-infection, cytokinin accumulation coincides with nodulin gene induction and phospholipid remodeling consistent with activation of the legume symbiosis program during syncytium maturation. Together, these findings establish that compatibility arises not from failed recognition but from progressive immune dismantling, including suppression of defense chemistry and co-option of the legume-rhizobium symbiosis machinery.
items.authors: Rai, M., Miraeiz, E., Dutta, M., Desai, V., Rai, A., Hudson, M.

items.title: Spatial transcriptomic profiling reveals candidate genes associated with male gametophyte development in CMS-D8 cotton F1 hybrids.
items.abstract: Gossypium trilobum cytoplasmic male sterility (CMS-D8) is characterized as being of the gametophytic type. Meiosis in F1 hybrids leads to the production of both fertile and sterile male gametophytes, making them a suitable material for studying the development of male gametophytes. Paraffin section analysis indicated that stage 8 represents a critical developmental period associated with male gametophyte abortion. Spatial transcriptomic analysis of 4.5-5 mm F1 buds revealed distinct spatial expression patterns, including enrichment of genes related to energy production and conversion in a putative meiotic-cell-associated spatial cluster. Cell-level analysis further resolved two transcriptionally distinct male gametophyte populations, between which genes associated with mitochondrial structure and cellular metabolic processes were differentially expressed. GhAAT showed differential expression between these two male gametophyte populations. Furthermore, phenotypic analysis of the Arabidopsis aat mutant revealed reduced pollen viability and a lower proportion of fully developed seeds, providing cross-species evidence consistent with a possible involvement of AAT in male reproductive development. In summary, this study provides a spatial transcriptomic profile of D8F1 buds and identifies GhAAT as a candidate gene associated with CMS-D8 pollen formation. These findings provide candidate genes and spatial information for further investigation of male gametophyte development in CMS-D8 cotton.
items.authors: Feng J, Han J, Zhang H, Zhang X, Zhang M, Tang H, Qi T, Guo L, Xing C, Wu J.
items.journal: Plant science : an international journal of experimental plant biology

items.title: Comparative accumulation and root-to-leaf partitioning of arsenic, lead, cadmium and mercury in indigenous and exotic tree species on a rehabilitated gold-mine landscape at Ayanfuri, Ghana
items.abstract: Abstract Trees are widely planted on rehabilitated gold-mine waste to stabilise degraded land, but species are usually chosen for growth performance, with little attention to how they take up and distribute potentially toxic elements (PTEs). We screened arsenic (As), lead (Pb), cadmium (Cd) and mercury (Hg) in the roots and leaves of 19 trees of 17 species, five indigenous to West Africa and twelve introduced, growing on three reclaimed waste dumps and in two reference forests at the Edikan concession, Ayanfuri, Ghana. On a whole-plant basis, indigenous trees had higher median concentrations than exotic trees of As (0.82 versus 0.22 mg kg − 1 ), Pb (0.61 versus 0.25 mg kg − 1 ) and Cd (0.52 versus 0.27 mg kg − 1 ) (Mann–Whitney U test; p = 0.022, 0.018 and 0.009; q = 0.029 for each after false discovery rate adjustment). Hg did not differ between the groups (p = 0.106). Median leaf-to-root translocation factors were 0.95–0.99 for all four elements, so leaf concentrations were close to, and in most trees slightly below, root concentrations. Ceiba pentandra had the highest As and Pb, Terminalia superba and Triplochiton scleroxylon the highest Cd, and the exotic Tectona grandis the highest Hg, with about twice as much in its leaves as in its roots. Indigenous species thus accumulated more As, Pb and Cd without concentrating them in foliage, making them candidates for phytostabilisation trials. The study is exploratory: no soil was analysed, so soil-to-plant transfer factors could not be calculated, and most species are represented by one tree.
items.authors: Antobre OO, Adu-Gyamfi AB, Gyampoh BA, Dakpo N, Kusi-Kyei V, Acquah E, Boadi S, Asante WA.

items.title: Integrated Molecular and Physiological Mechanisms Underlying Rice Adaptation to Heat, Salinity, and Drought Stress.
items.abstract: Rice faces increasing threats from climate change, driven by heat, salinity, and drought stresses. Although researchers have extensively studied individual stresses, growing evidence indicates that combined stresses elicit unique physiological, biochemical, and molecular responses that single-stress studies cannot predict. This review comprehensively synthesizes current knowledge of the integrated signaling networks and adaptive mechanisms underlying rice responses to heat, salinity, and drought stress, with particular emphasis on stress crosstalk and multi-stress responses. We examine the roles of mechanosensitive ion channels, calcium signaling, salt overly sensitive (SOS) pathway, heat shock response regulators, mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) cascades, and ABA-dependent and -independent signaling networks in stress tolerance systems. Furthermore, we discuss major adaptive responses involving reactive oxygen species (ROS) homeostasis, osmoprotectant accumulation, antioxidant defense systems, and phytohormone crosstalk involving abscisic acid, auxin, salicylic acid, cytokinin, brassinosteroids, ethylene, and gibberellins. Particular attention is given to the detrimental effects of combined stresses on growth, development, and yield. In addition, recent advances in enhancing stress tolerance through CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome editing, marker-assisted breeding, and molecular marker technologies are also highlighted. Despite significant progress, critical knowledge gaps remain regarding primary stress-sensing mechanisms, epigenetic stress memory, organelle-specific signaling, and the translation of laboratory findings to field conditions. By integrating current knowledge across molecular, physiological, and breeding perspectives, we provide a comprehensive integrated signaling network model and crosstalk among signaling pathways for understanding rice adaptation to combined stresses and highlight potential strategies for enhancing crop resilience and global food security.
items.authors: Khan A, Mas-Ud MA, Ahmad S, Ullah S, Matin MN.

items.title: Transcriptomic Analysis Revealed the Response Mechanism of Green Revolution Gene Rht-D1b in Wheat to Salt Stress.
items.abstract: The semi-dwarfing gene Rht-D1b (formerly known as Rht2) was introduced into modern wheat breeding during the Green Revolution to reduce plant height, improve lodging resistance, and increase harvest index. In this study, two wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) lines carrying Rht-D1b (dwarf) and Rht-D1a (tall), respectively, were used to assess the role of Rht-D1b in salt tolerance through physiological and transcriptomic analyses under salt stress. Compared with Rht-D1a, Rht-D1b showed less growth inhibition, with smaller decreases in plant height, root length, and shoot biomass, as well as higher SPAD values. Rht-D1b also accumulated less Na+, had lower ROS and MDA levels, and maintained stronger POD and CAT antioxidant enzyme activities. Transcriptome analysis showed that 20 POD genes were consistently upregulated in Rht-D1b to Rht-D1a at 0, 6, and 24 h, while ion-transport- and ROS-related genes showed time-specific activation patterns linked to Na+ homeostasis, calcium signaling, and antioxidant defense. Together, these findings suggest that Rht-D1b may contribute to wheat seedling salt tolerance by improving ion homeostasis and redox balance. The salt-responsive genes identified in this study may also serve as candidates for future functional studies and wheat breeding.
items.authors: Ni J, Yang F, Wang W, Chen Z, Guo X, Hao Y, Xu D, Ma W, Qu M.

items.title: A beneficial root endophyte buffers natural variation in pathogen susceptibility across Arabidopsis accessions.
items.abstract: Host genetic diversity shapes pathogen susceptibility within plant populations, raising the question of whether beneficial root microbes can buffer these differences. The fungal root endophyte Serendipita indica (Si) promotes plant growth and can mitigate disease caused by the pathogen Bipolaris sorokiniana (Bs). Here, we assessed how natural host genetic variation influences Si-mediated protection against Bs in Arabidopsis thaliana. We screened 47 A. thaliana accessions for susceptibility to Bs with and without Si colonization and performed phenotypic, transcriptomic, and comparative genomic analyses of two genetically and geographically proximate Swedish accessions, T510 and T530, that differed strongly in Bs colonization. Si conferred consistent protection against Bs across all accessions, despite variation in baseline susceptibility and immune-gene content. T510 and T530 differed in Bs colonization, disease symptoms, transcriptional responses, and immune-gene repertoires, including presence-absence variation of the TIR-NLR gene ISI. T530 lacks ISI, and mutation of ISI in Col-0 increased Bs susceptibility, demonstrating that ISI contributes to root immunity. However, Si-mediated protection was retained in the absence of ISI, demonstrating that ISI is not required for this protective effect. Beneficial fungal endophytes can thus buffer phenotypic consequences of natural variation in pathogen susceptibility, stabilizing disease outcomes across genetically diverse plant populations.
items.authors: Peltz N, Armbruster L, Stephens C, Joisten-Rosenthal V, Thomsen T, Yan AW, Dunken N, Granado R, Kopriva S, de Meaux J, Langen G, Koprivova A, Usadel B, Zuccaro A.

items.title: Genome-wide identification and characterization of the bZIP gene family in Siberian apricot (Prunus sibirica) and their role under cold stress.
items.abstract: The basic leucine zipper (bZIP) transcription factor functions not only as a key regulator of plant ontogeny but also as a critical mediator of cold stress responses. Currently, bZIPs have been subjected to genome-wide identification and functional annotation in multiple species; however, systematic characterization and mechanistic studies of this family remain lacking in the ecologically and economically important forest tree species Prunus sibirica. This study identified 41 PsbZIPs across the entire genome of P. sibirica, divided into 12 subfamilies. Exon-intron architecture and motif composition were largely conserved among PsbZIPs clustered within the same subfamily. No tandem duplication events were detected among the PsbZIPs. Instead, eight segmental duplication-derived gene pairs were identified. Protein-protein interaction analysis indicated potential interactions among most PsbZIPs. Further quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) analysis indicated that most PsbZIPs were highly expressed in petals, leaves, and stems. Under cold stress, unique expression profiles arose among PsbZIPs, with PsbZIP28 showing significant upregulation during the late stage of cold stress. Transient overexpression of PsbZIP28 in Populus ussuriensis markedly enhanced cold tolerance in the recipient plants. Subcellular localization analysis revealed that PsbZIP28 is localized in the nucleus, and yeast self-activation assays demonstrated that the C-terminus of PsbZIP28 possesses transcriptional activation activity. These results provide a conceptual basis for further elucidating the molecular basis underlying cold tolerance in woody plants and establish a valuable genetic resource for future stress-tolerance breeding and the development of novel cold-tolerant germplasm based on the bZIP gene family.
items.authors: Zhai K, Zhao X, Zhang H, Liu Y, Qu S, Long J, Dong S, Liu Q.

items.title: Post-Translational Regulation and Ubiquitination of Brassinosteroid Signaling Components in Plants.
items.abstract: Brassinosteroids (BRs), a group of steroidal phytohormones, play vital roles in plant growth and stress responses. The molecular pathways underlying BR signaling have been well characterized. A growing body of data demonstrates that BR signaling components also engage in crosstalk with components from other signaling pathways to modulate plant growth, development, immune defense, and stress adaptation, and such modulation displays BR-dependent or -independent characteristics. Hence, the core components of BR signaling are of paramount importance in the regulation of multiple physiological processes during the entire plant life cycle. As an important post-translational modification, protein ubiquitination is known to precisely modulate the activity and stability of BR signaling components, as well as to govern signal output. This review centers on recent advances and provides a systematic analysis of regulatory factors influencing the stability of core BR signaling components. Particular emphasis is placed on the pivotal role of E3 ubiquitin ligases in governing the degradation, accumulation, and functional activity of these components via ubiquitination, while also contrasting the functional conservation and divergence of relevant E3s between Arabidopsis and other crops. Further dissection of the molecular regulation of BR signaling core components will facilitate a better understanding of the underlying signaling network and enable the development of strategies for crop growth regulation, yield promotion, and stress adaptation.
items.authors: Jia Q, Du X, Wang T, Gao Z, Dong H, An R, Ji Y, Wei S, Zhang Y, Huang S.

items.title: Two conserved early effectors from Puccinia triticina are required for pathogenicity by suppressing callose deposition and hydrogen peroxide accumulation in wheat.
items.abstract: BackgroundWheat leaf rust, caused by the causal agent Puccinia triticina (Pt), poses a serious threat to wheat production worldwide. Pt secretes plenty of effectors into the host plant to manipulate host immune responses and facilitate successful colonization. However, effectors during the early stages of Pt infection remain largely unknown.ResultsHere, we employed deep RNA-sequencing on samples extracted from wheat leaves of a susceptible wheat cultivar, Thatcher, inoculated with Pt at 8 and 24 h post-inoculation, which enabled the identification of candidate effectors implicated in suppressing early plant immune responses. Through integrated transcriptomic analysis and an optimized effector identification workflow, early candidate effector-encoding genes that are highly expressed during Pt infection were identified and characterized. Functional assays revealed that two effector candidates, Pt01364 and Pt09156, exhibited the ability to suppress Bax-induced cell death in Nicotiana benthamiana. Quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) analysis demonstrated that both genes peaked at 8 h post-inoculation, and the yeast secretion trap assay showed that these two cell death-suppressing effector candidates possess functional signal peptides for secretion into host cells. Silencing of Pt01364 and Pt09156 significantly compromised Pt pathogenicity on a susceptible wheat cultivar. In addition, both effectors can inhibit callose deposition triggered by non-host bacteria and reduce hydrogen peroxide accumulation in wheat in response to avirulent Pt infection.ConclusionThis study provides a basis for identifying key effectors involved in the early stages of wheat-Pt interaction, highlighting Pt01364 and Pt09156 as promising candidate targets for developing innovative strategies to control wheat leaf rust. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry.
items.authors: Sun X, Wang Q, Wang M, Wang J, Gu J, Wang Y, Ma L, Wang D.

items.title: Life on the chalk: mechanisms of plant sensing and adaptation to high-pH soils.
items.abstract: Soil pH is a fundamental determinant of plant health, governing nutrient availability and physiological processes in the rhizosphere. High pH, especially in calcareous soils, reduces the solubility of iron, phosphorus, zinc, and manganese, causing nutrient deficiency, chlorosis, and yield loss. In this review, we summarize recent advances in plant responses to high-pH stress. Plants sense high external pH through changes in membrane potential and the rapid alkalinization factor-FERONIA and plant peptide containing sulfated tyrosine 1-PSY1R systems that regulate plasma membrane H+-ATPase activity. Hormonal signaling, particularly via auxin, integrates pH sensing with root growth regulation and ion homeostasis. Key regulators such as PHOSPHATE STARVATION RESPONSE 1, IRON MAN peptides, and basic leucine zipper 19/23 coordinate nutrient homeostasis under high-pH stress. We further discuss calcicole adaptations, microbial partnerships, and soil management practices that mitigate high-pH stress.
items.authors: Shekhawat K, Parween S, Fatima A, Singh N, Hirt H.

items.title: Tomato SlERF26 enhances drought tolerance by regulating SlPIP2;4-mediated ROS homeostasis.
items.abstract: Adverse environmental conditions severely limit plant growth and productivity, especially under an increasingly frequent and severe drought. Cultivated tomato is highly sensitive to drought, while wild tomato species exhibit remarkable drought tolerance. In this study, we identified SlERF26 as a drought-responsive gene that was differentially expressed between drought-tolerant Solanum pennellii introgression lines and the cultivated tomato background through combined introgression-line and transcriptomic analyses. SlERF26 encodes an AP2/ERF (APETALA2/Ethylene Response Factor) transcription factor. Under drought stress, overexpression of SlERF26 reduced the accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), including H₂O₂ and O₂-, which is consistent with its positive role in regulating drought tolerance. Transcriptome profiling further indicated that SlERF26 regulated a series of drought-responsive genes involved in membrane transport and ROS scavenging, such as aquaporin and peroxidases. Specifically, SlERF26 directly bound to the promoter of SlPIP2;4, an aquaporin gene, and activated its transcription. The slpip2;4 mutant accumulated higher ROS levels and exhibited significantly reduced drought tolerance. Moreover, analysis of SlERF26 OE × slpip2;4 hybrid plants confirms that SlERF26 acts upstream of SlPIP2;4 in drought tolerance. Consistent with this genetic relationship, biochemical quantification and histochemical staining demonstrated that SlERF26 and SlPIP2;4 act together to maintain ROS homeostasis during drought stress. Collectively, our findings define a SlERF26-SlPIP2;4 regulatory module that enhances drought tolerance in tomato by modulating aquaporin expression and ROS homeostasis.
items.authors: Wang Y, Hu X, Yang J, Mo Y, Hou H, Ding Y, Gong W, Zeng P, Shang C, Zhang X, Pan Y, Wu L, Song H, Hu N, Dai D, Hasan MM, Li J.

items.title: Functional characterization of the strawberry calcium-dependent protein kinase FvCPK28
items.abstract: Calcium-dependent protein kinases (CDPKs) translate cellular calcium signals into phosphorylation events that regulate plant development and immunity. In Arabidopsis thaliana , CPK28 restrains pattern-triggered immunity by limiting the accumulation of the receptor-like cytoplasmic kinase BOTRYTIS-INDUCED KINASE 1 (BIK1), and contributes to roles in development such as stem elongation. CPK28 orthologs have been described in several crops, but not in Rosaceae, a family that includes economically important fruits such as strawberry, apple, peach, and raspberry. Phylogenetic analysis of CDPKs and CDPK-related kinases (CRKs) in four Rosaceae species and Arabidopsis identified CPK28 orthologs forming a clade with Arabidopsis CPK28. Using the woodland strawberry ( Fragaria vesca ) ortholog, FvCPK28, as a case study, we show that FvCPK28 is a calcium-dependent kinase that phosphorylates both Arabidopsis AtBIK1 and a strawberry FvBIK1 homolog in vitro and associates with both proteins in planta . When expressed in the Arabidopsis cpk28-1 mutant, FvCPK28 restored stem elongation and immune responses to wild-type levels. These results show that the strawberry ortholog retains the biochemical and biological properties of CPK28. This work extends the functional study of CPK28 to the Rosaceae and identifies FvCPK28 as a candidate for modulating the balance between growth and defense in strawberry. Main Conclusion Strawberry FvCPK28 retains the biochemical and genetic properties of Arabidopsis CPK28, functioning as a Ca 2+ -dependent kinase that associates with and phosphorylates AtBIK1 and complements the cpk28-1 mutant.
items.authors: Goncalves-Dias, M., Monaghan, J.

items.title: Revisiting ethylene metabolism: Identification of an ethylene glycol-glucose conjugate reveals active ethylene metabolism in Populus.
items.abstract: In many plant species, the role of ethylene as a phytohormone signal has been well-studied, yet its direct metabolism in planta has received less attention. Consequently, this gap constrains our understanding of the full impact ethylene has on plant systems. During multiple evaluations of resilience in Populus spp., we detected an unidentified metabolite with plausible links to ethylene. In this study, we structurally characterize and identify this molecule as an ethylene glycol glucose conjugate (EGGC). Ethylene-perturbation experiments revealed EGGC abundance is positively correlated with endogenous ethylene production, supporting EGGC as an ethylene-derived metabolite. Stable-isotope labeled EGGC supplied to the media was detected in stem/leaf tissue, indicating long-distance translocation of the compound. These studies also revealed enzymatic conversion in stem/leaf tissue of EGGC to ethylene glycol (EG), with EG levels maintained and accompanied by shifts in downstream metabolites (i.e., glycolic acid and oxalic acid). These results suggest that EGGC participates in active metabolism rather than serves as a waste product. Collectively, the findings reported in this study demonstrate that EGGC is a biomarker of whole-plant ethylene production and position it as a tool for monitoring ethylene-associated stress responses.
items.authors: Brown LP, Baccile JA, Engle NL, Yao T, Ortega-Corretjer A, Jawdy SS, Kemmer S, Tschaplinski TJ.

items.title: Specialisation of photosynthetic biochemistry in C 4 chloroplasts potentiates distinct cell-specific functionality of different chloroplast-to-nucleus retrograde signalling pathways.
items.abstract: Chloroplasts are key environmental sensors for plant cells. Upon exposure to abiotic stresses such as excess sunlight and heat, reactive oxygen species (ROS) in chloroplasts are sensed to trigger chloroplast-to-nucleus signalling pathways for acclimatory nuclear gene expression. There is extensive biochemical- and cell type-specialisation of chloroplasts, such as those in heat-resilient plants performing C 4 photosynthesis, but how these specialisations intersect with chloroplast-to-nucleus signalling remains unclear. Here we show that specific chloroplast-to-nucleus signalling networks are functional in specialised leaf cell types of the C 4 model species, Setaria viridis . RNA-sequencing, electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy and metabolomics on cell type-enriched fractions, complemented with mutant analyses provided evidence for cell-specific enrichment of chloroplast-to-nucleus retrograde signalling pathways correlating with the photosynthetic specialisation in these cell types. Singlet oxygen ( 1 O 2 )-responsive beta-cyclocitral (β-CC) /dihydroactinidiolide (DHA) signalling and hydrogen peroxide (H 2 O 2 )-responsive 3'-phosphoadenosine 5'-phosphate (PAP) signalling pathways were specific to mesophyll cells, in line with enrichment of photosystem II and linear electron flow to photosystem I, respectively in this cell type. In contrast, bundle sheath cells were enriched for the rapid, ROS-independent retrograde signalling pathway mediated by the Calvin cycle product, dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP), consistent with the exclusive localisation of the Calvin cycle to C 4 bundle sheath cells. Taken together, our results provide insights into how chloroplast- and cell type-specialisation intersect with stress signalling in plant cells and identify photosynthetic biochemistry as a key driver of cell-specific cellular signalling.
items.authors: Yee, S., Furbank, R., Bhatia, G., Phua, S. Y., Micic, N., Naing, M. T., Bjarnholt, N., Cox, N., Pogson, B. J., Furbank, R. T., Chan, K. X.

items.title: A House Divided: Unifying the Classification of Plant Pathogen Effectors.
items.abstract: Plant pathogens deploy diverse effectors to interfere with host defense systems and create favorable conditions for infection. As effector biology has advanced, the terminology used to describe these effectors has become increasingly complex, reflecting differences in secretion pathways, molecular features, and subcellular localization across pathogens. This inconsistency complicates comparative studies and limits effective communication across research groups. Here, we propose a streamlined and broadly applicable classification framework based on the functional destination of effectors within host plants, dividing them into two categories: extracellular and intracellular effectors. Extracellular effectors operate beyond the host plasma membrane, acting in apoplast, cell wall, and xylem, whereas intracellular effectors act within host cells, targeting the cytoplasm, nucleus, and other organelles. This approach provides a common terminology applicable to effectors from fungi, Oomycetes, bacteria, nematodes, and viruses, while broadly reflecting the spatial organization of plant immune surveillance. Moreover, it establishes a practical foundation for the systematic organization and management of effector databases. Together, this classification facilitates standardized effector annotation, comparative analyses, and interdisciplinary understanding of molecular plant-pathogen interactions.
items.authors: Lim YJ, Lee YH.

items.title: Seed Priming with Plant Growth Regulators Improves Physiological and Biochemical Attributes of Pea and Plantago Seedlings Grown Under Artificial Magnetism
items.abstract: Seed-priming is an essential phenomenon of today’s agricultural practices which is widely being utilized for better seed stand development of plants. Priming of seeds with essential plant growth regulators (PGRs) such as; hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), salicylic acid (SA), ascorbic acid (AsA), gibberellic acid (GA3), potassium nitrate (KNO3) including H2O priming treatment for 12 hours is highly beneficial to promote plant effectiveness under different environmental circumstances including artificial magnetism (north, south and north/south). The present study was carried out during September 2022 in Department of Botany, University of Balochistan, Quetta to investigate the physiological and biochemical attributes of two important plant species; Plantago ovata Forrsk. (Plantago) and Pisum sativum (pea) under artificial magnetism. Design of experiment was completely randomized design (CRD) comprising three replications. Results of different parameters portrayed that priming of seeds with essential PGRs is a novel technique to enhance plant growth and development. The overall accumulation of secondary metabolites such as; anthocyanin, soluble sugars and phenolics, tannins contents in pea plants showed significant (p 0.05) results under artificial magnetic treatments in combination with supplementation of SA, KNO3, AsA and GA3 primed seeds as compared to plantago seedlings. Moreover, the status of nutrients, i.e., potassium in both shoots showed non-significant results by accumulating higher contents as compared to root, while in both plants seedlings, manganese content showed significant differences in root and shoot under priming. Astonishingly, the oxidative damage parameters (hydrogen peroxide and malondialdehyde) decreased by illustrating non-significant interactions among root and shoot. In overall study, pea seedlings performed very well under artificial magnetism by the pre-soaking of seeds with PGRs as compared to plantago seedlings. Therefore, the present study highly encourages the phenomenon of PGRs seed-priming along with artificial magnetic treatment for the better growth and development of plants seedlings and more importantly, pea and plantago.
items.authors: Nisa K, Shaukat K, Nizar M, Samad A, Ismail T.

items.title: Analysis of Microbial Communities Associated with Drought-Resistant Plants Using 16S rRNA Sequencing.
items.abstract: Microbial communities associated with plants influence their growth, physiological functions, and resistance to pathogens and environmental stresses. Nevertheless, the identification of beneficial bacterial taxa that support plant resilience to environmental stresses and can be incorporated into synthetic microbial communities is still far from complete. To address this problem, we analyzed the microbial communities associated with three drought-resistant plant species, Chenopodium album L. (from wetland and arid locations), Agropyron desertorum (Fisch. ex Link) Schult., and Alhagi pseudalhagi (Bieb.) Fisch., focusing on microbial signatures in the rhizosphere, roots, and stems. We showed that even under normal conditions, the microbiomes of drought-resistant plants are enriched with bacterial taxa associated with drought resistance, such as Bacillus (Bacillota), Burkholderiales and Pseudomonas (Pseudomonadota), as well as several representatives of Actinomycetota. The greatest diversity within the endospheric microbiome was found in stem samples of C. album from arid location. The specific bacterial genera identified in this study, such as Bacillus, Pseudomonas, Paenibacillus, and Streptomyces, could serve as sources for the creation of inoculants for other plants to help them overcome drought.
items.authors: Lyapina I, Fesenko I, Chizhevskaya E, Khudyaeva M, Lapenko N, Tikhonovich I, Chebotar VK.

items.title: Verticillium dahliae CFEM Effector VdCR Stabilises the Susceptibility Factor GhAGP31 to Suppress Host Vascular Immunity and Promote Cotton Verticillium Wilt.
items.abstract: Plant pathogenic fungi secrete a wide array of effector proteins to manipulate host immunity, including those containing CFEM (Common in Fungal Extracellular Membranes) domains. Here, we identified a CFEM domain-containing effector VdCR from Verticillium dahliae, the causal agent of cotton Verticillium wilt. The expression of VdCR was drastically upregulated during cotton infection. Targeted deletion of VdCR compromised fungal oxidative stress resistance and pathogenicity on cotton, establishing it as a key virulence factor. VdCR physically targets cotton non-classical arabinogalactan protein GhAGP31 via its CFEM domain. Virus-induced gene silencing (VIGS) of GhAGP31 significantly enhanced reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation, callose and lignin deposition, and plant resistance to V. dahliae, confirming that GhAGP31 acts as a negative regulator of vascular immunity. In addition, we identified GhAGP31 as a negative regulator of cotton vascular development, revealing its dual roles in coordinating plant immunity and development. We further verified that VdCR stabilises GhAGP31 to promote its accumulation both in vitro and in planta. Collectively, this study demonstrates that GhAGP31 functions as a novel cotton susceptibility factor that suppresses both vascular immunity and development and can be stabilised by the V. dahliae CFEM effector VdCR to facilitate fungal infection.
items.authors: Pu B, Yu H, Pan Z, Duan L, Liu T, Li H, Liu J, Zhang R, Hu X, Qin J.

items.title: Single-nucleus and spatial transcriptomics reveal dynamic cell differentiation and storage product accumulation in rice endosperm.
items.abstract: Rice (Oryza sativa) endosperm, a major food source worldwide, accumulates starch, proteins, and lipids. Understanding the cellular and molecular mechanisms that govern endosperm development and storage product accumulation is crucial for improving grain yield and quality. Through single-nucleus and spatial transcriptomic analyses of 177,820 nuclei and 60,003 spatial spots across four developmental stages of the rice caryopsis, we identified 12 distinct cell types and delineated seven precise anatomical regions, thereby establishing a spatially resolved single-cell transcriptomic atlas of the developing rice endosperm. Using these cell type annotations, we inferred the developmental trajectories of endosperm cells, uncovered gene regulatory networks underlying cell differentiation, and identified three key transcription factors that regulate aleurone cell-fate determination. Furthermore, we observed cellular heterogeneity in the aleurone layer and the starchy endosperm and showed how this heterogeneity coordinates nutrient transport and storage product biosynthesis during rice grain filling. This study establishes a comprehensive cellular foundation and genetic regulatory network for understanding rice endosperm formation and storage product accumulation.
items.authors: Xu X, Yang T, Wei W, Zhou J, Tang L, Cheng H, Wu M, Zhang Y, Li X, Bai AN, Qi X, He Y, Liu CM, Liu J.

items.title: Long Non-Coding RNA StlincPRI Enhances Resistance to Phytophthora infestans by Regulating Reactive Oxygen Species Homeostasis.
items.abstract: Potato (Solanum tuberosum) is the fourth-largest food crop worldwide. However, late blight, caused by oomycete Phytophthora infestans, poses a major threat to global production. Although long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) have emerged as key regulators of plant immune responses, their role in potato immune response remains largely unknown. Here, transcriptome profiling of resistant cultivar Qingshu No. 9 and susceptible cultivar Désirée identified a P. infestans-responsive long intergenic non-coding RNA (lincRNA), named StlincPRI, which is significantly upregulated upon infection. Overexpression of StlincPRI activates the expression of pathogenesis-related genes, inhibits pathogen growth, and decreases lesion area upon P. infestans challenge. Moreover, StlincPRI triggers a rapid reactive oxygen species (ROS) burst during the early stage of infection. Subsequently, it alleviates oxidative damage via enhancement of both enzymatic and non-enzymatic ROS scavenging systems to maintain cellular ROS homeostasis. Conversely, silencing StlincPRI results in opposite effects, demonstrating that StlincPRI functions as a positive regulator of potato immunity against P. infestans. These findings provide insights for developing strategies to enhance late blight resistance and hold potential for advancing sustainable potato production.
items.authors: Lin R, Zhou N, Hao J, Wu Y, Bai W.

items.title: The Transcription Factor PtrWOX4 Promotes Secondary Growth by Regulating Cambium Activity in Citrus.
items.abstract: In citrus cultivation, successful grafting depends on the vigorous growth of rootstock, particularly robust stem thickening, which is crucial for a strong and healthy graft union. However, the factors and molecular mechanisms that accelerate stem thickening remain largely unknown. Here, we functionally characterize PtrWOX4, a key regulator of secondary growth in trifoliate orange (Poncirus trifoliata L. Raf.). This study shows that PtrWOX4 encodes a nuclear protein with a conserved WUS-box motif activated by auxin and strigolactone but repressed by abscisic acid and gibberellin. Overexpressing PtrWOX4 in tobacco markedly increased stem diameter, reduced internode length, and upregulated the cambium-associated gene KNAT6 and the phloem-associated gene NEN4. These changes were concomitant with elevated auxin and jasmonic acid levels in tobacco. Furthermore, overexpressing PtrWOX4 in trifoliate orange accelerated stem thickening and activation of the cambium and vascular tissue development. Collectively, this study established PtrWOX4 as a transcriptional coordinator that promotes stem secondary growth in trifoliate orange by orchestrating cambium activity and vascular differentiation.
items.authors: Liu H, Zhou T, Luo Y, Srivastava AK, Thu AM, Liu Y, Dong Z.

items.title: Engineering the plant holobiont for enhanced abiotic stress resilience: current insights and future directions.
items.abstract: Climate change has intensified abiotic stresses such as drought, heat, and salinity, posing major threats to agricultural productivity and global food security. Conventional strategies to improve crop tolerance often face limitations in efficiency, sustainability, and environmental adaptability, underscoring the need for innovative approaches. This review focuses on the plant holobiont, which views plants and their associated microbiomes as an integrated functional unit in governing stress adaptation. Abiotic stress can disrupt plant-associated microbial communities, leading to dysbiosis and reduced holobiont resilience. Beneficial microorganisms, including plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria, endophytes, and arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, can enhance stress tolerance by improving nutrient acquisition, regulating phytohormone signaling, strengthening antioxidant defenses, maintaining osmotic balance, and modulating stress-responsive gene expression. Emerging evidence suggests that these interactions contribute to the establishment of holobiont stress adaptation through biochemical signaling, microenvironmental modification, and epigenetic regulation, enabling plants to respond more effectively to recurrent stress. Advances in microbiome engineering, particularly through the development of synthetic microbial communities (SynComs), offer promising opportunities to restore microbial functions and enhance crop resilience under changing climatic conditions. The integration of multi-omics technologies, artificial intelligence, and precision agriculture is expected to accelerate the development of microbiome-based solutions for sustainable crop production. Collectively, microbiome engineering represents a promising, environmentally sustainable strategy to enhance the holobiont's adaptive resilience and improve long-term plant performance under abiotic stress.
items.authors: Albert M, Alizadeh M, Jefferson TA, Prismantoro D, Hindersah R, Joshi RC, Harsonowati W, Chua KO, Permadi N, Miranti M, Doni F.

items.title: Root endophyte sulfur metabolites enhance redox balance and drought tolerance in Arabidopsis.
items.abstract: Drought is a major consequence of climate change and significantly limits crop productivity. Plant growth-promoting bacteria offer a promising solution to mitigate drought stress. The root endophyte Pseudomonas argentinensis SA190 has been shown to enhance plant performance under drought stress conditions, but the mechanistic basis of SA190's beneficial effects remained unclear. Given the pivotal role of sulfur-containing compounds in abiotic stress responses, we investigated multiple sulfur-related Arabidopsis mutants under PEG-induced drought stress. We found that SA190 enhances sulfate uptake and promotes glutathione (GSH) accumulation in shoots under stress conditions. SA190 treatment increased the GSH/GSSG ratio, providing an enhanced redox resilience under PEG stress. Inhibition of GSH biosynthesis in Arabidopsis with buthionine sulfoximine (BSO) provided evidence that SA190 contributes to elevated GSH levels under PEG-induced drought stress. Using bacterial mutants defective in GSH biosynthesis, we further show that SA190 contributes to Arabidopsis growth under PEG-induced stress, potentially through a mechanism involving bacterial GSH itself or its precursor, γ -glutamylcysteine (γ-EC). In summary, SA190 enhances tolerance to PEG-induced drought stress by modulating host sulfur metabolism and improving cellular redox homeostasis.
items.authors: Elkatmis B, Alkhateeb RS, Mannes C, Jalal R, Trapp M, Westhoff P, Ozkan C, Thelen GM, Han B, Saad MM, Kopriva S, Hirt H.

items.title: Ca2+-Driven Nanodomain Enrichment And Plasma Membrane Proteome Remodelling Govern Plant Response To Bacterial Outer Membrane Vesicles.
items.abstract: Phytopathogenic outer membrane vesicles (OMVs) can elicit protective immune responses and can be utilised for crop protection. Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae (Xoo), a Gram-negative bacterium that causes Bacterial Blight of rice, releases OMVs. However, the role of Xoo-OMVs in the Xoo-rice interaction remains unexplored. We investigated the early signalling events underlying the plant's response to Xoo-OMV to gain insight into plant-pathogen interactions. We observed that Xoo-OMVs trigger a rapid, unique Ca2+ signal in rice that is essential for evoking an immune response. By imaging and proteomic analysis of the rice plasma membrane (PM), we found that this Ca2+ signal is required for Xoo-OMV-induced nanodomain enrichment and aggregation of defence response-associated proteins in rice PM. The specific protein assembly in the PM helps the plant defend itself against Xoo. In the absence of the early Ca2+ signal, rice cannot respond effectively to Xoo-OMVs, resulting in a compromised immune response. Collectively, our study shows that rice responds to Xoo-OMVs via Ca2+-signal-induced nanodomain assembly and protein reorganisation at the PM, preparing the plant for an imminent pathogen invasion.
items.authors: Mondal I, Das H, Behera S.

items.title: Assessing Zymoseptoria tritici Candidate Effectors in the Non-Host Nicotiana benthamiana Reveals Immune Recognition and Potential Host-Independent Activities.
items.abstract: Zymoseptoria tritici is a significant wheat pathogen responsible for Septoria tritici blotch (STB) disease. Despite its economic impact, understanding of the molecular interactions between Z. tritici and its host remains limited, particularly the functions of many uncharacterized candidate effectors. Here, we assessed seven Z. tritici candidate effectors with elevated expression during the early biotrophic phase and transition to necrotrophy by transiently expressing them in the heterologous, non-host system Nicotiana benthamiana, with and without their predicted signal peptides. AlphaFold structural predictions revealed that two candidates share similarity with proteins of known function: a sterol-binding protein from Saccharomyces cerevisiae and a necrosis-inducing effector from Valsa mali. Effector-associated phenotypes did not always correlate with expression timing, and signal peptide presence significantly influenced observed activities. Because N. benthamiana is not a natural host of Z. tritici, observed responses may reflect conserved, host-independent activities of effectors or immune recognition by N. benthamiana, rather than their native functions in wheat. Consistent with this distinction, two candidate effectors, Mycgr3107904 and Mycgr394290, induced cell death in N. benthamiana while also modulating reactive oxygen species (ROS) burst, likely indicative of immune recognition. Some candidates attenuated ROS production, suggesting potential targeting of conserved cellular processes, whereas none suppressed PBR1-mediated cell death. Overall, our results indicate that candidate effector activities cannot be inferred from expression profiles alone, and that responses in the non-host N. benthamiana system reflect a combination of immune recognition and potential conserved activities, and primarily serve to prioritize candidates for validation in the native wheat-Z. tritici interaction.
items.authors: Gomez-Gutierrrez SV, Rodriguez-Diaz C, Jaiswal N, Gribskov M, Helm M, Goodwin SB.

items.title: Advancing Cadmium Remediation via Rhizosphere Engineering: From Microbial Mechanisms to Field Deployment.
items.abstract: Cadmium (Cd) contamination of agricultural soils threatens food security and ecosystem health worldwide, yet conventional cleanup methods remain costly and ecologically damaging. Phytoremediation offers a sustainable in situ alternative, but low metal bioavailability, insufficient plant biomass, and inconsistent microbial performance limit field deployment. This review provides a framework that links molecular plant-microbe interactions to practical rhizosphere engineering for Cd management. We compare how functional traits of plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria (PGPR), arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF), and endophytes influence Cd mobilization versus immobilization, pH tolerance, and persistence. Their functions overlap and depend on plant species, Cd concentration, soil properties, and microbial strain; nevertheless, the evidence points to general tendencies: PGPR often drive short-term Cd mobilization with limited persistence, AMF commonly promote more durable immobilization through hyphal sequestration, and endophytes frequently modulate internal metal transport. We also evaluate synthetic consortia, multi-omics-guided microbiome design, and soil amendments. Field outcomes are appraised against explicit criteria (trial duration, replication across sites, use of historically contaminated soils, and reporting of Cd removal rate, translocation factor, available soil Cd, biomass, and soil health indicators), which also underpin the proposed standardized validation protocols. Matching microbial traits to site-specific goals, alongside food-safety, cost, and regulatory considerations, can help move phytoremediation toward scalable deployment work provides environmental managers and policymakers with a comprehensive roadmap for sustainable Cd remediation in agricultural landscapes.
items.authors: Manda T, Tsigbey VE, Hammond KK, Rajasekar A, Dzinyela R.

items.title: Engineering Drought-Responsive ABA Signaling: Linking Physiological Stress Cues to Metal-Organic Framework-Mediated ABA Delivery and SnRK2 Activation.
items.abstract: Drought induces coordinated physiological, biochemical, and molecular responses that extend beyond changes in phytohormone concentrations. Rapid alterations in reactive oxygen species (ROS), apoplastic pH, Ca2+ and ionic dynamics, tissue hydration, and cellular redox status provide spatial and temporal information on developing water deficit and regulate stomatal behavior, photosynthesis, water relations, and stress-responsive gene expression. This review explores whether endogenous drought-associated signals can serve as biological triggers for stimulus-responsive metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) designed to regulate abscisic acid (ABA) delivery. We integrate drought-induced changes in redox state, apoplastic pH, ionic composition, and hydration with MOF transformation, host-guest interactions, ABA release, uptake, transport, metabolism, and engagement of the PYR/PYL/RCAR-PP2C-SnRK2 signaling pathway. We propose a framework in which responsive MOFs generate a temporally controlled ABA pulse that follows drought progression, activates protective signaling during water limitation, and attenuates after rewatering to facilitate recovery. Particular emphasis is placed on ROS-Ca2+ crosstalk, SnRK2/OST1-dependent guard-cell regulation, hydraulic adjustment, photosynthetic protection, and recovery dynamics. Current studies demonstrate MOF-mediated phytohormone protection, controlled release, and drought-related physiological improvement. Current advances have established the feasibility of MOF-based ABA protection and controlled delivery; however, the integration of drought-responsive carrier activation with receptor-accessible ABA delivery and PYR/PYL/RCAR-PP2C-SnRK2 pathway validation remains an emerging research frontier. We therefore outline a claim-matched validation framework integrating spatial drought-signal analysis, isotope-resolved ABA tracing, carrier localization, phosphorylation-based pathway assays, drought-rewatering experiments, and physiological assessment. This integration of plant stress physiology with responsive nanomaterials provides a conceptual basis for developing more precise ABA delivery strategies for crop resilience under increasingly variable water availability.
items.authors: Jan MF, Shah MA, Azeem I, Ahmad H, Ullah R, Liaqat W, Aasim M, Altaf MT.

items.title: Auxin and Cytokinin Differentially Regulate Growth, Bud initiation, and Leaf Morphology in the Dryland Moss Syntrichia caninervis Brid
items.abstract: Abstract Although the role of auxin and cytokinin in growth and plant development from the cellular level to the whole plant are largely conserved across plant lineages; this does not exclude the possibility of divergence, especially in deep-splitting plant lineages. Here, the independent effects of exogenous auxin and cytokinin on the growth and development of S. caninervis are demonstrated, revealing concentration-dependent and antagonistic hormonal responses in development. At high concentrations, auxin promoted ectopic protonema proliferation but suppressed normal gametophore growth and pronounced disruption of leaf morphology. Cytokinin significantly enhanced bud production in a dose-dependent manner and produced comparatively modest leaf morphological changes, except for the hairpoint. In general, these findings suggest partial conservation of core auxin-cytokinin signaling mechanisms in S. caninervis relative to P. patens and vascular plants, while also revealing species-specific differences in hormonal sensitivity that likely reflect evolutionary and ecological distinctiveness of dryland mosses. From an applied perspective, the stimulatory effect of cytokinin on bud formation and/or stimulatory outgrowth protonema growth under auxin highlights the potential of targeted applications as a strategy for biocrust restoration in dryland ecosystems.
items.authors: Jauregui-Lazo J, Lujan I, Brady S.

items.title: Trichoderma elicitor CP3 induces phosphorylation and nuclear export of SRP to enhance tomato resistance to gray mold.
items.abstract: Beneficial Trichoderma fungi enhance plant immunity, but the molecular mechanisms of elicitor-mediated immune priming are still not well defined. Here, we identified a cerato-platanin (CP) family elicitor, CP3, from T. asperellum that enhances tomato resistance to Botrytis cinerea. CP3 is secreted and localizes to the host nucleus, where it interacts with the tomato protein SRP. This interaction recruits casein kinase 1 to phosphorylate SRP at Ser-185, thereby triggering its nuclear export to the plasma membrane. Subsequently, SRP binds the ubiquinone biosynthesis protein COQ9, forming a signaling module that activates reactive oxygen species production and jasmonate/ethylene defense pathways to establish induced systemic resistance. Genetic disruption of CP3, SRP, or COQ9 abolishes CP3-induced resistance, confirming their essential roles. Our findings reveal a complete CP3-SRP-COQ9 signaling axis through which a beneficial fungal elicitor reprograms host nucleocytoplasmic trafficking to activate tailored immunity, offering new molecular targets for engineering disease-resistant crops.
items.authors: Yin Y, Fu Y, Yu X, Hou J, Khalid MZ, Ahammed GJ, Liu T.

items.title: Overexpression of PlPAT1, a GRAS transcription factor from Paeonia lactiflora, enhances salt stress tolerance in transgenic tobacco.
items.abstract: BackgroundSoil salinization poses a significant threat to agricultural productivity worldwide, including the cultivation of Paeonia lactiflora. Understanding the molecular mechanisms of salt stress response and identifying key salt-tolerant genes are essential for breeding resilient varieties. The GRAS family of transcription factors is known to regulate plant growth, development, and abiotic stress responses; however, its role in P. lactiflora remains poorly characterized.ResultsIn this study, we identified a novel GRAS transcription factor from P. lactiflora, designated PlPAT1, based on its homology to Arabidopsis GRAS members. Under salt stress, PlPAT1 expression was up-regulated in leaves and stems but down-regulated in roots. Subcellular localization revealed that PlPAT1 protein localizes to both the nucleus and cytoplasm.
