Transgenic tobacco lines overexpressing PlPAT1 exhibited enhanced salt tolerance, accompanied by increased chlorophyll content, elevated levels of soluble sugars and proteins, and higher activities of antioxidant enzymes (SOD, POD, CAT). In contrast, malondialdehyde (MDA) and hydrogen peroxide accumulation were significantly reduced compared to wild-type plants.ConclusionOur results demonstrate that PlPAT1 functions as a positive regulator of salt stress tolerance, likely through modulating osmotic balance and enhancing reactive oxygen species scavenging capacity. These findings highlight the potential of PlPAT1 as a candidate gene for improving salt tolerance in plants and provide a genetic resource for the utilization of saline-alkali land.
items.authors: Cai J, Zhang X, Yan C, Lu C, Fu Z, Liu Y, Li G.

items.title: Nanoscale selenium confers broad-spectrum antifungal activity and reprograms antioxidant, phenylpropanoid and hormonal defense metabolism in tomato.
items.abstract: Sustainable crop protection requires strategies that suppress pathogens while supporting host defense. Here, selenium nanomaterials (SeNMs) were investigated for their combined antifungal activity and effects on tomato defense metabolism across three pathogens with contrasting infection strategies. SeNMs inhibited mycelial growth of phytopathogenic fungi in a concentration-dependent manner and disease severity was significantly reduced in planta against Colletotrichum gloeosporioides, Fusarium oxysporum and Fusarium solani. SeNMs treatment alleviated infection-induced physiological damage, restoring plant growth, chlorophyll content, gas-exchange parameters and PSII efficiency. Oxidative injury, indicated by H2O2, malondialdehyde and proline accumulation, was consistently greater in roots than shoots and was reduced by SeNMs in both tissues. Antioxidant and phenylpropanoid responses diverged sharply between tissues: infection suppressed SOD, CAT and APX activities and lignin accumulation in shoots while inducing them in roots and SeNMs treatment restored shoot responses and further amplified root responses. Phytohormone profiling revealed a strongly root-biased response, with salicylic acid (SA), jasmonic acid (JA) and abscisic acid (ABA) rising under the soil-borne pathogens; SeNMs treatment significantly lowered root SA under both Fusarium species and root ABA under F. oxysporum, indicating attenuation rather than induction of stress-associated hormonal signaling. Transcript profiling of antioxidant, phenylpropanoid and defense-signaling genes, including SlPAL, SlMYB14, SlPR1, SlCHS and SlFLS, mirrored these tissue-specific patterns. Together, these findings show that tomato concentrates defense metabolism at the site of infection and that SeNMs act differentially on directly challenged and systemically affected tissues, supporting their potential in broad-spectrum fungal disease management.
items.authors: Shen JJ, Ye B, Munawar A, El-Ela AA, Li H, Shi XX.

items.title: Volatile organic compounds of L. enzymogenes LEC suppress the growth of fungal and oomycete pathogens and modify the cell physiology of Rhizoctonia solani
items.abstract: Lysobacter enzymogenes LEC is a plant disease-suppressive bacterium. To obtain a more comprehensive understanding of its biocontrol activity and to identify further potential application methods, we investigated the function of its volatile organic compounds (VOCs). VOC activity was assessed in vitro using split-plate assays with eight different fungal and oomycete isolates and in planta against Pseudoperonospora cubensis on cucumber plants. The volatilomes of LEC and the less active L. enzymogenes DSM2043 were analysed by GC-MS analyses. Further, the effects of VOCs on cell physiology of Rhizoctonia solani were analyzed by fluorescence and transmission electron microscopy. The strongest inhibition of LEC VOCs was observed for Phytophthora infestans (94%) and Phoma lingam (83%), while inhibitions were lower for Rhizoctonia solani (42%) and Alternaria spp. (24% and 29%) and not detectable for two Fusarium isolates. VOC exposure also significantly reduced downy mildew caused by P. cubensis on cucumber plants (39%), although this effect was locally restricted to the leaf directly above the VOC source. In R. solani, VOC exposure reduced nuclei abundance and increased lipid accumulation. GC MS analyses revealed distinct volatile profiles between LEC and L. enzymogenes DSM2043 and identified ketones, such as 2-dodecanone and undecanone as candidate bioactive compounds, which is in agreement with previous findings. Our results demonstrate broad-spectrum VOC-mediated biocontrol activity, and thereby provide a more comprehensive understanding of its biocontrol activity and highlight new ways for potential applications of LEC.
items.authors: Maier, J., Gallinger, J., Molthan, M., Heil, N., Schaefer, P., Linkies, A.

items.title: Genome-Wide Identification and Expression Analysis of the S-Locus-Specific Glycoprotein/EP1 Gene Family in Cotton (Gossypium hirsutum L.).
items.abstract: The S-locus-specific glycoprotein/EP1 gene family encodes a class of epidermis-specific secretory glycoproteins involved in plant responses to abiotic stress. However, their role in cotton (Gossypium hirsutum) drought response remains unclear. Here, we identified 12 GhEP1 genes from the G. hirsutum genome, clustered into three subfamilies. Structural predictions indicated that most GhEP1 proteins are hydrophilic and localised to the outer side of the plasma membrane or nucleus, with a few containing transmembrane domains. Collinearity analysis revealed that segmental and tandem duplications drove family expansion, with a high degree of collinearity conservation among dicotyledonous plants. Transcriptomic data showed generally low GhEP1 expression across tissues, but GhEP1-2, GhEP1-6, GhEP1-7 and GhEP1-8 responded significantly to NaCl, PEG-induced drought and cold stresses. qRT-PCR further confirmed that the expression of most GhEP1 genes was significantly up-regulated in roots under drought stress, while GhEP1-3 was induced in leaves, indicating tissue-specific regulatory divergence. This study systematically characterises the GhEP1 family and provides potential genetic resources for improving drought tolerance in cotton.
items.authors: Feng C, Liu Y, Liu S, Geng J, Sun H, Li D, Liu R, Qian Y, Guo B.

items.title: Trait-based Machine-Learning Identifies Functional predictors of Plant Responsiveness to Arbuscular Mycorrhizal Fungi
items.abstract: Abstract Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) are widespread plant symbionts that enhance nutrient acquisition, growth, and stress tolerance, yet plant responsiveness to AMF varies substantially and remains difficult to predict. We developed Trait2Myco, a Random Forest–based machine-learning framework that integrates plant functional traits and environmental variables to predict mycorrhizal growth response (MGR). The framework was trained using 80 observations spanning four grass species grown under four precipitation regimes. Predictor variables included leaf and root economic traits and precipitation, while total MGR served as the response variable. A full model incorporating ten functional traits and precipitation was trained using 80% of the observations and evaluated on an independent testing dataset (20%, n = 16). The full model explained 41% of variation in MGR (R² = 0.41), whereas a reduced ecological model containing only specific leaf area, specific root area, root carbon concentration, and precipitation explained 51.7% of the variation (R² = 0.517). Ten-fold cross-validation of the full model yielded an R² of 0.983, RMSE of 0.046, and MAE of 0.036. Variable importance analysis identified specific leaf area, precipitation, root carbon concentration, and specific root area as the strongest predictors of MGR. Partial dependence analysis revealed nonlinear relationships between these predictors and MGR, while principal component analysis showed that highly responsive plants occupied distinct regions of functional trait space characterized by more resource-acquisitive trait syndromes. Leaf and root traits contributed nearly equally to model performance, accounting for 41.9% and 41.3% of cumulative importance, respectively, while environmental factors contributed 16.8%. An exploratory analysis using an independent AMF colonization dataset produced comparable predictive relationships, suggesting that trait-based machine-learning approaches may provide a useful framework for predicting plant responsiveness to AMF across environmental contexts.
items.authors: Shah T, Errahmouni MA, Hijri M.

items.title: The SCHENGEN pathway regulates lignin barrier formation via the receptor-like cytoplasmic kinase BIK1 in plant immunity.
items.abstract: Lignin deposition is a hallmark of plant immunity, forming a physical barrier that restricts pathogen spread and confines hypersensitive cell death. However, how immune signalling triggers this barrier remains unclear. Here we show that in Arabidopsis thaliana, the SGN3 (also referred to as GSO1) receptor kinase and CIF peptides, known for their roles in Casparian strip surveillance in the root endodermis, also function in leaves during effector-triggered immunity to control lignin barrier formation and disease resistance. Mechanistically, SGN3 preferentially uses BAK1 as its coreceptor and directly activates the receptor-like cytoplasmic kinase BIK1, which functions as the primary downstream signalling component during immune-associated lignification. Genetic and molecular analyses further reveal that NLR-driven CIF-SGN3-BIK1 signalling cooperates with pattern recognition receptor pathways to promote reactive oxygen species production and lignin polymerization during effector-triggered immunity. These findings uncover a previously unrecognized immune function of SGN components and establish a signalling module linking pathogen recognition to lignin-based barrier formation.
items.authors: Jang E, Jeon HS, Cho H, Lee H, An M, Jeon S, Soe MT, Chung EH, Tobimatsu Y, Oh E, Park OK.

items.title: Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi provide better agronomic performance in the production of 'Hass' avocado seedlings: a multivariate approach
items.abstract: Abstract Among the fruit trees that stand out in the current scenario is the avocado tree, which is widely cultivated worldwide due to the nutraceutical properties of its fruit, which are beneficial to human health. In this context, the adoption of sustainable practices at different stages of the avocado production chain is essential, aiming at reducing inputs and minimizing environmental impacts. This research aims to validate the use of mycorrhizal fungi in the I) production of rootstocks and II) production of ‘Hass’ avocado seedlings. For this purpose, the following treatments were proposed: 0 g.L − 1 (T1), 2 g.L − 1 (T2), 4 g.L − 1 (T3), and 6 g.L − 1 (T4) of the commercial product EcoRhiza® ( Glomus spp. 1 x 10 3 CFU g − 1 ), composed of four strains of arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi from the genus Glomus ( Glomus aggregatum , G. mosseae , G. intraradices , and G. etunicatum ) in a completely randomized design. The results showed significant responses when using the dose of 4 g.L − 1 for variables associated with gas exchange in rootstocks. For the seedlings, the same dose provided not only improvements in gas exchange variables but also increases in variables associated with chlorophyll indices, leaf area, and dry mass of the root system. These results indicate that the dose of 4 g.L − 1 of EcoRhiza® is the most effective for optimizing the development of ‘Hass’ avocado rootstocks and seedlings, contributing to a more sustainable avocado nursery production.
items.authors: Santos MFSd, Milan RJ, Costa BM, Avilés TEC, Belloti M, de Lara IAR, Silva SRd.

items.title: Mitochondrial C1-FDX Depletion Perturbs ROS Homeostasis and Iron Metabolism in Arabidopsis.
items.abstract: Mitochondrial complex I (CI) is a major source of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in plant cells, and iron-sulfur (Fe-S) cluster proteins are critical for maintaining CI structure and electron transport. C1-FDX, a mitochondrion-localized ferredoxin containing a [2Fe-2S] cluster, acts as a structural component and assembly factor of mitochondrial CI and complex V (CV) in Arabidopsis. In this study, we further characterized the physiological and molecular functions of C1-FDX in regulating ROS production, NADH/NAD+ homeostasis, and iron metabolism. Histochemical staining demonstrated that loss of function of C1-FDX in Arabidopsis c1-fdx mutants accumulated excessive superoxide anions (O2•-) but exhibited reduced hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) relative to the wild type (WT). Biochemical assays further confirmed that there was an elevated NADH/NAD+ ratio in mutant seedlings, which facilitated O2•- overproduction at mitochondrial CI. Loss of C1-FDX also led to Fe3+ accumulation in mutant tissues. Immunoblot and qRT-PCR results showed that the abundance of MnSOD markedly increased, while other antioxidant proteins, including FeSOD, CAT1, and GR, were downregulated in c1-fdx mutants of Arabidopsis. The enhanced MnSOD activity accelerated the conversion of O2•- into H2O2, and the subsequently accumulated Fe3+ may be derived from the Fenton reaction, which consumes H2O2, ultimately resulting in decreased H2O2 levels. Additionally, deficiency of C1-FDX disturbed the abundance of mitochondrial chaperones, proteases, and alternative respiratory pathway proteins. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that C1-FDX participates in the regulation of mitochondrial ROS balance and iron homeostasis and suggest there is a novel regulatory link between ferredoxin, the electron transport chain, and the Fenton reaction in plant mitochondria.
items.authors: Huang M, Zhang K, Wang T, Li P, Xin Y, Chen B.

items.title: Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi and mycorrhizal helper bacteria co-inoculation alters drought-associated physiological traits and leaf abscisic acid concentration in citrus rootstocks.
items.abstract: Plants rely heavily on root-associated microflora to mitigate various environmental stresses such as drought and the use of arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) as a biological instrument to enhance plant drought tolerance, through the formation of mutualistic associations, seems like a novel strategy for sustainable agriculture. Thus, a glasshouse study was undertaken with two citrus rootstocks (Troyer citrange and Cleopatra mandarin) under 20 days of differential moisture regimes (well-watered and water-stress condition), after 270 days of inoculation with two AMF strains (Glomus intraradices and mixed strains of Gigaspora decipiens + Glomus mosseae) alone or in combination with mycorrhizal helper bacteria (MHB), i.e., phosphate solubilising bacteria (PSB), Azospirillum or Providencia, with an objective of testing the hypothesis that AMF and MHB might influence ABA accumulation in citrus leaves, thereby altering physio-biochemical response to declining soil water status. The seedlings dually inoculated with AMF and MHB exhibited significantly higher relative water content of leaf as well as rhizospheric soil. Glomus intraradices in association with PSB or Azospirillum accumulated higher concentrations of osmolytes (phenols, proline and total soluble sugars) and antioxidant metabolites (glutathione and carotenoids) in leaves under WS condition. Significantly altered leaf tissue ABA accumulation was noticed in dual inoculated treatment of Glomus intraradices and Azospirillum for Troyer citrange (3.517 µg g-1 F.W.) and G. intraradices and PSB for Cleopatra mandarin seedlings (3.079 µg g-1 F.W.), under water-stress condition, as compared to other microbial inoculants including control. Thus, water deficit stress induced physiological and biochemical response pathways could be modified by AMF and MHB. Under these experimental conditions, Troyer citrange exhibited higher relative water content, photosynthetic activity, and stomatal conductance under drought conditions than Cleopatra mandarin seedlings, offering a potential microbial intervention strategy for mitigating osmotic stress in semi-arid environments.
items.authors: Barman P, Singh SK, Kumar R, Mishra DS, Shukla A, Pandey AK, Khadivi A, Tunç Y.

items.title: The SPL transcription factor MdSPL2 positively regulates drought tolerance in apple.
items.abstract: SQUAMOSA promoter-binding protein-like (SPL) transcription factors play crucial roles in plant abiotic stresses. In this study, the MdSPL2 gene was isolated from apple. Ectopic expression of MdSPL2 in Arabidopsis conferred enhanced tolerance to drought stress. Under drought stress, reduced malondialdehyde (MDA) content and decreased reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation were observed. Meanwhile, Apple calli, tomato seedlings and apple plantlets with ectopic overexpression of MdSPL2 all displayed markedly reduced sensitivity to drought stress. MdSPL2 was shown to play a vital role in drought tolerance by modulating ROS production. These results demonstrate that MdSPL2 acts as a crucial positive regulator under drought stress, providing novel insights into the function of MdSPL2 in abiotic stress responses.
items.authors: Wang TT, Chen GL, Wang Q, Yuan X, Guo XS, Li Y, Zhang LY, Wang DR, You CX.

items.title: bZIP-Mediated Activation of a Late Embryogenesis Abundant Protein MsLEA2 Enhances Aluminium Tolerance in Medicago sativa.
items.abstract: The phytohormone abscisic acid (ABA) is rapidly induced in roots exposed to aluminium (Al) stress, yet the mechanisms by which it modulates Al-detoxification genes remain elusive. Here we uncover a hierarchical ABA-responsive regulatory network that orchestrates a Late Embryogenesis Abundant (LEA)_2 protein MsLEA2, which modulates Al tolerance in alfalfa (Medicago sativa L.). Using yeast one-hybrid (Y1H) assays, luciferase complementation imaging (LCI), mutagenesis, and electrophoretic mobility shift assays (EMSA), we show that three antagonistic bZIP transcription factors-MsABF2 (activator), MsDPBF3 (hyper-activator) and MsGBF1 (repressor)-dynamically regulate MsLEA2 expression through spatially distinct ABRE motifs, enabling precise transcriptional control. Functional analyses reveal that MsLEA2 acts as a multifunctional hub, that promotes (i) oxalate exudation via interactions with aquaporins (MsPIP2;1, MsPIP2;2, MsTIP1;1), (ii) reactive oxygen species (ROS) scavenging, and (iii) cell wall remodelling through binding to UDP-xylose synthase (MsUXS1). Golgi-targeted MsLEA2 facilitates apoplastic Al exclusion, a mechanism distinct from its cytoplasmic homologue AtLEA14, underscoring the importance of subcellular compartmentalisation in Al detoxification. Our findings establish LEA_2 proteins as pivotal components of secretory-pathway-mediated Al tolerance and provide actionable targets for engineering crops resilient to acidic soils.
items.authors: Sun L, Mo X, Lv A, Liu X, Zhao E, Zhang Y, Hu W, Zhang Y, Xing Q, An Y, Zhou P.

items.title: Helotiales fungi as potential nutritional partners for non-mycorrhizal plants: a machine learning and experimental approach.
items.abstract: BackgroundMost land plants benefit from the ancestral arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) symbiosis for phosphorus (P) acquisition. However, several plant lineages have independently lost this symbiosis, raising fundamental questions about how these 'non-mycorrhizal' plants meet their nutritional requirements without this crucial partnership.ResultsComparative genomic analyses confirmed that Cyperaceae, Caryophyllaceae, and Brassicaceae lack genes essential for AM symbiosis, indicating that these lineages independently abandoned this association 90-122 million years ago. Field surveys of 42 wild populations across seven sites revealed that non-mycorrhizal plants generally maintain shoot P levels comparable to those in AM neighbors. To identify fungal taxa potentially associated with P nutrition in non-mycorrhizal plants, we applied a machine-learning approach to predict plant P-accumulation from root microbiome composition. The model explained substantial variance in plant P-accumulation (57-69%), and identified 85 fungal taxa as key predictors of shoot P-accumulation, predominantly belonging to the Helotiales (28%) and Pleosporales (23%) orders. Experimental validation of two phylogenetically distant Helotiales lineages (Tetracladium maxilliforme OTU29 and Helotiales sp. OTU7), using isotopic tracing, demonstrated their capacity to enhance plant growth and transfer P (and N) to their native non-mycorrhizal hosts under P-limiting conditions.ConclusionsOur findings suggest that non-mycorrhizal plants engage in nutritional partnerships with diverse Helotiales lineages that could collectively contribute to their mineral nutrition. However, given the widespread distribution of these Helotiales fungi, including in roots of AM plants, they may play a broader role in plant nutrition, i.e. also in mycorrhizal hosts. This study provides proof of concept for a novel framework integrating machine-learning predictions with experimental validation to identify functionally important microbial partnerships in natural plant communities. Video Abstract.
items.authors: Bruyant P, Gillespie LM, Doré J, Courty PE, Moënne-Loccoz Y, Almario J.

items.title: Arbuscular mycorrhizal symbiosis enhances salt tolerance in Eucalyptus grandis by coordinating antioxidant defense, hormone accumulation and ion homeostasis.
items.abstract: Eucalyptus is a globally important timber species, yet its productivity is markedly constrained by salt stress. Although arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) fungi play crucial roles under environmental stress, the integrated physiological and molecular mechanisms by which they confer salinity tolerance in E. grandis remain incompletely understood. In this study, we explored the impact of inoculation with the AM fungus Rhizophagus irregularis on the physiological, biochemical, and transcriptional responses of E. grandis seedlings across a NaCl gradient (0-200 mM). The results indicated that AM symbiosis significantly alleviated salt-induced growth inhibition, membrane damage and water deficit. Relative to non-mycorrhizal plants, AM-colonized seedlings exhibited lower accumulations of osmolytes and oxidative stress markers, while maintaining higher activities of key antioxidant enzymes. Hormonal profiling revealed a coordinated downregulation of stress-related phytohormones in mycorrhizal plants under salinity. Additionally, AM plants accumulated less sodium (Na+) and more potassium (K+) than non-mycorrhizal controls, suggesting enhanced Na+ efflux and K+ uptake under salt stress. Genome-wide analysis identified 23 candidate SOS pathway genes in E. grandis, and qPCR expression profiling revealed that all of these responded to AM symbiosis under salt stress, suggesting that AM symbiosis may regulate SOS pathway gene expression as part of its salt tolerance mechanism. Redundancy analysis suggested strong correlations among enhanced antioxidant enzyme activity, hormonal adjustments, ion homeostasis and the expression of specific EgSOS genes. Collectively, these findings provide integrated physiological and molecular evidence that AM symbiosis improves salt tolerance in a woody species through modulation of antioxidant defenses, hormonal balance, ion homeostasis and SOS pathway gene expression.
items.authors: Wang S, Xu G, Yu Y, Zhong Y, Li S, Wang J, Chen H, Tang M.

items.title: Physiological Responses and Transcriptomic Characteristics of Exogenous Trehalose Alleviating Cadmium Toxicity in Maize Seedlings.
items.abstract: Cadmium (Cd) contamination poses a severe ecological risk to ecosystems. Trehalose (TR) is a non-reducing disaccharide which can mitigate the adverse effects of heavy metals. The physiological responses and transcriptomic characteristics underlying TR-mediated heavy metal tolerance remain unclear in maize. In this study, maize seedlings were exposed to 200 mg L-1 CdCl2·2.5H2O with or without 23 mM exogenous TR for 5 days. By phenotypic observation, although TR supplementation could not fully restore maize growth under Cd stress, it significantly alleviated Cd-induced inhibition, increasing shoot and root dry weight by 33.80% and 36.67%, respectively, compared with Cd treatment alone. Exogenous TR also improved the photosynthesis under Cd stress. Cd stress triggered excessive ROS accumulation and membrane lipid peroxidation, whereas trehalose application alleviated oxidative damage by significantly reducing O2-, H2O2, and MDA contents while further enhancing SOD and CAT activities. Compared with Cd treatment, cell-wall fractionation revealed a 20.53% increase in root cellulose under Cd+TR combined treatment. Further, exogenous TR reduced Cd concentrations in roots and shoots by 19% and 33%, respectively. RNA-seq identified enriched GO categories related to cell communication, signal transduction, amino acid transmembrane transport, and membrane components, suggesting possible involvement of these processes in the TR response. These findings collectively demonstrate that exogenous trehalose enhances maize cadmium tolerance through coordinated physiological responses and transcriptional adjustments.
items.authors: Li C, Zhao J, Dong X, Yang S, Tang Y, Huang W, Chen J, Qiao Q, Zhu J, Ruan Y, Dong X, Fan J.

items.title: Type III Effectors of Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato DC3000: Molecular Mechanisms, Host Manipulation Networks, and Implications for Plant Disease Resistance.
items.abstract: Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato DC3000 (Pst DC3000) is a reference system for dissecting how type III-secreted effectors (T3Es) suppress plant immunity and reconfigure host physiology. Here, we reassess the DC3000 effector repertoire through an evidence-graded framework that links experimentally resolved effector-target mechanisms to repertoire-level genetic interactions and, ultimately, to disease-resistance strategies. We distinguish findings demonstrated with Pst DC3000 from mechanistic examples derived from other P. syringae pathovars and from computationally generated hypotheses. At the molecular level, validated DC3000 effectors perturb pattern-recognition receptor signaling, protein turnover, vesicle trafficking, plasmodesmatal communication, organelle function, and hormone-associated processes. At the repertoire level, deletion and reconstruction studies reveal functional redundancy, specialization, conditional suppression, and context-dependent interactions; importantly, convergence on a common host phenotype is not treated as evidence of direct physical cooperation between effectors. We further evaluate how effectoromics, multi-omics, single-cell and spatial approaches, structure prediction, and machine-learning tools can prioritize new hypotheses while emphasizing their need for genetic, biochemical, and infection-based validation. Finally, we consider how conserved effector targets, susceptibility factors, NLR engineering, and CRISPR-based editing may translate mechanistic knowledge into more durable bacterial-disease resistance. This synthesis positions the DC3000 system as a bridge between mechanistic effector biology, quantitative effector-network analysis, and experimentally testable strategies for crop protection.
items.authors: Zhong X, Huang J.

items.title: Regulatory Pathways of Endophytic Fungi in Promoting Flavonoid Biosynthesis in Medicinal Plants.
items.abstract: Endophytic fungi form complex symbiotic associations with medicinal plants via long-term coevolution. Such cross-kingdom interactions substantially modulate flavonoid biosynthesis in host plants. This review dissects the mechanisms through which endophytic fungi elevate flavonoid accumulation in medicinal plants. We first summarize symbiotic and growth-promoting relationships between endophytic fungi and medicinal plants, outlining four core synergistic functions: nutrient supply, phytohormone homeostasis, stress resistance enhancement, and secondary metabolism activation. We then elaborate on three primary regulatory patterns underlying endophyte-modulated flavonoid biosynthesis, including direct activation of plant flavonoid biosynthetic pathways, indirect regulation via stress mitigation and host metabolic reprogramming, and autonomous flavonoid production by endophytic fungi. Notably, most current evidence for autonomous flavonoid biosynthesis by endophytic fungi is derived from axenic cultures, whereas its occurrence and quantitative contribution within colonized plant tissues remain to be established. We further discuss state-of-the-art technologies for untangling plant-fungus symbiotic interactions, including multi-omics integration, spatial metabolomics, single-cell sequencing, synthetic microbial consortia, and CRISPR-Cas genome editing. Lastly, we propose future research perspectives covering green cultivation of medicinal plants, targeted improvement of medicinal quality, and efficient microbial biosynthesis of flavonoids.
items.authors: Gao Y, Dong H, Fang Z, Liu S, Xu Y, Guo Y, Yang Y, Luo J, Yan L.

items.title: Natural Variation in CYCLIC NUCLEOTIDE-GATED ION CHANNEL 16 Controls Fruit Weight in Tomato.
items.abstract: Fruit weight is a crucial agronomic trait influencing yield and quality in tomato domestication. Although numerous quantitative trait loci (QTLs) controlling fruit weight have been reported, the underlying molecular mechanisms remain largely unresolved. Here, we identify natural variation in the promoter region of CYCLIC NUCLEOTIDE-GATED ION CHANNEL 16 (CNGC16) associated with both fruit weight and gene expression differences via genome-wide association study (GWAS) in tomato accessions. Geographical and subpopulation analyses reveal that the large-fruit CNGC16 haplotype was selectively favoured during domestication and may contribute to local environmental adaptation. Functional assays demonstrate that CNGC16 regulates fruit weight by promoting cell division and maintaining cytosolic Ca2+ homeostasis in fruit cells. Mechanistically, CNGC16 physically and genetically interacts with calmodulin 6 (CaM6) to mediate calcium signalling that controls fruit size. These findings uncover a novel calcium-dependent pathway regulating tomato fruit weight and propose CNGC16 and CaM6 as promising molecular targets for crop improvement.
items.authors: Wang X, Huang Y, Miao H, Dai Y, Wang Y, Ding Z, Li N, Wu G.

items.title: Plant resilience: harnessing bioactive compounds for sustainable disease protection.
items.abstract: Plants have evolved complex phytochemical and immune defense mechanisms in response to pathogen invasion. Plants deploy phytochemical defense system-signaling molecules, secondary metabolites, antimicrobial proteins and peptides-to mitigate the pathogens they encounter. Pathogens have developed strategies-effector proteins, efflux pumps and detoxification mechanisms-to manipulate or overcome plant defenses. This review offers insights into how these bioactive compounds are biosynthesized and activated following pathogen recognition. We provide an overview of the dynamic crosstalk between PTI and ETI and their role in optimizing plant defense. Additionally, we discuss the potential of advanced genetic engineering approaches, nanocarrier-mediated elicitor delivery, and microbiome engineering to enhance these natural defenses. Finally, we address the technical bottlenecks of engineering plant immunity and provide a roadmap for future research directions. This review provides a stronger mechanistic foundation for breeding crops with durable, broad-spectrum resilience for sustainable crop protection.
items.authors: Latif MZ, Deng M, Asghar N, Kong L, Kousar S, Zhang H, Rehman SU, Jiang Y, Humza M, Lu C, Ding X.

items.title: Multilevel response to heat and cold stress in cauliflower (Brassica oleracea var. botrytis)
items.abstract: Abstract Abiotic stress, including heat and cold stress, are among the most detrimental to crop production. Despite previous studies, our understanding of how physiological and molecular responses enable crop plants to adapt to temperature stress remains unsatisfactory and requires further exploration. Under cold and heat stress, as well as during recovery after direct stress treatments, we observed increased electrolyte leakage in cauliflower leaves. Furthermore, after exposure to heat, a decrease in chlorophyll levels and photosynthetic conversion capacity was observed, indicating chloroplast senescence induction progressed throughout. This decrease was also observed after the recovery phase, suggesting irreversible changes in chloroplast function. Interestingly, chloroplasts under cold stress do not exhibit functional and most likely, structural changes. At the molecular level, heat stress, particularly heat recovery, had a negative impact on the cauliflower transcriptome by decreasing the abundance of numerous transcripts in cauliflower leaves. Cold and heat stress also affected a variety of transcription factors (e.g., MYB and WRKY family members). In the future, our results may contribute to the development of cauliflower varieties with improved tolerance to both high and low temperatures. That may be crucial for the global crop industry and food safety.
items.authors: Taube M, Kasprowicz-Maluśki A, Bielewicz D, Stolarska E, Taube M, Polcyn W, Nowak W, Rurek M, Wojtaszek P.

items.title: Submergence Response and Tolerance of Rice: Morphological and Physiological Strategies, and Regulatory Mechanisms.
items.abstract: Rice, as a globally vital food crop, is frequently threatened by flooding, which adversely affects its growth and yield. The most immediate and prominent influence of waterlogging or submergence induced by flooding on rice is hypoxia (reduced oxygen availability) or anoxia (absence of oxygen) stress and the consequent energy deficiency. Rice has evolved specific acclimation strategies to counteract or alleviate flooding stress, including leaf gas film (LGF) formation, adventitious root (AR) emergence, aerenchyma formation, radial oxygen loss (ROL) barrier development, and the stunted or elongated growth of coleoptiles or internodes, all of which serve to secure oxygen supply and maintain energy homeostasis for sustaining survival. These adaptive traits and strategies are governed by the regulatory genes involved in the reprogramming of energy and carbohydrate metabolism, the accumulation and scavenging of reactive oxygen species (ROS), and the programmed cell death (PCD) process, as well as the phytohormone biosynthesis and signaling pathways. To facilitate a comprehensive understanding of the submergence response and tolerance and the intricate regulatory mechanisms in rice, this review integrates the impacts of flooding on the growth and development, the strategies employed to adapt to submergence, the physiological and biochemical characteristics, the phytohormonal signaling and crosstalk, and the molecular mechanistic framework of rice subjected to submergence stress. It also highlights the importance of key superior genes for flooding-tolerance, flooding-tolerant germplasms, and molecular breeding technologies in developing submergence-tolerant rice varieties. By aligning these advances, this review provides valuable insights into and guidance for improving resilience to submergence stress and enhancing crop production under constantly changing climate conditions.
items.authors: Feng T, Liu S, Shi B, Lv L, Huang X, Li R, Ai H, Sun Z, Zhou A, Liu Y, Cui R, Liu Y, Huang X.

items.title: Stress signaling and physiological modulation by glycine betaine for cadmium-resilient maize.
items.abstract: Glycine betaine (GB), a naturally occurring osmoprotectant, stabilizes proteins, membranes, and osmotic balance under abiotic stress. It effectively mitigates oxidative damage and maintains redox homeostasis, making it a promising candidate for cadmium (Cd) tolerance. Cd toxicity is a major constraint to sustainable agriculture due to its phytotoxicity and bioaccumulation. This study evaluates the effect of GB applied via seed priming and foliar spray on Cd stress in two maize cultivars with contrasting tolerance ( CZP and MMRI). Plants were exposed to 500 mM CdCl₂ under controlled conditions, and morpho-physiological and biochemical traits - including biomass, chlorophyll, protein, reactive oxygen species (ROS), malondialdehyde (MDA), hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂), proline, GB, soluble sugars, phenolics, and flavonoids - were measured. Cd exposure reduced biomass, chlorophyll, and protein, while increasing ROS, MDA, and H₂O₂. Treatments, particularly seed priming, enhanced osmoprotectants and antioxidants, restoring osmotic balance and redox homeostasis. CZP showed greater biochemical resistance and lower Cd translocation than MMRI. Overall, GB-mediated stress modulation involves physiological reprogramming, with seed priming proving more effective than foliar spray. This study provides novel insights into GB-driven amelioration of Cd stress in maize.
items.authors: Hashmat S, Zaki M, El-Beltagi HS, Zulfiqar U, Alotaibi MS, Rebouh NY, Jobborov B, Daghash Alqahtani M, E Semary H, Ullah S.

items.title: Loss of SPATULA Function Partially Suppresses Root Growth and Meristem Organization Defects in GCN5 Mutants in Arabidopsis thaliana.
items.abstract: GENERAL CONTROL NON-DEREPRESSIBLE 5 (GCN5) is a histone acetyltransferase that plays a central role in regulating plant development and responses to environmental stimuli. In root development, GCN5 promotes the maintenance of the stem cell niche and proliferation of transit-amplifying cells. SPATULA (SPT) is a basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) transcription factor with established roles in gynoecium and carpel development, as well as broader functions in plant growth. In roots, SPT negatively regulates quiescent center size, root meristem size, and overall root growth, without substantially affecting root patterning or cell-type differentiation. To investigate a potential genetic interaction between SPT and GCN5 in root meristem development, we generated and characterized spt;gcn5 double mutants. Notably, loss of SPT partially suppressed some of the developmental defects associated with gcn5, including abnormalities in root meristem size, meristem organization, and root growth. These data suggest that a complicated genetic interaction between SPT and GCN5 regulates important aspects of root meristem growth and organization.
items.authors: Poulios S, Tersenidis C, Sidiropoulou S, Staikoglou CM, Kaftantzi MA, Vlachonasios KE.

items.title: Metabolic Regulation of Phenanthrene-Degrading Strain Sphingobium abikonense GHP1 in Response to Phenanthrene Stress and Its Effects on Endorhizosphere Microbiota of Lettuce.
items.abstract: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) are persistent organic pollutants with high ecotoxicity and bioaccumulation potential, and plant-microbe-assisted remediation is a promising green strategy for their removal. This study investigated Sphingobium abikonense GHP1, a phenanthrene-degrading bacterium isolated from a municipal solid waste incineration site, to elucidate its potential remediation mechanism using untargeted metabolomics and root endophytic bacterial community analysis. GHP1 completely degraded phenanthrene (50 mg L-1) within 3 days using it as the sole carbon source. During degradation, aromatic intermediates, including 1-hydroxy-2-naphthoic acid, salicylic acid, and hydroxybenzoic acid derivatives, accumulated, while central carbon metabolism, 2-oxocarboxylic acid metabolism, aromatic compound degradation, and benzoate degradation pathways were activated. Increased levels of NAD, purine metabolites, phosphatidylcholine, and phosphatidylethanolamine suggested enhanced redox regulation, energy metabolism, and membrane homeostasis under phenanthrene stress. In lettuce, GHP1 inoculation promoted plant growth, increased biomass and chlorophyll content, and reduced phenanthrene residues in roots and leaves. Moreover, GHP1 increased the richness of the root endophytic bacterial community and enriched Actinobacteriota, Firmicutes, and other bacterial taxa. These findings demonstrate that GHP1 enhances phenanthrene remediation through coordinated pollutant degradation, metabolic regulation, and plant-microbe interactions, providing a promising microbial resource for the remediation of PAH-contaminated environments.
items.authors: Zhang L, Wang Z, Jia Y, Liu L, Yang Y, Ren W, Gu H.

items.title: Warming winters can increase the risk of root frost damage in boreal tree seedlings.
items.abstract: Boreal winters are warming rapidly, but associated changes in snow cover, precipitation phase, and freeze-thaw conditions vary geographically. Where warming reduces or interrupts snow insulation while freezing conditions persist, root-zone temperatures may become more strongly coupled to atmospheric variability, potentially increasing episodic exposure of tree-seedling roots to damaging temperatures despite higher mean air temperatures. This review synthesizes our current understanding of snow-soil thermal processes and root physiological responses, evaluates the consequences of changing winter conditions for boreal forest regeneration, and assesses the capacity of empirical, forest growth, and land-surface modelling approaches to represent winter root frost risk. Evidence from boreal conifers shows that roots are generally less frost hardy than above-ground tissues and that root frost hardiness (FH) varies seasonally with root-zone temperature and thermal history. Experimental studies further demonstrate that root freezing injury can impair root regeneration, physiological function, shoot growth, and subsequent survival, with effects sometimes becoming apparent only after budburst or during later growing seasons. However, these responses depend strongly on species, injury severity, recovery capacity, and post-injury conditions. Altered winter environments can also impose interacting stresses, including ice encasement, hypoxia, waterlogging, and frost heaving. Ectomycorrhizal fungi show substantial taxon-specific freezing tolerance, but the consequences of repeated winter freezing and thawing for functioning of intact root-fungus symbioses remain poorly resolved. Existing modelling frameworks increasingly represent snow, frozen soils, plant hydraulics, and in some cases dynamic FH or frost mortality, but these components are rarely integrated with root-specific FH, root injury, and delayed seedling performance. Building on this synthesis, we propose a process-based framework linking winter climate forcing, snowpack and root-zone thermal dynamics, dynamic root FH, cellular and hydraulic injury pathways, and subsequent seedling growth and survival. The framework highlights that root frost damage risk emerges from the interaction between environmental exposure and dynamic physiological vulnerability rather than from air temperature extremes alone, and identifies key processes for improving prediction of boreal forest regeneration under changing winter conditions.
items.authors: Wu D, Domisch T, Kilpeläinen J, Repo T, Zhang D, Gong R, Vauhkonen J, Peltola H.

items.title: Cloning, Expression Analysis, and Functional Characterization of the NAC Transcription Factor SlNAC2-like from Tomato.
items.abstract: To investigate the regulatory function of the tomato NAC transcription factor SlNAC2-like under high-temperature stress, the high-temperature-tolerant line Hm 2-2 and the high-temperature-sensitive line BY 1-2 were used as experimental materials. The SlNAC2-like gene was cloned from tomato leaves via reverse transcription PCR (RT-PCR), and its encoded protein was characterized using bioinformatics tools, phylogenetic analysis, and expression profiling. Subcellular localization and yeast self-activation assays were performed to determine protein localization and transcriptional activity. Virus-induced gene silencing (VIGS) was employed to generate SlNAC2-like-silenced plants, and the activities of superoxide dismutase (SOD), peroxidase (POD), and catalase (CAT), as well as proline (Pro) and malondialdehyde (MDA) contents, were measured under high-temperature stress using spectrophotometry. The results showed that the SlNAC2-like cDNA fragment was 1044 bp in length, with an 876 bp open reading frame encoding 291 amino acids containing a highly conserved NAM domain. The protein was localized in the nucleus and exhibited transcriptional activation activity. Quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) analysis revealed that SlNAC2-like expression was tissue-specific and induced by high temperature (42 °C), abscisic acid (ABA), salicylic acid (SA), and methyl jasmonate (MeJA). Silencing of SlNAC2-like compromised tomato high-temperature tolerance, as evidenced by reduced SOD, POD, and CAT activities, decreased Pro content, and a marked increase in MDA content, along with significant downregulation of genes involved in ABA, SA, and jasmonic acid (JA) signaling pathways. Collectively, these findings suggest that SlNAC2-like acts as a positive regulator of tomato tolerance to high-temperature stress and that its function is associated with antioxidant defense and the ABA, SA, and JA signaling pathways. However, the present study does not establish how SlNAC2-like regulates ROS homeostasis or hormone signaling, and identification of its direct target genes and interacting partners requires further experimental validation. This study provides valuable genetic resources and a theoretical basis for molecular breeding of stress-resistant tomato varieties.
items.authors: Lv L, Duan L, Liu J, Li H, Shao Q, Chen N.

items.title: Enhancement of growth and salt tolerance in Clematis chinensis by the plant growth- promoting fungus Trichoderma compactum SZ01.
items.abstract: BackgroundSalt-tolerant rhizosphere microorganisms with multiple plant growth-promoting (PGP) traits represent cost-effective biological inoculants for enhancing plant tolerance to abiotic stress.ResultsIn this study, a salt-tolerant fungal strain, SZ01, was isolated from the rhizosphere of Clematis chinensis using PDA medium supplemented with 1% NaCl and identified as Trichoderma compactum based on morphological and molecular analyses. SZ01 tolerated NaCl concentrations up to 9%. Functional characterization revealed that SZ01 exhibited potassium solubilization, nitrogen fixation potential, and siderophore production, although it lacked the ability to solubilize organic or inorganic phosphorus. Pot experiments demonstrated that under salt stress, inoculation with SZ01 spore suspension significantly increased the fresh and dry weights of underground tissues, reduced Malondialdehyde (MDA) accumulation, and enhanced soluble sugar and proline contents compared with non-inoculated controls, indicating effective mitigation of salt-induced physiological damage. Transcriptomic analysis of C. chinensis leaves further showed that SZ01 treatment triggered extensive transcriptional reprogramming, particularly through modulation of MAPK and metabolic pathways, thereby optimizing stress-responsive gene expression. Secondary metabolite profiling of SZ01 under salt stress revealed the accumulation of chlorine-containing molecules potentially contributing to plant growth promotion.ConclusionThese findings highlight the potential of SZ01 as a microbial inoculant to promote plant growth and productivity in saline-alkaline environments, with implications for both medicinal and agricultural crop production.
items.authors: Wu Y, Xue X, Zhang S, Rong Y, Sun Y, Liu W, Yang L, Wang M, Jiang T.

items.title: Aquatic moss by-products offer an alternative to algal biomasses for phytostimulant bioproduction.
items.abstract: IntroductionAquatic mosses are recently gaining attention for commercial use, stimulating the development of new biomass cultivation approaches. This study explores the potential of by-products from aquatic moss propagation as natural plant biostimulants, addressing the need for low-waste production and sustainable agricultural strategies.MethodsUsing Temporary Immersion Bioreactors, Leptodictyum riparium and Taxiphyllum barbieri were cultivated, yielding solid non-viable biomass and liquid spent culture medium capable of offering a convenient and eco-sustainable alternative to similar products from algal and plant biomasses. Chemical analyses were performed to identify key plant hormones, including cytokinins (e.g., cis-zeatin, N6-isopentenyladenosine), auxins (indole-3-acetic acid, 2-oxindole-3-acetic acid), and abscisic acid (ABA). To evaluate efficacy, in vitro Nicotiana tabacum plants were grown under optimal, salt, and osmotic stress conditions and treated with various moss-derived preparations.ResultsCytokinins dominated the extract fraction with higher concentrations than auxins in both moss species. Cytokinin totals in the extracts were up to three orders of magnitude above the minimum threshold typically required for cytokinin-responsive phenotypic changes. In some cases, auxin concentrations approached, though remained below, the ~100 nM threshold commonly cited for bioactivity. Under optimal conditions, T. barbieri extract at 0.1% was the most effective treatment, increasing root length by up to 49% and shoot fresh weight by 93%. Under salt stress, L. riparium culture water applied at 3% of medium induced the strongest response, enhancing root length and biomass by up to 260% and 301%, respectively. Under osmotic stress, moderate biomass increases were observed, reaching 94% with L. riparium by-product and 48% with T. barbieri extract.DiscussionOverall, biostimulant efficacy was species- and matrix-dependent, with extracts mainly promoting growth under optimal conditions and culture water mitigating salinity stress. These findings indicate that moss-derived by-products are promising candidates for the development of innovative plant biostimulant formulations within a circular and low-input production framework, offering an alternative to other phytohormone-rich biomasses.
items.authors: Anglana C, Capaci P, Stigliano E, Plačková L, Doležal K, Barozzi F, Di Sansebastiano GP.

items.title: Tylosema esculentum (Marama Bean) as a Climate-Resilient Opportunity Crop: A Review of Nutritional, Medicinal, andGenomics Insights and Drought Adaptation.
items.abstract: Tylosema esculentum (Burch.) A. Schreib. (also known as marama) is a perennial legume native to the arid and semi-arid regions of southern Africa, where it thrives under extreme climatic conditions, particularly in hot and water-limited environments and nutrient-poor soils. This review outlines current knowledge on marama's nutritional and medicinal potential, as well as genomic insights and drought adaptation mechanisms, to ensure sustainable food systems. Marama has added advantages since the entire crop, including grains/beans, stems and tubers, can be used as a source of food for animals and humans. However, the nutritional value and safe consumption of different tissues are dependent on developmental stages and appropriate processing to reduce anti-nutritional compounds and improve digestibility. Marama beans possess exceptional nutritional value, being rich in protein; unsaturated lipids; essential micronutrients; and health-promoting phytochemicals including phenolics, flavonoids, saponins and phytosterols. To date, the chloroplast and mitochondrial genomes of Tylosema esculentum (marama) have been sequenced and assembled, while its nuclear genome size has been estimated at approximately 1 gigabyte, providing valuable genomic resources for further research. Marama exhibits a predominantly drought-avoidance strategy characterized by the development of deep tubers for water and nutrient storage, reduction in transpiration through leaf senescence and stomatal regulation, and maintenance of plant water status during prolonged dry periods. Marama also exhibits osmotic adjustment, which further enhances cellular protection and stress tolerance under water-deficit conditions. Despite these promising attributes, marama remains largely underutilized due to limited agronomic data to support its cultivation and insufficient data on its metabolic and genetic architecture that drives drought adaptation and socio-economic potential. Thus, there is an urgent need for integrated research efforts that will facilitate the transition of this crop from a wild-harvested resource to a sustainable, climate-resilient crop suited to arid and semi-arid agroecosystems.
items.authors: Gavhi P, Nkuna M, Nemauluma GL, Mogwaduba L, Murovhi NR, Mulaudzi T.

items.title: extracellular ATP: an emerging primer for plant stress memory.
items.abstract: Plants can retain information from prior stress exposure as strong and durable memory, but the proximal signals that establish the primed state remain elusive. Extracellular ATP (eATP), a ubiquitous damage-associated molecular pattern released upon cellular perturbation, is emerging as an early orchestrator of plant stress adaptation. Herein, we advance a framework positioning eATP as a regulatory hub that integrates stress perception via the purinoceptor 2K1/2 (P2K1/2), amplifies Ca2+ and reactive oxygen species signaling, and interfaces with phytohormone networks, energy sensors, chromatin regulation, and noncoding RNAs. We propose eATP as an integrative priming hub, explicitly separating established signaling from hypothesized epigenetic memory, and discuss how this framework can guide plant resilience strategies.
items.authors: Shan Y, Li T, Zhang D, Duan X, Jiang Y.

items.title: Host identity and fungal source pools shape mycorrhizal assembly under carbon removal interventions in large-scale afforestation
items.abstract: Large-scale afforestation is central to global carbon dioxide removal (CDR) commitments. Soil inoculation and enhanced rock weathering (ERW) may increase tree biomass carbon stocks during woodland establishment. Both can alter soil fungal communities, but whether they change the root-colonising mycorrhizal fungi that support tree nutrition and growth is largely unknown. In a fully-factorial field trial on former upland pasture in Wales (11.5 ha; ∼25,000 saplings), we tested the effects of soil inoculation (addition of soil from nearby mature, donor forests) and ERW (basalt amendment) on root-associated ectomycorrhizal (EcM) and arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) fungi, and tree growth in mixed-broadleaf and conifer plantations, two and four years after planting. To identify key colonisation sources, we also characterised mycorrhizal fungi in roots and soils of surrounding hedgerows, source tree nursery, non-forested control plots, donor woodlands and soil inoculum. Soil inoculation caused a subtle shift in conifer EcM community composition (3% of variation) but had no detectable effect in broadleaves. Basalt amendment raised soil pH but did not change mycorrhizal composition, diversity, or colonisation. Root-associated EcM communities were distinct from those detected in plantation soils and shared far more taxa with the tree nursery than with the donor inoculum (41-48% vs. 2-9% of plantation EcM taxa) whereas AM communities largely reflected fungi present in pre-existing pasture. Host identity was the dominant factor structuring mycorrhizal communities, overshadowing both treatments, and was the strongest predictor of aboveground biomass. Synthesis and applications : This field-scale evaluation shows early mycorrhizal assembly during woodland establishment is strongly structured by tree species identity and pre-existing fungal source pools, limiting the effect of inoculation at planting. Mycorrhizal management should therefore target the nursery stage and be tailored to individual tree species. Basalt amendment for ERW is unlikely to harm mycorrhizal communities during establishment. Because soil fungal communities did not reflect root symbiosis, our findings also stress that monitoring of belowground outcomes in CDR-focused planting should include root sampling rather than relying on soil DNA alone.
items.authors: Thomson, I. J., Lindsay, O., Allen, H., Averill, C., Brekke, T. D., Nicholls, C., Steidinger, B., Vanguelova, E., Waring, B., M. Suz, L., Bidartondo, M. I.

items.title: Drought resistance is influenced by soil water uptake depth in dryland shrubs.
items.abstract: Climate change exacerbates aridity in dry shrublands leading to different responses of coexisting shrubs to drought, including different resistance (capacity to sustain growth during droughts). However, it is unknown how resistance depends on shifts in soil water uptake depth and functional traits. To address this issue, we studied seven shrub species in two semi-arid Mediterranean sites. Using the isotopic composition of oxygen and hydrogen in soil and xylem water samples (δ18O, δ2H), we quantified depth of soil water uptake. Traits (height, leaf mass per area-LMA and wood specific gravity-WSG) were measured to evaluate whether they were related to intrinsic water-use efficiency (iWUE) and radial growth resistance to drought. The iWUE was positively correlated with LMA and increased during dry periods in the less arid site. Soil water uptake depth, height and WSG were positively associated with drought resistance. Species that shifted from shallow to deep water sources during the dry season, such as Pistacia lentiscus, Quercus coccifera and Rhamnus lycioides, were more resistant, whereas less resistant species such as Juniperus phoenicea, Juniperus oxycedrus, Rhamnus alaternus and Ephedra spp. used more shallow and stable soil-water sources. Synthesis. Drought resistance depended on shifts in soil water uptake depth. Drought resistance should be integrated in future analyses of dryland plant communities given its linkages with functional traits.
items.authors: Tamudo E, González de Andrés E, Camarero JJ, Gazol A.

items.title: Advances in the transcriptional regulation of seed vigor and its application in molecular breeding for rice.
items.abstract: Rice seed vigor is a life-cycle trait whose performance after sowing depends on physiological capacity established during seed development, preserved during storage, and reactivated during germination and seedling establishment. Rather than functioning as isolated stage-specific pathways, transcriptional networks coordinate a series of transitions between protection and growth. During seed development, transcription factors establish embryo competence, reserve organization, desiccation tolerance, and proteostasis, thereby creating the physiological capacity for subsequent performance. During storage, ABA- and auxin-associated bZIP networks, including the OsARF12-OsbZIP23 and OsbZIP23-PER1A modules and SAG9-associated regulation, maintain longevity through antioxidant and protective processes; emerging salicylic acid-associated signaling further extends this hormone-redox regulatory framework. After imbibition, ABA-GA balance, sugar and energy signaling, reserve mobilization, reactive oxygen species homeostasis, and cell expansion determine the timing and uniformity of germination, while related regulatory modules support establishment under salinity, chilling, water deficit, and oxygen limitation. Importantly, current evidence varies substantially in strength: some regulators are directly supported by germination, longevity, dormancy, or stress-vigor phenotypes, whereas others remain developmental candidates inferred mainly from grain composition or seed-development traits. Field-emergence validation and natural-storage evidence also remain limited. We therefore propose that rice seed-vigor improvement should prioritize stage-appropriate regulatory alleles and precise modulation of transcription-factor activity, while jointly considering storability, dormancy and pre-harvest sprouting resistance, field establishment, yield, and grain quality.
items.authors: Chen F, Zhang Y, Wu Z, Zhang H, Gao Y, Fan J, Wei Q, Xie H, Zhang J.

items.title: Bioinformatics-Driven Identification of Flooding-Tolerance Genes and Their Structural and Molecular Characterization in Soybean.
items.abstract: Flooding stress is one of the important abiotic factors restricting soybean production globally. Despite numerous efforts, the genetic mechanisms of flooding tolerance are not fully understood. This work used a bioinformatics-driven, integrative approach combining structural analysis, molecular docking, expression profiling, and biochemical phenotyping to prioritize and characterize genes associated with flooding tolerance (FTgenes) during the early stages of soybean seedling development. Functional annotation of 83 previously prioritized FTgenes was used to classify them into five functional categories, with one candidate per category identified for further study: enolase (energy supply); phytocyanin (reactive oxygen species; ROS management); glycoside hydrolase family 17 (GH17; cell wall adjustment); ethylene and sulfur compound biosynthesis-related protein (ESCBp; hormonal signaling); and alfin zinc-finger protein (gene regulation). Comprehensive sequence analyses, phylogenetic relationships, motif predictions, and homology modeling were performed for these five candidate genes. Molecular docking analyses demonstrated that enolase, GH17, and ESCBp had conserved residues necessary for catalysis and forming stable complexes with respective ligands. Expression analysis showed distinct but coordinated transcriptional activation of the FTgenes during short-term flooding stress. Levels of salicylic acid and abscisic acid changed as a function of time upon flooding. In addition, protein levels, chlorophyll a content, total phenolics, flavonoids, and antioxidant capacity were modulated in an organ-dependent manner. Overall, this study has provided evidence for a coordinated network of energy metabolism, ROS homeostasis, cell wall adjustment, hormone signaling, and regulation of gene expression that characterizes the early molecular response of soybean seedlings to flooding stress. These genes provide structurally and molecularly characterized candidate genes for future genetic improvement.
items.authors: Baiya S, Kao CF, Kao PH, Juntaropakorn M, Kitjaruwankul S, Promkatkaew M.

items.title: Tartary buckwheat cotyledon size varieties undergo distinct transcriptional reprogramming of phytohormone signaling under cold and UV stresses.
items.abstract: Fagopyrum tataricum (TB) is a characteristic high-altitude crop in China. The cotyledon, as a key photosynthetic and nutrient storage organ at the seedling stage, plays critical roles in early growth and stress tolerance, but the molecular linkage between cotyledon size and abiotic stress resistance remains unclear. In this study, 279 TB accessions were phenotyped for cotyledon area, height, and width across three ecological regions over two consecutive years, and were classified into large, medium, and small cotyledon types via phenotypic clustering analysis. Two representative accessions, Ft104 (large cotyledon) and Ft32 (small cotyledon), were selected for further experiments. Cytological observations showed that cotyledon size was associated with differences in epidermal cell size and density, with small-cotyledon accessions exhibiting a higher number of cells per unit area. Physiological assays at the germination stage demonstrated that small-cotyledon accessions exhibited faster water absorption, stronger seedling emergence capacity, and more stable degradation of storage substances. Under low-temperature and UV-B stress, small-cotyledon accessions accumulated less malondialdehyde (MDA) and displayed significantly higher activities of peroxidase (POD), superoxide dismutase (SOD), and catalase (CAT), indicating enhanced stress tolerance. Transcriptomic analysis and WGCNA identified 18 co-expression modules, of which MEcoral4 was associated with cotyledon morphology and stress-related physiological traits and was enriched in plant hormone signal transduction. Three candidate genes, FtAUX22D, FtARG7, and FtPYL4, were further examined by qRT-PCR across multiple accessions. Heterologous expression in yeast provided preliminary evidence that FtPYL4 enhances cold-stress tolerance. Targeted LC-MS/MS profiling further revealed genotype-dependent changes in endogenous phytohormones and auxin-related metabolites, with Ft32 showing higher accumulation of several indole-related metabolites and SA under stress, whereas Ft104 exhibited a pronounced JA response to UV-B. Together, these results indicate an association between cotyledon-size phenotype and abiotic-stress responses involving phytohormone-related transcriptional and metabolic reprogramming in Tartary buckwheat.
items.authors: Liu L, Sai F, Shao J, Zhang W, Fan J, Ma M, Liu Z, Xu S, Jiao X, Hou S, Sun Z.

items.title: Recognition-dependent activation of the Arabidopsis RRS1-R/RPS4 TIR-NLR immune receptor pair.
items.abstract: Plant TIR domain-containing proteins exhibit NADase activity upon pathogen effector recognition, creating small molecules that activate defense via EDS1 and its associated proteins. Arabidopsis RPS4 and RRS1 comprise a TIR-NLR immune receptor pair that recognizes multiple effector proteins including AvrRps4 and PopP2. We show here that RPS4 and RRS1 acquire NADase activity upon recognition of a cognate effector. However, both in the presence and absence of effector, RPS4 and RRS1 form an oligomer that does not change in size upon effector provision. Effector-dependent defense activation by RPS4 and RRS1 requires the catalytic glutamate residue and the BB-loop motif of RPS4, which is absent in RRS1 and other RRS1-like TIR domains in Arabidopsis. Oligomerization of RPS4 and RRS1 occurs through multiple domains, but oligomerization does not require enzymatic activity. We propose that conformational changes or reconfiguration within the RPS4/RRS1 oligomer upon effector recognition derepresses the complex for immune activation.
items.authors: Ahn HK, Guo G, Skłenar J, Keh SPY, Huh SU, Hulin MT, Burdett H, Sindalovskaya M, Na S, Choi J, Mukhi N, Zhao H, Knorr LS, Paek E, Banfield MJ, Menke FLH, Ma W, Jones JDG.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
also: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Low ambient temperatures regulate Arabidopsis abscisic acid signaling and seed germination via CBFs-ABI3/ABI5-ICE1 interactions.
items.abstract: Seed germination is profoundly influenced by diverse environmental stimuli (e.g., temperatures), but the associated underlying molecular mechanisms remain largely uncharacterized. In this study, we demonstrated that low ambient temperatures, such as 16°C, suppress Arabidopsis thaliana seed germination, with endogenous abscisic acid (ABA) signaling revealed as a critical part of the underlying mechanism. The germination suppression and ABA response regulation by low ambient temperatures require ABSCISIC ACID INSENSITIVE3 (ABI3) and ABI5, two indispensable transcriptional activators in the ABA signaling pathway. In-depth analyses demonstrated physical associations between ABI3/ABI5 and low-temperature-responsive C-REPEAT BINDING FACTOR1 (CBF1), CBF2, and CBF3 (i.e., CBFs). Genetic evidence confirms that CBFs are essential for low-temperature- and ABA-mediated germination repression. Furthermore, CBFs and ABI3/ABI5 synergistically mediate the inhibitory effects of both low temperatures and ABA on germination. Mechanistically, these factors reciprocally enhance each other's transcriptional activities and promoter enrichment at downstream target genes. Notably, CBFs also directly bind INDUCER OF CBF EXPRESSION1 (ICE1), establishing an antagonistic regulatory axis with ABI5. Collectively, our findings underscore the critical modulatory effects of low ambient temperatures on ABA signaling and seed germination, thereby elucidating the mechanism by which the CBFs-ABI3/ABI5-ICE1 module functions as a signal transducer that converts environmental stimuli into endogenous hormone signals.
items.authors: Ye J, He K, Yu C, Lou Y, Du J, Zhang J, Han X, Hu Y.

items.title: Response differences in seed germination and seedling growth of three Asteraceae plants under saline-alkali stress.
items.abstract: Soil salinization severely restricts plant growth and threatens ecological sustainability, particularly in soda saline-alkali regions such as the Songnen Plain. Asteraceae plants are widely used in vegetation restoration due to their strong ecological adaptability. In this study, Tagetes erecta L., Cadendula officinalis L., and Leucanthemum maximum (Ramood) DC were selected as experimental materials. Two types of stress (salt and alkali) were applied at five concentration levels each (excluding the distilled-water control), which respectively constituted a salinity gradient and an alkalinity gradient. Seed germination parameters, seedling growth traits, and physiological indicators were measured, and field validation was conducted in areas with mild, moderate, and severe saline-alkali soils in the Songnen Plain. T. erecta L. showed optimal germination at the low concentration of salt and alkalinity (25 mmol/L), exhibiting a "low promotion and high inhibition" pattern, and maintained relatively high vigor under high stress. L. maximum had the highest germination rate under non stress conditions but was highly sensitive to increasing salt and alkalinity, while its root growth remained relatively stable under salt stress. C. officinalis L. was highly sensitive to alkali stress. Alkali stress consistently exerted stronger inhibitory effects on seed germination and seedling growth than salt stress. Field validation further demonstrated that T. erecta L. maintained a significantly higher survival rate under severe saline-alkali conditions (HS) compared to L. maximum and C. officinalis L. (p < 0.05). This study identified interspecific differences in saline-alkali tolerance among three Asteraceae species, offering a data basis and scientific reference for plant selection and breeding in ecological restoration and landscaping of saline-alkali areas.
items.authors: Yang S, Yang X, Li R, Ji Y, Hu Y, Jin D, Wei R, Liu Y.

items.title: From the rhizosphere to systemic circulation: cross-kingdom signaling and health effects of soil microbial metabolites.
items.abstract: Plant roots and soil microorganisms engage in continuous, complex chemical dialogues at the rhizosphere-a highly dynamic interface. The rhizosphere not only serves as a "black box" where root exudates and microbial metabolites converge but also functions as a critical site for shaping microbial community structure. Small-molecule metabolites produced by either plant roots or microbes mediate plant-microbe interactions locally and can further influence shoot physiology through systemic signaling. Similarly, in animal and human systems, gut microbes produce bioactive metabolites - such as short-chain fatty acids, indole derivatives, and secondary bile acids - that enter systemic circulation and participate in host metabolic regulation, immune modulation, and even neural function. Although the rhizosphere and gut belong to distinct ecosystems, they exhibit remarkable parallels in metabolite-mediated cross-kingdom signaling mechanisms: microbial metabolites in both systems can traverse biological barriers, enter systemic circulation, and modulate host phenotypes. Thus, from the rhizosphere to systemic circulation, soil (or gut) microbial metabolites are being redefined as pivotal mediators linking environment, microbiota, and host health. Elucidating the chemical nature, transmission pathways, and biological effects of these metabolic signals will not only advance the development of green, microbiome-based inputs for sustainable agriculture but also offer novel ecological perspectives for understanding human metabolic and neurodegenerative diseases.
items.authors: Ji M, Li L, Gao L, Xu J, Liu H, Yao Y, Niu G, Hao B.

items.title: When Roads Remove Trees, Conservation Must Move Fast: A Rescue Translocation Model for Keralam's Native Epiphytic Orchids.
items.abstract: Development-related tree removal can immediately eliminate epiphytic orchids and specialised canopy habitats, yet evidence for rescue translocation remains limited. We assessed 27,324 mature native orchids representing 21 species, rescued during road widening in Keralam, India, and translocated to three contrasting recipient landscapes. Of the 27,324 translocated orchids, 19,511 survived (71.4%) after 12-24 months. Among the surviving plants, 5224 flowered (26.8%), of which 1934 produced capsules (37.0%). Recovery differed among recipient sites, orchid species and phorophytes. The buffered urban site supported the highest survival, whereas the exposed coastal site imposed a strong establishment filter but supported relatively high flowering and capsule production among survivors. Regional endemic and cool-growing orchids also survived and reproduced, although establishment was lower and more site-dependent. Phorophyte identity was most strongly associated with establishment, while root growth consistently predicted survival, flowering and capsule production. Embryo-containing seeds occurred in all sampled capsule collections, but formal physiological viability and germination tests were not undertaken. Rescue translocation can therefore reduce otherwise likely losses when tree removal is unavoidable. The findings support pre-felling surveys, timely rescue, recipient site screening, testing across candidate phorophytes and staged long-term monitoring, while the operational allocation design prevents causal attribution or prescriptive species-phorophyte matching.
items.authors: Venugopal M, Sukumaran PN, Sarasan V.

items.title: Multi-Omics Analysis of the Enhancement of Bioactive Components in Glycyrrhiza uralensis Fisch. through Combined Inoculation with Rhizobium and PGPR under Salt Stress
items.abstract: Abstract Background and objective Licorice, an important forage crop widely cultivated worldwide, faces increasing scarcity of wild resources, making artificial cultivation the primary means of market supply. Salt stress negatively impacts the quality and yield of licorice, while microbial inoculation can not only effectively alleviate the damage caused by salt stress but also enhance its quality. To elucidate the response mechanism of licorice to salt stress, this study investigated the physiological, transcriptomic, and metabolomic changes under salt stress. Results The results showed that the combined inoculation group exhibited significant increases in osmotic substance and chlorophyll content. Transcriptome and metabolome sequencing analysis, along with pathway validation, identified 34, 76, and 54 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in the CK vs CKNaCl, GM9ZNaCl vs CKNaCl, and GM10NaCl vs CKNaCl groups, respectively. These genes were primarily enriched in pathways such as ABC transporters, oxidative phosphorylation, plant hormone signal transduction, and jasmonic acid biosynthesis. The contents of metabolites including linoleic acid, amino acids, and jasmonic acid in licorice were significantly increased. Conclusion It is inferred that combined inoculation may enhance the osmotic regulation capacity and antioxidant defense ability of G. uralensis roots under salt stress, activate phytohormone signaling pathways such as jasmonic acid, and thereby coordinately regulate the expression of related functional genes, effectively improving the salt tolerance of G. uralensis and promoting the synthesis of secondary metabolites. This study provides an important theoretical basis for utilizing microbial agents to improve the growth of medicinal plants in saline-alkali soils.
items.authors: Hao¹·² Y, Yubo¹·² Y, Shengjun¹·² M, Wenfeng³ C, Kunhong D.

items.title: Adjustment of Root System Architecture and Root Function in Response to Multifactorial Abiotic Stress.
items.abstract: The root of land plants is a remarkably adaptive organ. Unlike the shoot with its main functions in light harvesting and photosynthesis, sexual reproduction and diaspore distribution, the root explores the soil for nutrient resources and water, while preferably avoiding zones of unfavorable conditions. Roots realize an extraordinarily flexible architecture and perceive and integrate environmental input parameters to optimize growth, architecture, and physiology. In nature, roots encounter a heterogeneous rooting environment characterized by combinations of negative and positive growth parameters, for example, nutrient availability, temperature, hypoxia, toxic metal ions, or compacted soil, necessitating research on multifactorial stress effects on roots. While many studies have addressed the combination of altered nutrient status, in particular nitrogen and phosphorus, and other environmental stress factors such as drought, temperature, and soil compaction, fewer studies addressed climate change-related combinations of stressors such as heat, drought, and hypoxia. The decisive mechanism of environmental input integration targets root growth and architecture, but also exudation. The adjustment is realized by altered activity of apical meristems for root elongation, the pericycle for lateral root initiation and formation, the development of adventitious roots, and root thickening by cambial activity and senescence. This review presents selective case studies to exemplarily summarize current experimental approaches and obtained knowledge on root responses to multifactorial environmental constraints with focus on assimilate-, redox-, and auxin-dependent regulation. The review pinpoints the need to advance and harmonize our experimental approaches by investigating the sensory role and growth response of roots at the local and systemic level.
items.authors: Dietz KJ.

items.title: Together we "CAM": 12 open questions in Crassulacean acid metabolism biology.
items.abstract: BackgroundCrassulacean acid metabolism (CAM) is a remarkable example of convergent evolution and is a versatile photosynthetic adaptation across the tree of life. It often receives less research attention than C3 or C4 photosynthesis, but as the consequences of climate change become more drastic, research into bioengineering CAM has become increasingly timely for its adaptive advantage during drought. Regardless of a biotechnological application, several aspects of CAM biology are still poorly understood.ScopeHere, we highlight 12 questions that have the potential to advance the field of CAM biology, covering a wide range of topics, from mechanistic, physiological, evolutionary to applied themes, including stomatal kinetics, vacuolar malate transport, mitochondrial respiration, the circadian clock, phenotypic definitions, sensing stress to induce CAM, ecophysiological significance of CAM, phytohormone signaling, multi-level molecular regulation, genetic engineering, climate change, and evolution of CAM. Overall, we also highlight the ultimate need for exploring the numerous CAM phenotypes instead of only model species.ConclusionsThis perspective article provides a broad yet detailed overview of CAM biology and aims to inspire more work in the field. We aimed to highlight key knowledge gaps and future research opportunities, thereby underscoring the timely significance and relevance of CAM.
items.authors: Daems S, Perez-Lopez AV, Pritchard J, Chomthong M, Hartzell S, Messerschmid TFE, Morris BA, Siadjeu C, Subaylaa M, Reichel-Deland V, Leverett A, Callegari Ferrari R.

items.title: Integrated Transcriptome and MicroRNAome Analysis Reveals Dynamic Responses Underlying ZmWAK-Mediated Resistance to Head Smut in Maize.
