items.abstract: The maize wall-associated kinase gene ZmWAK confers partial resistance to head smut caused by Sporisorium reilianum, yet how it coordinates dynamic immune responses remains poorly understood. Here, we integrated transcriptome and microRNAome analyses of near-isogenic maize lines differing at the ZmWAK locus to dissect the regulatory landscape underlying ZmWAK-mediated resistance during mesocotyl infection. We found that ZmWAK was associated with a stage-specific defense trajectory characterized by dynamic shifts in phytohormone networks, intermediate cellular reprogramming, and late-stage cell wall remodeling. A conserved extracellular defense signature was maintained through sustained activation of apoplastic oxidoreductase-associated processes. Meanwhile, ZmWAK-associated miRNAs were preferentially reprogrammed during peak pathogen proliferation, and their predicted targets were enriched in phenylpropanoid metabolism, lignin biosynthesis, secondary metabolism, and apoplastic oxidoreductase activity. These patterns suggest that transcriptional and post-transcriptional responses converge on extracellular redox and cell wall-associated defense processes. Together, our findings define a dynamic, multilayered regulatory landscape associated with ZmWAK-mediated quantitative resistance and provide insights into how resistance loci coordinate temporal immune responses during pathogen infection.
items.authors: He S, Liu Y, Fan W, Zhang Q, Deng S, Xu M.

items.title: The Anatomy of Phi Thickening Development in Brassica oleracea Roots.
items.abstract: In response to jasmonic acid, inner cortical cells in Brassica oleracea roots sequentially form two different secondary cell wall arrays. Initially, these cells develop phi thickenings, thick bands looped around the radial walls that are coordinated between adjacent cells to form a reinforcing scaffold. These thickenings develop later than the formation of the Casparian strip and protoxylem. Subsequently, inner cortical cells develop a reticulate network of delicate thickenings on their inner face adjacent to the endodermis. While phi thickenings initially develop in a single layer in the inner cortex, we demonstrate that multiple rings can develop in two ways, either through the occasional development of isolated thickenings in individual cells in the middle cortex, or through cell divisions in the endodermis that generate a new inner cortical layer which forms extensive phi thickenings. We also show that the phi thickening network in developing lateral roots remains separate from the network in the primary root, even as the Casparian strip re-forms a contiguous network. These anatomical observations have implications not only for understanding the developmental pathways leading to phi thickening formation but also for investigating the rare example of two different secondary wall structures being deposited in the same cell type.
items.authors: Collings DA, Aleamotuʻa M, McCurdy DW.

items.title: Two paralogous seed protein trait-associated genes influence light and phytohormone signaling, maturity, and seed storage in soybean.
items.abstract: The soybean gene Glyma.20G085100 (Gm20P), contributing to the cqSeed protein-003 QTL, and its paralog Glyma.10G134400 (Gm10P), were edited using the CRISPR/Cas9-based genome editing reagents. Two mutants, a gm20p single mutant and a gm10p gm20p double mutant devoid of editing reagents, were identified. Additional gm10p and gm20p single mutants were isolated from F2 population of the cross between the gm10p gm20p double mutant and the wild-type Thorne. The above mutants were characterized in different growing conditions. Seed protein content of the gm10p single and the gm10p gm20p double mutant were significantly reduced relative to the gm20p single mutant and Thorne, with a concomitant increase in oil and starch content. A delayed maturity phenotype was observed in the gm20p single, the gm10p single, and gm10p gm20p double mutants under field conditions across multiple environments. Under controlled conditions in a growth chamber, prominent delayed maturity was only observed under short-day conditions, while long-day conditions induced phenotypic changes in growth in the gm10p gm20p double mutant, but slight delay in maturity. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that the gm10p gm20p double mutant exhibited repression of genes involved in light signaling, enhanced expression of JAZs in JA signaling, suppression of ABA-responsive and senescence-related genes, and elevation of genes that inhibit IAA signaling. Furthermore, the gm10p gm20p double mutant displayed higher sensitivity to salt and ABA during germination. Collectively, these results suggest that both Gm10P and Gm20P modulate light signaling and impact soybean development, maturity and seed reserve content.
items.authors: Quach T, Nguyen H, Meyer O, Sato S, Yang W, Kumar V, McDaniel L, Hancock CN, Parrott W, Stacey MB, Hudson ME, Diers BW, Butler NM, Cahoon EB, Clemente TE, Zhang C, Guo M.

items.title: Transcriptomic and Epigenetic Reprogramming in Solanum tuberosum L. Micropropagation: A Systematic Review of Elicitor-Driven Acclimatization and Scalable Biofactories.
items.abstract: Solanumtuberosum L. relies heavily on in vitro propagation for pathogen-free seed tuber production; however, the transition to ex vitro environments causes severe plantlet mortality due to transplant shock. Exogenous elicitors have emerged as pivotal preconditioning tools, but their underlying molecular mechanisms remain fragmented. This systematic review aims to elucidate the translational architecture of elicitor-driven preconditioning in Solanum tuberosum, systematically organized across a tripartite continuum-(1) epigenetic chromatin plasticity, (2) transcriptomic defense reprogramming, and (3) scalable biofactory platforms (temporary immersion bioreactors and sensor-actuated aeroponics)-required to validate ex vitro physiological competence. Adhering to PRISMA 2020 guidelines for systematic reviews, we conducted a structured search across Scopus, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect (January 2010 to August 2026). Inclusion criteria targeted original research evaluating transcriptomic or epigenetic responses to in vitro elicitation in S. tuberosum. Following quality appraisal, data from 58 high-quality studies were synthesized using a critical narrative approach. The evidence is clearly stratified into our three core layers. (1) Transcriptomic Reprogramming: Exogenous elicitors systematically reactivate dormant defense networks prior to ex vitro transfer, converging strictly on salicylic acid (SA), jasmonic acid (JA), and ethylene (ET) signaling pathways alongside reactive oxygen species (ROS) detoxification. (2) Epigenetic Plasticity: Concurrently, morphological adaptation is heavily modulated by reversible chromatin remodeling; specifically, transient DNA hypomethylation and histone acetylation ensure in vitro cellular totipotency and stress memory. (3) Translational Scalability: Automated bioreactors and aeroponic platforms provide the essential physical microenvironment to validate these molecular outcomes and reverse vitrotype disorders at commercial scales. Elicitors drive an integrated tripartite preconditioning continuum that mitigates transplant shock and enables scalable hardening. We delineate a comprehensive translational framework to the transition from empirical micropropagation to targeted, genomics-informed biofactory platforms.
items.authors: Sarchi GAJ, Sarchi SAC, Ortega JIM, Hernández F, Martínez RTS.

items.title: Chloroplast dysfunction under engineered nanoparticle stress: consequences for photosynthesis and plant growth.
items.abstract: Annual production of engineered nanoparticles (ENPs) now exceeds thousands of metric tons because of their expanding applications in agriculture, waste management, and environmental technologies. This review provides a mechanistically integrated synthesis of ENP-induced chloroplast dysfunction and its downstream consequences for photosynthesis, plant growth, and reproduction. A bibliometric analysis of 239 publications (1983-2026) highlights a critical gap between primary empirical studies and integrative reviews, establishing a strong rationale for the present work. At the cellular level, the chloroplast is a central target of ENP toxicity within the broader context of whole-plant stress responses. Within the photosynthetic machinery, Photosystem II (PSII) is vulnerable; dissolved metal ions disrupt the Mn4CaO5 oxygen-evolving complex, while reactive oxygen species (ROS) accelerate D1 protein degradation and impair the PSII repair cycle. Under phytotoxic exposure conditions, ENP treatment is frequently associated with reduced Fv/Fm, impaired electron transport, and lower net photosynthetic rates. Furthermore, photosynthetic pigment content declines across species, impairing light harvesting and photoprotection. RuBisCO activity may be impaired through oxidative modification and, for some ENP types, through particle- or ion-associated effects on redox-sensitive protein residues. Transcriptomic analyses reveal coordinated downregulation of photosynthesis-associated genes, such as LHCB2.4 and chlorophyll biosynthesis loci, alongside miRNA-mediated post-transcriptional reprogramming. Integrated across the whole plant, these molecular disruptions culminate in biomass reductions, delayed flowering, and impaired germination. This review critically highlights the detrimental effects of high ENP doses on plant health and associated risks for agricultural productivity.
items.authors: Banerjee S, Anand V, Rajput P, Sen A, Paul S, Chernikova N, Alliluev I, Mandzhieva S, Minkina T, Rajput VD.

items.title: Single-cell insights into plant responses to biotic and abiotic stresses: cellular heterogeneity and regulatory mechanisms.
items.abstract: Plants are continuously challenged by biotic and abiotic stresses that compromise growth, productivity, and stress resilience. Although bulk omics approaches have identified numerous stress-responsive pathways, they obscure the cellular heterogeneity and spatial organization that underlie stress perception, signal transmission, and response execution. Single-cell and spatial omics now enable plant stress responses to be resolved at the levels of cell type, cell state, and spatial location. In this review, we synthesize recent applications of single-cell RNA sequencing, single-nucleus RNA sequencing, single-cell chromatin accessibility profiling, spatial transcriptomics, and emerging single-cell proteomics in plant stress biology. We systematically compare biotic and abiotic stresses in terms of spatial response patterns, cellular division of labor, cell-state transitions, and gene regulatory networks. Biotic stress typically generates localized, infection-centered immune landscapes characterized by sentinel-cell activation, vascular defense hubs, and receptor-triggered transcriptional cascades. In contrast, abiotic stress more commonly involves organ-scale homeostatic adjustment, developmental plasticity, and sustained growth-tolerance trade-offs. Despite these distinctions, both stress classes share core regulatory modules, including reactive oxygen species, hormone signaling, transcription factor networks, and vascular long-distance communication. We further discuss technical challenges related to protoplast and nuclei preparation, cell-type annotation, spatial resolution, and multimodal data integration. By linking stress-responsive genes to the specific cell types, states, and spatial domains in which they function, single-cell approaches provide a mechanistic framework for precision engineering and breeding of stress-resilient crops.
items.authors: Wang J, Li H, Wang Z, Xu L, Cheng Y.

items.title: Nanotechnology-Enabled Strategies for Enhancing Plant Abiotic Stress Tolerance.
items.abstract: Amid increasingly complex climate scenarios, abiotic stresses such as drought, extreme temperatures, and soil salinization have emerged as primary bottlenecks limiting the sustainable development of modern agriculture. Because of their unique nanoscale effects and physicochemical properties, nanoparticles (NPs) can penetrate plant tissue barriers, offering a novel approach to enhance crop resilience to environmental stresses. This review systematically summarizes the core mechanisms by which NPs enhance plant stress tolerance. NPs primarily mitigate the overaccumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and cellular oxidative stress by modulating antioxidant systems, thereby maintaining the physical integrity of photosynthetic apparatuses and cell membranes. Additionally, NPs regulate phytohormone signaling networks and the transcription of stress-responsive genes, while supporting ion compartmentalization and osmotic homeostasis in complex habitats such as coastal saline environments. Integrating multi-omics analyses, this review discusses plant metabolic responses to NPs and their dose-dependent toxicological effects. Addressing bottlenecks in practical application, we evaluate barriers to field-scale translation, the environmental release and migration of nanomaterials across water, air, and the food supply, and associated detection methods and safety risks, including the specific case of widely used silver nanoparticles. Future research must rely on multidisciplinary integration to optimize targeted delivery networks, premised on well-defined risk-assessment standards and viable cost-benefit balances, ultimately providing a scientific basis for enhancing agricultural climate resilience.
items.authors: Li Y, Hussain S, Wang L, Chen S, Wang W, Jing X, Wu Y, Liu J, Ulhassan Z, Khan MN.

items.title: Nuclear Architecture Related 1-Dependent H2 Reshapes Root Plasticity Through Targeting Root Meristem Cell Division Activity.
items.abstract: Root system architecture plasticity is critical for optimizing anchorage and nutrient and water uptake. However, whether and how biogenic molecular hydrogen (H2) influences root plasticity remains further explored. Here, using ABA-inhibited plant root growth as a research model, we show that Arabidopsis hydrogenase Nuclear Architecture Related 1 (NAR1)-dependent H2 reshapes root plasticity. First, we observed that NAR1 overexpression promotes primary root elongation and meristem cell division, whereas RNAi-NAR1 lines show impaired root growth, particularly upon ABA administration. Consistently, ABA-inhibited CYCB1;1 expression, a G2/M marker, was substantially recovered or aggravated in OE-NAR1 or RNAi-NAR1 lines. Further analysis revealed that NAR1 preserves DR5 activity, and AUX1, PIN1, and PIN2 signals under ABA. In parallel, NAR1 sustains cellular homeostasis by limiting ABA-triggered oxidative stress, as evidenced by upregulation of antioxidant defense and reduced ROS and lipid peroxidation. The functional requirement for NAR1-derived H2 was further corroborated by H2 supplementation, which effectively rescued the inhibited phenotypes of RNAi-NAR1 lines. Together, our findings reveal a convergence of meristem cell division activity, auxin signaling and ROS homeostasis governed by NAR1-dependent H2, which reshapes root plasticity under ABA treatment. These observations provide new molecular insights into endogenous H2 signaling for shaping plant plasticity in complex environments.
items.authors: Jiang K, Cheng P, Liu Z, Du H, Shen W.

items.title: The art of multi-tasking: plant responses to their environment.
items.abstract: Plant growth, development and survival are a continuous balancing act, integrating numerous environmental signals with core developmental programs. Nevertheless, in plant physiological research we usually study responses to the environment one factor at the time. It was the advent of microarray-based transcriptomics, and specifically the demonstration that combined treatments produce unique transcriptional signatures, that transformed stress combination into a defined molecular research program. We highlight how the field has evolved from the first seminal reports that combined severe abiotic stress treatments to a more comprehensive understanding of plant response to a range of conditions, including temperature, water availability, nutrients and light. We propose to broaden the conceptual framework from "combined stress" to a more inclusive consideration of context-dependent integration of environmental signals into responses. Integration of dose-, time- and location-dependent responses to the key plant hormones auxin, abscisic acid, ethylene and jasmonate are discussed. To further this research domain, we recommend accurate recording of environmental conditions and routine incorporation of treatment gradations, from mild to severe, in our research. Realizing this integrative view will require combining data-rich omics and machine-learning approaches with focused, hypothesis-driven experiments.
items.authors: Testerink C, Pierik R.

items.title: Nitrate metabolism and regulation of legume nitrogen fixation.
items.abstract: The interaction between nitrate and symbiotic nitrogen fixation is complex, diverse, and tightly regulated at multiple levels. The effects of nitrate are strongly dependent on the specific legume-rhizobia symbiosis and on the concentration and exposure time to nitrate. This has hampered studies on nitrate inhibition of nodule development and function. Here, we critically review most of the proposed mechanisms, which include carbohydrate deprivation, inactivation of nitrogenase and/or leghemoglobin by nitrite and/or nitric oxide, feedback regulation of nodule activity by an increase of nitrogenous metabolites in the phloem, and oxygen limitation through an oxygen diffusion barrier (ODB) mainly located in the inner cortex. Several hypotheses to explain the limitation of oxygen access to the nitrogen-fixing zone include glycoprotein occlusion of intercellular spaces, shifts in K+ and H2O2, and enhanced 'protective' respiration and activity of the ascorbate-associated enzymes in the cortical cells. Important progress has been made with the identification of nitrate transporters (NPF and NRT2 families) and transcription factors involved in nitrate regulation of nodulation (NIN, NLPs, and FUN) and in nitrate-induced nodule senescence (NAC094 and SNAP1/2/3/4). However, with the exception of a genetic study showing that suberin deposition in the endodermis is involved in nodule oxygen permeability, the molecular mechanisms underlying the ODB remain a mystery.
items.authors: Becana M, Duanmu D, Minchin FR, Chiurazzi M.

items.title: Cell-cycle-driven epigenetic resetting maintains meristematic cell fate for shoot branching.
items.abstract: Cell proliferation generally promotes differentiation, whereas proliferative quiescence maintains stem cell identity-a paradigm well-established in adult mammalian stem cells. Here we report that in Arabidopsis bud precursor cells, meristematic cell fate maintenance depends on active cell-cycle progression. We identify two opposing mechanisms that balance trimethylated histone H3 Lys27 levels to regulate transcription of the shoot meristem marker gene SHOOT MERISTEMLESS (STM). On one hand, two classes of transcription factors recruit Polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2) to epigenetically silence STM. On the other hand, cell proliferation reduces trimethylated histone H3 K27 levels to counteract this silencing. We demonstrate that inhibiting cell division suppresses STM expression and promotes differentiation. The interplay between these forces establishes a cell-cycle-coupled epigenetic resetting mechanism that sustains pluripotency. This cell fate switch is bistable; both modelling and experimental data confirm that prolonged quiescence triggers irreversible differentiation. We propose that in plants, sequence-dependent PRC2 recruitment enables precise silencing of fate-determining genes, while cell proliferation maintains pluripotency through periodic resetting of epigenetic marks.
items.authors: Guo Y, Yang Y, Shi B, Wang H, Cao X, Peng Z, He Y, Xiao J, Tao L, Umeda M, Sablowski R, Jiao Y, Wang Y.

items.title: Mycelial Production and Mycorrhizal Establishment of Terfezia arenaria and Tirmania pinoyi on Helianthemum canariense: A Morphological and Molecular Study.
items.abstract: Desert truffles are hypogeous edible fungi of ecological and economic importance in arid and semi-arid ecosystems, where they establish mycorrhizal associations with Helianthemum species. This study evaluated the effects of pH, culture medium, and fungal species on the apical growth and mycelial biomass production of Terfezia arenaria and Tirmania pinoyi under controlled conditions. Fungal identification was confirmed by sequencing the ITS region. Both species were cultured on Potato Dextrose Agar and Malt Extract Agar at four pH levels (4.55, 5.6, 6.0, and 6.5) at 28 °C. Mycelial biomass was further evaluated at pH 6.0 and 6.5, and the resulting mycelial suspensions (100 mL) were used to inoculate Helianthemum canariense seedlings under controlled conditions. The resulting suspension was applied directly to the root system of young seedlings at a rate of 20 mL per plant. The results revealed highly significant effects of pH and culture medium, slightly significant effects of fungal species, and highly significant interactions between all factors, including the three-way interaction medium, pH and fungal species. T. arenaria exhibited strong growth across all pH levels on PDA but showed marked inhibition on MEA at pH ≥ 6.0. In contrast, T. pinoyi responded more favorably to PDA than MEA at higher pH levels. For mycelial biomass production, no significant effect of species, pH, or medium was found when considered individually. However, a highly significant interaction was detected between species and solid-state culture for both wet- and dry-weight mycelium biomass production. T. arenaria has produced a greater biomass on MEA, while T. pinoyi performed better on PDA. In contrast, pH has shown no significant effect within the tested conditions. Inoculated H. canariense roots exhibited abundant fungal hyphae, vesicles, and endospores, together with a fungal mantle and Hartig net, confirming the establishment of a dual ectomycorrhizal-endomycorrhizal symbiosis. Overall, the results highlight strong species-specific responses and demonstrate that successful desert truffle cultivation requires optimization of culture medium and pH according to fungal species.
items.authors: Hicham K, Abdessamad T, Hamza K, Lahcen O.

items.title: Genetic determinants of Brevundimonas -mediated attenuation of plant pattern-triggered immunity
items.abstract: Root-associated commensal bacteria from diverse taxonomic groups can attenuate plant pattern-triggered immunity (PTI), yet the bacterial mechanisms underlying immune attenuation remain poorly understood. Brevundimonas sp. MF374 is a root-associated Alphaproteobacterium previously identified as a strong attenuator of flg22-triggered immunity. Here, to identify the genetic determinants underlying this phenotype, we conducted transposon mutagenesis and screened 4,032 MF374 mutants for defects in immune attenuation. Deletion and complementation of candidate loci identified tonB1 (BLR19_RS15045) as the strongest determinant of immune attenuation, with ppiD (BLR19_RS02880) making a weaker contribution. A panel of GUS reporter assays designed to distinguish among different mechanisms of attenuation showed that intact MF374 cells directly reduced the immune-eliciting activity of flg22 in a tonB1 -dependent manner. TonB1 also contributed to attenuation of responses triggered by a distinct flg22 sequence and the endogenous plant elicitor AtPEP1. Together, these findings implicate TonB-dependent transport in attenuation of flg22-induced immunity by MF374 and reveal a previously uncharacterized mechanism of immune attenuation by a root-associated commensal.
items.authors: Liao, C., Zheng, D., Zhang, A., Georges, J. C., Conway, J. M.

items.title: Near-Infrared Imaging of H2O2 in Plants With Nanosensors Under Environmentally Changing Conditions.
items.abstract: Optical sensors are powerful tools to monitor biological systems. However, their practical deployment is often limited by environmental interferences such as autofluorescence, mechanical motion, and fluctuating illumination. These challenges are particularly pronounced in plants because they require and use light, which has impaired the use of (fluorescent) sensors for plant stress signals such as H2O2. Here, we present a ratiometric sensing platform that overcomes these limitations by integrating three spectrally distinct components: 1) an H2O2 sensor based on aptamer modified near infrared (NIR) fluorescent single walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs, ∼1000 nm), 2) a stable NIR reference based on polyethyleneglycol modified Egyptian Blue nanosheets (EB-NS, 900-955 nm) and 3) a visible (VIS) signal (∼641 nm) to correct for the NIR autofluorescence tail of plants (>835 nm). This ratiometric approach enables robust signal correction under relevant perturbations, including leaf rotation and wind-induced motion. Furthermore, it allows continuous H2O2 monitoring under dynamically varying illumination conditions (>300%), resulting in a 75% enhancement in signal contrast compared to single-channel detection. By spectrally resolving nanosensor signals and endogenous plant autofluorescence, this strategy enables in vivo monitoring of stress-induced H2O2 under realistic environmental conditions. It establishes interference-resistant optical sensing and advances field-deployable nanosensor technologies for precision agriculture.
items.authors: Li J, Hill BF, Ma C, Gretz J, Kistwal T, Wartmann JAC, Metternich JT, Giraldo JP, Kruss S.

items.title: OsYchF1 suppresses OsEF1Bγ-mediated ER detoxification to co-involve the growth-maintenance trade-off in rice.
items.abstract: Translation elongation is a fundamental biological process, yet its direct role in stress adaptation remains unclear. In this study, we uncover a novel regulatory axis in rice involving the unconventional G protein OsYchF1, which gates the detoxification activity of the elongation factor 1Bγ (OsEF1Bγ) in the endoplasmic reticulum. OsEF1Bγ is a subunit of the eEF1B complex and possesses an N-terminal glutathione S-transferase (GST) domain. We demonstrate that overexpression of OsEF1Bγ enhances rice tolerance to osmotic and saline stress by lowering malondialdehyde levels, suggesting its role as a positive regulator via GST-mediated detoxification. Conversely, we found that OsYchF1 interacts with OsEF1Bγ across multiple domains. This interaction competitively inhibits the binding of reduced glutathione to OsEF1Bγ by approximately 40-fold, thereby suppressing its GST activity in vitro. Consistently, OsYchF1 knockout mutants phenocopy OsEF1Bγ overexpressors, displaying enhanced stress tolerance, reduced reactive oxygen species accumulation, and increased antioxidant enzyme activities. Furthermore, we show that stress-induced downregulation of OsYchF1 acts as a physiological trigger, releasing this molecular brake to enable rapid activation of OsEF1Bγ-mediated detoxification in response to challenging environments. Collectively, our findings reveal a post-translational mechanism where OsYchF1 serves as a molecular brake on the ER-localized detoxification engine of OsEF1Bγ, fine-tuning abiotic stress adaptation and establishing an unexpected link between the translation machinery and cellular redox homeostasis.
items.authors: Gao L, Yu L, Chen D, Li R, Wang Y, Liao Y, Meng Y, Li Q, Miao Y, Hao G, Miao R.
items.journal: The Plant journal : for cell and molecular biology

items.title: Analysis of Spatiotemporal Changes in Jasmonic Acid, Salicylic Acid, and Indole-3-Acetic Acid in Tea Plants Based on Silylation and Gas Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry.
items.abstract: Phytohormones play a vital role in plant responses to biotic stresses. Although phytohormone determination mainly employs ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (UHPLC-MS/MS), its high costs and technical requirements limit utility, whereas gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) is more widely used. To determine jasmonic acid (JA), salicylic acid (SA), and indole-3-acetic acid (IAA) in tea plants, a GC-MS method was developed, including selection of silylating reagents and establishment of metabolism quenching and purification methods. SA, JA, and IAA contents in tea leaves increased significantly after storage at -80 °C or extraction at room temperature. These increases were prevented by immersing samples in a 95 °C water bath. Quantification limits for SA, JA, and IAA were 0.020 ng mg-1, 0.015 ng g-1, and 0.015 ng g-1, similar to or exceeding those obtained by UHPLC-MS/MS. Recoveries and RSD were 93.1-98.9% and 2.1-9.9%, respectively. Only 10 mg of tea leaves was sufficient for simultaneous analysis of the three phytohormones. The JA response to geometrids was strong compared with the SA response, whereas the opposite trend was observed for leafhoppers. The systemic responses of JA and SA were rapid, similar to the local response. These results indicate that the proposed method is sensitive and reliable.
items.authors: Sun C, Hu K, Bian L, Luo Z, Li Z, Xiu C, Fu N, Chen Z, Gao Y, Cai X.

items.title: Coordinated cell division and growth drive meristem notch formation in Ceratopteris gametophytes.
items.abstract: Meristems drive organogenesis and shape plant body plans, yet their morphology and cellular organization vary widely across land plants. Fern gametophytes develop a multicellular meristem that initiates at one flat margin of the prothallus and progressively forms a distinctive concave notch, producing the characteristic cordate gametophyte. Despite its importance for gametophyte growth and sexual organ formation, the cellular basis of meristem notch morphogenesis remains unclear. Here, we address this question in the fern Ceratopteris richardii using long-term time-lapse confocal imaging, chemical perturbations, and quantitative analyses at single-cell resolution. We reconstructed complete cell lineages and generated dynamic maps of cell division, size, growth rate, and collective cell displacement throughout development. Our analyses reveal that position-specific cell proliferation and division patterns, coordinated with differential cell expansion and dynamic cell displacement between the notch-forming lineage and adjacent wing regions, drive notch morphogenesis. Chemical perturbations disrupting microtubule function or cell-cycle progression disrupted notch formation, demonstrating that coordinated cell division and growth are required. Together, these findings establish a quantitative cellular framework for understanding meristem morphogenesis across land plants.
items.authors: Yang X, Khoudari N, Yan A, Geng Y, Liu X, Volkening A, Zhou Y.

items.title: SbMYB44 transcription factor from halophyte Salicornia brachiata confers salt and drought tolerance through physio-biochemical, oxidative and molecular modulation in transgenics.
items.abstract: Abiotic stresses significantly disrupt the morphological, physiological and biochemical functions of plants, ultimately limiting crop productivity. Salicornia brachiata is a succulent halophyte that can grow in extreme saline conditions by manoeuvring molecular and physio-biochemical adaptations. MYB family transcription factors are involved in various metabolic and stress-responsive pathways, however, their functional characterization from Salicornia remains limited. Therefore, the present study functionally validate the R2R3-type MYB TF SbMYB44 isolated from S. brachiata. Overexpression of SbMYB44 in tobacco plants, conferred improved tolerance to salt and drought stress by modulating a various morpho-physiological, biochemical and molecular responses. Transgenic plants exhibited improved membrane stability, higher levels of photosynthetic pigments and increased elemental content, alongside reduced electrolyte leakage and sodium accumulation compared to wild-type (WT) plants under both stress conditions. Biochemically, SbMYB44 transgenic lines demonstrated elevated levels of osmolytes, phenolics and antioxidative enzymes activity, and decreased accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS). At the molecular level, SbMYB44 overexpression was associated with the upregulation of several stress-responsive genes under salt and drought stress. However, the detailed direct target-gene regulatory study by which SbMYB44 TF regulates these stress-responsive genes remains to be elucidated. Under stress conditions, SbMYB44 overexpression was associated with maintained pigments and ion homeostasis, enhanced accumulation of osmoprotectants and antioxidant enzyme activities, which may contribute to reduced oxidative damage and improved stress tolerance. Overall, present study shows that SbMYB44 overexpression strengthens the plant's ability towards abiotic stresses, suggesting potential applications in developing stress-resilient crops.
items.authors: Dangariya M, Agarwal P, Agarwal PK.
items.journal: Plant science : an international journal of experimental plant biology

items.title: Growth Promotion of Delayed-Transplanted Strawberry Plug Seedlings by Single- and Combined-Strain Inoculation of Bacillus spp.
items.abstract: Delayed transplanting of plug seedlings frequently causes root coiling and growth retardation in strawberry (Fragaria × ananassa), compromising transplant quality and commercial nursery performance. While plant growth-promoting bacteria (PGPB) are widely used to enhance crop growth and resilience, their effects on delayed-transplanted strawberry remain poorly understood. This study investigated the individual and combined effects of two Bacillus strains (KP3P9 and K13C) on the growth and root architecture of 12-week-old 'Benihoppe' strawberry plug seedlings, which had been delayed-transplanted for approximately 5-8 weeks. Moreover, root metabolomic profiles were analyzed to uncover metabolic reprogramming associated with Bacillus inoculation. Results showed that all Bacillus treatments promoted plant growth, enhanced fresh weight, and improved root development of delayed-transplanted strawberry. Metabolomic analysis revealed that all Bacillus treatments increased steroid levels but decreased flavonoids, ketones/aldehydes/esters, lignans, nucleotides, phenylpropanoids, and sugars in roots of delayed-transplanted strawberry plants. Furthermore, distinct metabolic signatures were found among treatments: the single KP3P9/K13C treatment elevated polyphenols and terpenoids; K13C uniquely increased alcohols, alkaloids, and coumarins, while their co-application (KK) specifically enhanced amino acid accumulation. KEGG enrichment analysis further revealed varied metabolic reprogramming: KP3P9 significantly enriched pantothenate and CoA biosynthesis, cornified envelope formation, and aminoacyl-tRNA biosynthesis; K13C enriched tyrosine metabolism and alpha-linolenic acid (ALA) metabolism, whereas KK specifically enriched flavonoid metabolism. This study reveals the promoting effects of single and combined KP3P9 and K13C applications and provides novel insights into the metabolic basis of Bacillus-mediated growth enhancement on delayed-transplanted strawberry.
items.authors: Liu F, Zhang L, Zhao H, Xia J, Guo S, Cheng C.

items.title: Synergistic effects of optimized foliar calcium silicate spray and NPK fertilization on growth, flowering, stem mechanical strength and vase life in herbaceous peony.
items.abstract: Herbaceous Peony (Paeonia lactiflora Pall.) is a high-value cut flower and landscape ornamental crop popular for its aesthetically appealing flowers. Its high global demand highlights the Western Himalayan region of India as a promising area for commercial floriculture. However, inadequate agronomic practices limit the quality and marketability of cut flower spikes. Thus, the present study evaluated the effect of soil-drenched NPK fertilization and foliar calcium sprays under field conditions on morpho-physio-biochemical responses, nutrient uptake, stem mechanical strength, and vase life of herbaceous peony. Soil was drenched with NPK (19:19:19) at 0.5 and 1.0 g L-1 concentration, whereas foliar sprays of calcium chloride (CC), calcium nitrate (CN), and calcium silicate (CS) were carried out at 0.5 and 1.0 g L-1 concentration. Among all treatments, 0.5 g L-1 NPK + 0.5 g L-1 CS yielded superior vegetative and reproductive growth, including improved plant height, stem diameter, flower number, flower diameter, and fresh weight. This optimized treatment enhanced photosynthetic performance, photosynthetic pigments, phenolics, flavonoids, and nutrient (N, P, K, and Ca) uptake and accumulation in plant tissues. Reduced stem bending was observed in treated cut spikes, as revealed by Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) analysis showing enhanced secondary cell wall thickening in xylem tissues. This was supported by increased calcium accumulation in stems, lignin deposition, associated with enhanced expression of key lignin biosynthesis-related genes, including PAL, CAD, COMT, CCR, and POD. Consequently, treated stems exhibited enhanced water uptake and prolonged vase life, supporting sustainable commercial floriculture and postharvest management of herbaceous peony.
items.authors: Bhardwaj R, Verma V, Priti, Thakur D, Gupta H, Shailja, Kumar A, Yadav SK, Bhargava B.

items.title: Artificial microRNAs against hypoxia-responsive small protein encoding genes reveal HRSP41 and 42 as regulators of development and stress tolerance.
items.abstract: BackgroundSmall proteins remain poorly characterized in Arabidopsis thaliana, partly because of genetic redundancy and the difficulty of identifying loss-of-function mutants. To address this gap, we investigated 58 hypoxia-responsive small protein genes (HRSPs) encoding proteins of 80-100 amino acids using a homology-based artificial microRNA (amiRNA) strategy.ResultsHomozygous amiRNA lines were screened for developmental traits and stress-related phenotypes. Two closely related paralogs, HRSP41 and HRSP42, emerged as key regulators with both shared and distinct functions. HRSP41 promoted flowering under short-day conditions, whereas HRSP42 delayed flowering and specifically increased seed tolerance to oxidative stress. Both genes acted together to reduce the inhibitory effect of abscisic acid on seed germination. Transcriptome profiling revealed distinct downstream effects: HRSP42 silencing was associated with repression of glutathione metabolism, whereas HRSP41 silencing affected glycerolipid metabolism and cell wall-related pathways. Under hypoxia, simultaneous downregulation of HRSP41 and HRSP42 altered transcriptional, post-transcriptional, and translational responses and intensified the repression of photosynthesis-related genes.ConclusionsDespite their high sequence similarity, HRSP41 and HRSP42 control plant development and stress adaptation through partially overlapping but clearly distinct molecular mechanisms. Our results identify these paralogs as previously uncharacterized regulators of flowering, oxidative stress responses, ABA sensitivity, and hypoxia-responsive gene expression.
items.authors: Castillo MC, Sánchez-Palomares S, León J.

items.title: Endosperm secretion remodels the maternal seed coat
items.abstract: In flowering plants and mammals, maternal tissues must accommodate the growth of the offspring they enclose. The maternal seed coat expands around the developing embryo and endosperm. Endosperm pressure and hormonal signals coordinate seed-coat development1,2, but whether the endosperm directly promotes maternal cell elongation remains unclear. Here we show that the coenocytic Arabidopsis endosperm directly supplies cell-wall-loosening proteins to maternal seed-coat walls. The seed-size-regulating HAIKU-WRKY10 pathway activates an endosperm secretory programme enriched in cell-wall-associated proteins. These proteins spread through a shared extracellular domain across multiple inner seed-coat layers, revealing an extensive functional maternal-filial interface through which the endosperm reaches maternal cells it does not directly contact. Among these proteins, three expansins are necessary and sufficient for maternal cell elongation and seed growth. The endosperm therefore promotes its own growth by enabling expansion of the maternal tissues that enclose it. Paternal DNA methylation and maternal Polycomb activity jointly regulate this programme, with Polycomb also required for timely shutdown of expansin expression. These findings link parental epigenetic states to maternal tissue expansion through proteins supplied by the offspring. This cross-generational control of growth parallels epigenetically regulated signaling from mammalian extraembryonic tissues3, suggesting a shared strategy for adapting the maternal environment to offspring development.
items.authors: Ke, Y., Guo, W., Tang, Y., Li, Y., Zhu, Y., Xi, X., Meng, M., Wang, Z., Axelsson, E., Ye, H., Xia, C., Xie, W., Yao, J., Zhu, Y., Lv, P., Zhao, P., Sun, M.-x., Berger, F., Xu, R., Li, J.

items.title: Nucleoredoxin Proteins in green lineage: Insights about its Roles in Biotic and Abiotic Stress Resilience.
items.abstract: Oxidative stress and reactive oxygen species (ROS) in plants are inevitable, and plants employ enzymatic and non-enzymatic system for cell homeostasis. Nucleoredoxins (NRX) are a family of thioredoxin (TRX) superfamily and being nuclear oxidoreductase, NRX are an important class of proteins present in many organisms including plants. Unlike TRXs, plant NRXs are larger proteins comprising of multiple TRX domains and conserved active redox motif 'WCPPC', displayed evolutionary conservation across various plants. NRX maintains oxidative stress tolerance by maintaining the reduced state by thiol-disulphide chemistry via conserved cysteine residues present in active site. Subcellular localization of NRX is mostly cytoplasmic and the putative protein interacting partners predicted their correlation with oxidative stress tolerance. We have also attempted to correlate plant NRXs with the available patent documents and observed that very little information is available. Compared to TRX research that started in 1960s, NRX have been discovered later and their structural complexity, multiple isoforms have led to their functional characterization more challenging. NRXs have roles in abiotic and biotic stresses and emerging roles indicate its role in plant immunity and modulation of plant defense response at molecular level by -OMICS studies. In view of the above, the present review discusses the sequence analysis, structure, and functional genomics associated with NRXs in plants. This is also correlated with the futuristic aspect of NRX roles being delineated in molecular stress response and signaling using CRISPR-Cas genome editing and related techniques.
items.authors: Gupta A, Thakur R, Yadav S.
items.journal: Plant science : an international journal of experimental plant biology

items.title: Identification of Calcium-Sensing Receptor (CAS) as a Phytaspase Interactor: Implications for the CAS Trafficking Pathway.
items.abstract: Proteolytic enzymes play important and diverse roles in regulating protein homeostasis in living cells. Phytaspase, a member of the plant subtilisin-like protease family possessing a 'caspase-like' selectivity and specificity of hydrolysis of its targets, is a cell death-related protease. Phytaspase displays a peculiar trafficking pattern and is involved in the execution of plant cell death induced by biotic and abiotic stresses. To elucidate the molecular mechanisms of phytaspase functioning, a search for Nicotiana tabacum phytaspase (NtPhyt)-interacting proteins was performed using the BioID approach. This search identified the calcium-sensing receptor (CAS) protein as a candidate NtPhyt interactor. Direct interaction of NtPhyt with N. tabacum CAS (NtCAS) was corroborated by an in vitro analysis utilizing the purified proteins. Furthermore, NtPhyt was shown to introduce five cleavages in the CAS molecule in vitro. For NtCAS-EGFP produced in N. benthamiana leaves, dual localization to chloroplasts and the cell periphery, including the plasma membrane, was observed, whereas NtPhyt proteolytic activity was undetectable in the chloroplasts. A CAS precursor protein apparently preserving the chloroplast transit peptide was found to accumulate upon a light-to-dark transition and to disappear in the presence of elevated levels of NtPhyt. A requirement for CAS for stress-induced retrograde transport of NtPhyt was uncovered, and partial co-localization of CAS with NtPhyt was observed in cells subjected to oxidative stress. Our results are consistent with the model according to which CAS transiently localizes to the plasma membrane as an intermediate location on its way to its final destination, the chloroplasts, and interacts with NtPhyt at this stage.
items.authors: Litvinova AV, Pigidanov AA, Torosian TA, Zgoda VG, Serebryakova MV, Kovaleva IE, Mamedov MD, Golyshev SA, Safronov GG, Chichkova NV, Vartapetian AB.

items.title: Coordinated suppression of photosynthesis- and nitrogen-related gene expression is associated with Citrus bark cracking viroid stunting in hop
items.abstract: Abstract Background. Citrus bark cracking viroid (CBCVd, Cocadviroid rimocitri ) causes severe stunting in hop ( Humulus lupulus L.), but the host response has rarely been resolved across disease stages. We asked how the hop transcriptome changes between early and late season and how this relates to the whole-plant phenotype. Results. In a 2 × 2 factorial RNA-seq experiment (CBCVd-infected vs. CBCVd-free controls × 2 post-dormancy timepoints, sampled in spring and summer, 18 and 21 months post-inoculation, respectively), with differential expression cross-validated against a second hop genome and validated by RT-qPCR and Sanger sequencing, the response was broader in May (162 differentially expressed genes, DEGs) than in August (12 DEGs), although biomass deficit was larger at the later timepoint. Only one gene, a glycine-rich cell-wall structural protein, was significant at both timepoints; the largest and most consistent suppression was found for two high-affinity nitrate-transporter (NRT2.5-like) loci, each significant at one of the two timepoints. Viroid titre was at similar height at both timepoints. At the whole-plant level, infected plants showed a leaf-chlorophyll deficit (9 % in May, 14 to 17 % from late July) and strongly reduced biomass accumulation (3 to 16 % of the control biomass across the season), in line with the transcriptome. GSEA identified coordinated suppression of photosynthesis and chloroplast function together with nitrate assimilation as the dominant signature at both timepoints, alongside repressed cell-wall and starch/sucrose metabolism. Cytosolic ribosome and translation programmes were suppressed in May but rebounded by August (treatment × timepoint interaction at pathway level), pointing to a temporal switch even as the suppression of photosynthesis- and nitrogen-related genes persisted. Conclusions. Our data suggest that at the two analysed timepoints CBCVd-associated stunting is accompanied by an early, coordinated transcriptional suppression of photosynthesis- and nitrogen-related genes rather than the immune-signalling-dominated response reported in other viroid studies. The growth deficit is already established at the spring sampling and persists through the season. The two NRT2.5-like loci are among the strongest and most consistent molecular correlates (log₂FC about −4 in May and −7 in August); whether they contribute to stunting or result from it, and whether they are useful as markers, remains to be tested.
items.authors: Hagemann M, Jagani S, Born U, Jakše J.

items.title: Characterization of the MeWRKY12-MeSSIV Regulatory Module and MeWRKY12 Promoter Activity in Cassava.
items.abstract: BackgroundSoluble starch synthases are essential for starch formation, but their transcriptional regulation remains poorly understood in cassava. Starch synthase IV (SSIV) is an important enzyme in starch biosynthesis, and this study aimed to investigate the transcriptional regulation of cassava MeSSIV.MethodsYeast one-hybrid, transcriptional activation, subcellular localization, and dual luciferase assays were performed to evaluate MeWRKY12 binding to and activation of the MeSSIV promoter. Quantitative real-time PCR was used to analyze MeWRKY12 expression in different tissues. Histochemical staining and quantitative GUS assays were conducted using proMeWRKY12 reporter plants grown under field conditions for six months. Promoter responses to abscisic acid (ABA), methyl jasmonate (MeJA), and gibberellic acid (GA3) were examined in storage root slices.ResultsMeWRKY12 bound to the tested MeSSIV promoter region in yeast, exhibited transcriptional activation activity, localized to the nucleus, and enhanced MeSSIV promoter activity in plant cells. MeWRKY12 transcript abundance was highest in storage roots. GUS activity was also highest in storage roots, followed by fibrous roots. Histochemical staining revealed broad promoter activity in vascular, cambial, and parenchymatous tissues, including the xylem parenchyma of storage roots. Promoter activity increased following ABA, MeJA, and GA3 treatments, with distinct temporal response patterns.ConclusionsThese findings provide evidence at the promoter level supporting MeWRKY12 as a candidate positive regulator of MeSSIV transcription and reveal variation in proMeWRKY12 activity across tissues and hormone treatments. This study provides a basis for investigating WRKY transcription factors in the regulation of starch biosynthesis in cassava.
items.authors: Guo YQ, Lu XH, Wang YH, Wang LH, Wang Y, Guo WY, Li RM, Liu J, Yao Y, Guo JC, Wang YJ, Geng MT.

items.title: The endophytic fungi as natural elicitors of secondary metabolites, antioxidant enzymes, physiological traits, and associated genetic indicators of Polygonatum sibricum
items.abstract: Abstract This study explores the impact of four fungal endophytes, Fusarium oxysporum, Aspergillus terreus, Alternaria alternata, and Penicillium chrysogenum, on the metabolics, antioxidants, physiological, and genetic traits of Polygonatum sibiricum. The experiment performed in randomized complete block design (RCBD) and fungal strains were applied to plants through root dipping. The results indicated significant (p≤0.05) variations in secondary metabolites, physiological traits and antioxidant enzyme activities. F. oxysporum illustrated the significant rise alkaloids, saponins, phenolics, and antioxidant enzyme activities (POD, SOD, CAT). Likewise, P. chrysogenum significantly enhanced flavonoid content, and A. terreus showed a marked increase in terpenoids, while A. alternata depicted mild impact on saponins and phenolics. Additionally, fungal treatments significantly influenced Pn and chl content, with F. oxysporum resulting in the highest net Pn and chl. Gene expression analysis showed that F. oxysporum and P. chrysogenum significantly (p≤0.05) upregulated the defense-related genes, such as PAL, CYP450 and BAS, correlating with enhanced secondary metabolite production. Furthermore, the correlation analysis and principal component analysis (PCA) confirmed strong relationship between fungal treatments and plants metabolic, physiological and genetic responses. Besides, these results further illustrated the potential of fungal endophytes as natural modulators for enhancing plant physiological, biochemical and molecular ability that reshape overall response of P. sibricum.
items.authors: Alzahrani Y, Alsamadany H.

items.title: Mangrove-Derived Halotolerant Endophytic Bacteria Confer Strain-Specific and Consortium-Mediated Salt Tolerance in Peanut (Arachis hypogaea L.).
items.abstract: Soil salinity is a major abiotic stress that severely limits crop productivity worldwide. This study evaluated the potential of halotolerant endophytes isolated from mangrove plants to enhance salinity tolerance in the peanut (Arachis hypogaea L. cv. JL24). A two-step approach, including screening and validation methods, was applied. Initially, six mangrove endophytes, ACR52, EAR173, EAR191, EAR195, EAL318, and ACL463, were tested for their capacity to colonize the non-host peanut. Histochemical detection of gusA-tagged derivatives confirmed early tissue-associated colonization of peanut seedlings by all six isolates. Seed inoculation of six endophytes improved germination under severe salinity, with ACR52 maintaining 83% final germination at 200 mM NaCl, compared with 67% in the uninoculated controls. The six-strain consortium accelerated germination, giving the highest germination at every NaCl level on Days 1 and 4. Among the isolates, EAL318 (Bacillus subtilis), EAR195 (Proteus mirabilis), and ACR52 (Klebsiella quasipneumoniae subsp. similipneumoniae) exhibited strong PGP traits and were selected for further evaluation. In greenhouse experiments with 300 and 500 mM NaCl, inoculated plants showed significantly higher plant height (32-40% increase), shoot dry weight (28-35% increase), and chlorophyll content (20-30% increase) compared with uninoculated controls. Under severe greenhouse salinity, ACR52 showed the most consistent preservation of reproductive performance, whereas C3 produced the broadest antioxidant response, with elevated CAT and POD activities and reduced H2O2 and MDA accumulation. These findings identify mangrove-derived endophytes as potential candidates for future field evaluation under saline-soil conditions.
items.authors: Yammanuri N, Chinreddy SR, Naik Kt P, Vallepu VB, Akila CS, Puli COR.

items.title: Glutamate promotes cold tolerance through CsGLR3.2- and Ca2+-associated CBF signaling in tea plants.
items.abstract: Low temperature limits the productivity and quality of tea plants, particularly when spring cold spells damage vulnerable young shoots. However, the metabolic signals that regulate C-repeat binding factor (CBF)-mediated cold responses remain unclear. Time-series metabolomic analysis revealed progressive glutamate accumulation in cold-treated tea shoots, accompanied by a marked decline in theanine content. Exogenous glutamate enhanced cold tolerance in tea shoots. By contrast, co-silencing of CsGGT2 and CsGGT4 attenuated cold-induced glutamate accumulation and compromised cold tolerance, indicating that CsGGT2/CsGGT4-associated theanine turnover contributes to cold-induced glutamate accumulation. Silencing CsGLR3.2 attenuated the protective effect of glutamate and reduced glutamate-enhanced CsCBF1-CsCBF4 expression. Pharmacological treatments provided complementary support for the involvement of GLR- and Ca2+-associated signaling in this response. Transcriptomic analysis further showed that glutamate altered the expression of genes associated with flavonoid biosynthesis and redox homeostasis. Collectively, these findings connect the characteristic theanine metabolism of tea plants with cold-responsive glutamate signaling and support a model in which glutamate enhances CsCBF expression through CsGLR3.2- and Ca2+-associated signaling. Glutamate metabolism and GLR-associated signaling therefore represent potential targets for improving cold tolerance in tea plants.
items.authors: Zhang X, Fu Q, He M, Fang J, Zhang Y, Hao Y, Yang Y, Ye M, Ding C, Li N, Wang L, Zeng J, Dai W, Wang X, Huang J.

items.title: Structural determinants of hydrogen peroxide tolerance in plant peroxidases: Distinct H2O2 accommodation and electrostatic profiles.
items.abstract: Hydrogen peroxide is both the oxidizing substrate of plant peroxidases and a major cause of their irreversible inactivation. Understanding how structurally related peroxidases accommodate H2O2 is therefore relevant to enzyme robustness and catalytic performance. Here, three class III plant peroxidases, horseradish peroxidase (HRP), peanut peroxidase (PNP), and royal palm tree peroxidase (RPTP) were compared using a reproducible structure-based workflow that evaluated heme geometry, distal-pocket accessibility, geometry-constrained H2O2 sampling, protein-derived electrostatic potentials, and residue-level peroxide contacts. Relative heme exposure differed substantially among the enzymes, with HRP showing the lowest exposure and RPTP the highest, indicating that cofactor burial alone does not account for their distinct peroxide responses. Geometry-constrained sampling revealed a markedly smaller population of sterically allowed and productive-like H2O2 configurations in HRP than in PNP and RPTP. Across independent sampling seeds, productive-like configurations represented 23.1% of allowed poses in HRP, 66.8% in PNP, and 78.1% in RPTP. Electrostatic analysis further distinguished RPTP by a predominantly positive distal-to-proximal potential difference across productive-like configurations, whereas HRP and PNP showed predominantly negative values. Residue-contact analysis confirmed conservation of the catalytic His42-Arg38 framework and indicated stronger local steric restriction around Phe41 in HRP. Taken together, these results show that the three enzymes differ in how their distal heme environments accommodate H2O2 and suggest that peroxide tolerance reflects a combination of accessibility, local geometry, and electrostatic organization rather than heme burial alone. These structural trends are qualitatively consistent with published biochemical evidence on peroxide processing and inactivation.
items.authors: Castillo JJ.

items.title: Genome-wide identification of the CPA family in Ipomoea pes-caprae reveals their roles in salt stress tolerance and ion homeostasis regulation.
items.abstract: High soil salinity is a major environmental constraint that limits global agricultural productivity and plant development. The current research aimed to perform a comprehensive assessment of the cation/proton antiporter (CPA) gene family in the highly adaptable coastal halophyte beach morning glory (Ipomoea pes-caprae (L.) R. Br.). Thirty-two CPA genes were identified across 15 chromosomes and categorized into three distinct subfamilies: sodium/hydrogen exchanger (NHX), potassium efflux antiporter (KEA), and cation/hydrogen exchanger (CHX). To characterize the regulatory architecture and transcriptional dynamics during high-salinity exposure, promoter evaluations and quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) analyses were utilized. Computational scanning of upstream regulatory sequences revealed a high abundance of cis-acting motifs linked to environmental adversity and phytohormone signaling in CPA gene promoters. Transcriptomic and RT-qPCR expression profiles further demonstrated that the CPA genes display organ-specific and temporally dynamic expression under high-salinity conditions. Functional validation was performed through heterologous overexpression of selected genes (IpcNHX2, IpcKEA6, IpcCHX3, and IpcCHX5) in Arabidopsis, and this overexpression significantly enhanced the salt tolerance of transformed lines during extreme saline treatments (up to 150 mM NaCl). Physiological analyses further demonstrated that IpcCPA overexpression improved biomass maintenance and promoted ionic homeostasis by reducing Na + accumulation, maintaining higher K+ levels, and increasing the K+/Na+ ratio under salt stress. Furthermore, yeast complementation assays revealed that these CPA proteins partially restored the growth defect of the potassium-deficient CY162 mutant for growth defect of the potassium-deficient CY162 mutant, suggesting their potential involvement in potassium homeostasis. In summary, this study provides a comprehensive genomic evaluation of the CPA family in I. pes-caprae, highlights the potential roles of CPA members in salt stress adaptation, and offers valuable candidate genes for crop improvement.
items.authors: Lin X, Qu T, Chen X, Li X, Wang X, Zhang M, Li X, Wu T, Si S, Feng H, Hu J, Cai J, Yang S, Pan C, Wang L, Niu X, Qin Y, Cheng Y.

items.title: Botrytis cinerea uses effective detoxification mechanisms to overcome the plant RBOHD-dependent extracellular oxidative burst.
items.abstract: The necrotrophic fungus Botrytis cinerea rapidly kills host tissue with its secreted proteins and metabolites. Necrotrophs can trigger the hypersensitive response, which is accompanied by reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, but it remains unclear whether this ROS burst promotes or restricts B. cinerea infection. We have combined Arabidopsis RESPIRATORY BURST OXIDASE HOMOLOG D (RBOHD) mutant analysis, luminol-based in vivo assays, and the use of CRISPR/Cas9-generated B. cinerea ROS detoxification mutants to analyze the toxic effect of the ROS burst. In addition, RNA-sequencing, transcript analyses and redox imaging were used to study RBOHD-dependent signaling and redox homeostasis. RBOHD mutants showed slightly increased susceptibility to B. cinerea infection, and the apoplastic ROS burst was found to be dependent on RBOHD. Fungal mutants confirmed the importance of SOD1 and AP1 for ROS detoxification and virulence. Unexpectedly, the transcriptomes of B. cinerea-infected Arabidopsis Col-0 and an activation-impaired RBOHD mutant were highly similar 48 hours after inoculation, providing no evidence for a connection of extracellular ROS production and intracellular ROS-induced transcriptional signaling. Nevertheless, RBOHD activity was found to be involved in the maintenance of cellular redox homeostasis under phytotoxic stress. Our results indicate a protective role of the RBOHD-dependent oxidative burst against B. cinerea, but this can be overcome by the fungus via different ROS detoxification mechanisms.
items.authors: Vielba-Fernandez A, Sommer L, Ross D, Ingelfinger J, Wachtmeister T, Hecht J, Safari N, Müller-Schüssele SJ, Hahn M.

items.title: Integrated Transcriptomic and Proteomic Analyses Reveal Wheat Responses Associated with High-Temperature All-Stage Resistance to Puccinia striiformis f. sp. tritici.
items.abstract: The obligate biotrophic fungus Puccinia striiformis f. sp. tritici (Pst) frequently overcomes host immunity through rapid evolution. The wheat landrace Paozimai exhibits high-temperature all-stage resistance (HTAS) to Pst, a type of resistance expressed at relatively high temperatures across all growth stages. In this study, we investigated host-pathogen interactions using integrated transcriptomic and data-independent acquisition proteomic analyses. Dual RNA-seq analysis at 192 and 216 h post-inoculation (hpi) revealed a shift in enriched Pst pathways during the late latent period, from endoplasmic reticulum protein processing and fatty acid metabolism at 192 hpi to carbohydrate and glutathione metabolism at 216 hpi. In the host, differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were enriched in defense-related signaling pathways at 192 hpi and in metabolic pathways at 216 hpi. Co-expression network analysis identified ribosomal and protein biosynthesis processes that may contribute to defense. Proteomic analysis showed greater overlap across time points, with oxidative phosphorylation enriched at 192 hpi and glycan biosynthesis at 216 hpi. Furthermore, integrated multi-omics and co-expression network analysis identified 16 candidate wheat genes, including genes encoding ribosomal proteins and stress-response proteins. These findings describe temperature-associated host and pathogen responses during HTAS and nominate candidates for functional validation.
items.authors: Su C, Lyu X, Tu Y, Lu D, Li G, Ma D, Zhang S, Yang L, Li C, Hu Y.

items.title: Cold Tolerance in Alfalfa: Physiological Mechanisms, Regulatory Networks, and Molecular Breeding Prospects.
items.abstract: Alfalfa (Medicago sativa L.) is a perennial legume forage whose winter survival determines stand persistence, spring green-up, and long-term yield in cold regions. Low-temperature stress causes membrane phase transitions, cellular dehydration, impaired photosynthetic electron transport, and excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation. Tolerance depends on coordinated antioxidant protection, osmotic adjustment, membrane stabilization, photosynthetic maintenance, and carbon-nitrogen allocation to the root crown. At the molecular level, this process is mediated by calcium ion signaling, phytohormone pathways, and the cold-responsive ICE-CBF/DREB-COR regulatory cascade. Reported molecular resources include calmodulin-like protein modules (MsCML10 and MsCML50), CBF/DREB factors, autophagy and circadian regulators, sugar-metabolism genes, and genes from yellow-flowered alfalfa. This review integrates low-temperature injury, physiological responses, molecular regulatory networks, evaluation methods, genetic resources, and breeding progress. It emphasizes that evidence strength differs among cultivated-alfalfa functional studies, heterologous validation, and omics-based candidate discovery. Major gaps include inconsistent phenotyping, insufficient root-crown and overwintering-bud characterization, limited validation under natural overwintering, and weak translation of candidate genes into breeding populations. Future research should combine standardized multi-environment phenotyping with multi-omics, functional validation in alfalfa, marker development, genomic selection, and multi-trait improvement of cold tolerance, yield, forage quality, and stress adaptation.
items.authors: Yang W, Shi X, Lu J, Liu X.

items.title: The plant nuclear mechanome: nuclear envelope-chromatin mechanics in environmental stress sensing, memory and recovery.
items.abstract: Plant responses to drought, salinity, heat and mechanical loading are usually interpreted through hormones, redox signals and transcriptional networks, but these frameworks incompletely capture the physical state of the nucleus. In wall-bounded, turgor-driven plant cells, environmental and growth-derived forces can be transmitted through the cytoskeleton to the nuclear envelope, nucleoskeleton and chromatin. Evidence from osmotic and heat-stress studies indicates that nuclear shape, stiffness, lamina organization, peripheral chromatin tethering and three-dimensional genome architecture are stress responsive. We synthesize these findings into the concept of the plant nuclear mechanome: an integrated system comprising nuclear geometry, viscoelasticity, envelope-cytoskeleton coupling, lamin-like scaffolds, nuclear pores, chromatin organization and nuclear-body dynamics. We propose that this system acts as a tunable interface that can buffer, transmit or amplify mechanical inputs and thereby influence chromatin accessibility, transcriptional competence, acclimation, stress memory and recovery. Particular attention is given to nuclear envelope and nucleoskeletal modules that may connect force transmission with genome regulation. We distinguish established observations from mechanistic hypotheses and outline experiments combining realistic stress treatments, live nuclear imaging, quantitative mechanics, targeted genetic perturbation, single-nucleus omics and physiological validation. This framework positions nuclear mechanics as a testable dimension of plant cell biology and environmental adaptation.
items.authors: Ali S, Naseem MT, Zaman W.

items.title: RDAR biofilm formation and in silico analysis of putative amyloid proteins in Azospirillum baldaniorum Sp245.
items.abstract: Azospirillum baldaniorum Sp245 is a plant growth-promoting rhizobacterium (PGPR) whose ability to benefit host crops depends on robust root colonization, a process driven by the transition from a planktonic state to a sessile, biofilm-associated lifestyle. This study investigated the capacity of A. baldaniorum Sp245 to form Red, Dry, and Rough (RDAR) morphotype biofilms. Through macroscopic evaluation and confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM), we visualized the presence of exopolysaccharides, putative amyloid proteins, and extracellular DNA (eDNA) within the RDAR biofilm matrix using Calcofluor White (CFW), Thioflavin S (TS), and Propidium Iodide (PI) fluorescent probes, respectively. Furthermore, formic acid treatment of extracellular matrix proteins extracts suggests the presence of resistant, putative amyloid proteins. Because genomic screening revealed the absence of homologs of a canonical curli-dependent amyloid system, we performed a genome-wide in silico analysis to identify genes encoding alternative biofilm-associated proteins. Using the Staphylococcus aureus Biofilm-Associated Protein (Bap protein) as a reference, we identified 20 candidate proteins characterized by extensive domain reiteration and diverse architectures, including bacterial immunoglobulin (Ig-like) domains, VCBS repeats, SWM motifs, DUF4347, PKD domains, and RTX β-roll structures. Three-dimensional modeling indicates that these candidates possess elongated, filament-like conformations with repetitive β-strand motifs typical of amyloid-like assembly and calcium-dependent adhesion. These findings suggest that in the absence of traditional curli machinery, A. baldaniorum Sp245 could be using a diverse, domain-rich repertoire of alternative matrix proteins to facilitate cell surface interactions, coordinate structural stability, and establish the RDAR biofilm morphotype. Ultimately, this study establishes a foundation for understanding the role of amyloid proteins in Azospirillum biofilm matrix formation and offers new insights into the potential mechanisms of bacterial persistence and ecological fitness in the rhizosphere.
items.authors: Cortés-Sotres DR, Xiqui-Vázquez ML, Reyes-Carmona SR, Barrera-Olvera NG, Baca BE, Mancilla-Simbro C, Ramírez-Mata A.

items.title: Characterization and Multiplicity of Infection: Xanthomonas Oryzae Bacteriophages XOPW and XOP2 for Biofilm Control
items.abstract: Abstract Xanthomonas oryzae is a bacterial pathogen that causes leaf blight disease (BLB), a devastating rice disease that is globally epidemic and causes significant crop losses of 50%. This bacterium shows resistance to antibiotics and chemicals because of the misuse of chemicals and antibiotics, so bacteriophages are used as an alternative treatment against X. Oryzae. Bacteriophages are considered biocontrol agents because they target specific bacterial strains and lyse bacteria rapidly, controlling infection. For the first time, the current study was designed to isolate and characterize the specific lytic bacteriophage against X. oryzae from Hazara Division, Shinkiari, KPK Province, Pakistan, the major cause of BLB in rice, as well as evaluate the efficiency of bacteriophages in terms of multiplicity of infection for controlling X. Oryzae infection. In this study, all isolated phages showed a very narrow host range; XOPW and XOP2 infect only X. oryzae. All phages showed excellent stability at pH 6–8 while phage treatment was for 1 hour. Heat treatment results showed that even a 1-hour exposure at 80 o C has a significant effect on phage stability, and phages become completely inactivated. Phages tolerated 60 o C heat treatment to varying degrees, resulting in a 2–3 log reduction in titer. Similarly, heat treatment at 50 o C had a minor effect on phage titer. Phages suspended in SM buffer stored at 4 o C showed a minor reduction in titer even after three months of storage. According to the findings, isolated phages were causing bacterial lysis by forming transparent plaques. The MOI studies were conducted at MOI 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, and 100, and the spectrophotometric technique was used to record the net decrease in the bacterial population. Phages XOP2 and XOPW showed diverse levels of efficacy, with bacterial growth being significantly suppressed at various MOIs. The isolated bacteriophages were highly effective at reducing the growth of bacteria. At MOI 1, 10, and 100, a slow but moderate decline in bacterial growth over time was seen in comparison to other MOI levels. 1, 10, and 100, bacterial growth was comparatively unchanged until 20 hours, remaining nearly parallel to the control. The XOPW and XOP2 phage effectively reduced the optical density (OD) of a 4-day-old biofilm in a dose-dependent and time-dependent manner. At all-time points (6, 8, and 24 hours), the higher concentration of phage (MOI 1) consistently resulted in a lower OD compared to the lower concentration (MOI 0.1). The antibacterial activity of all phages was sustained, despite some partial resistance, indicating their potential for therapeutic use. In this pressing situation, employing phages as a therapeutic tool to combat antibiotic-resistant X. oryzae provides another approach.
items.authors: ullah Z, Khan I, Alvi IA.

items.title: Gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA): an integrative metabolite connecting plant growth, metabolism, and stress adaptation.
items.abstract: Gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), a ubiquitous non-protein amino acid, has emerged as an important integrative metabolite and signaling regulator in plants. Initially studied mainly as an intermediate of carbon and nitrogen metabolism, GABA is now known to participate in developmental regulation and stress responses. Its cellular abundance is shaped primarily by the GABA shunt and polyamine-degradation pathways and is further controlled by Ca2+/calmodulin signaling, pH, transcriptional regulation, transport, and environmental cues. GABA has been associated with seed germination, vegetative growth, reproductive development, and fruit ripening, but the strength of evidence differs among processes. Direct molecular evidence for GABA signaling is best established for regulation of aluminum-activated malate transporter (ALMT) anion channels, whereas many reported interactions with phytohormones, redox signals, and stress responses are supported mainly by genetic, pharmacological, metabolic, or exogenous-application studies. Under drought, salinity, temperature extremes, metal stress, and pathogen challenge, changes in endogenous GABA metabolism and exogenous GABA application are frequently associated with improved osmotic adjustment, antioxidant capacity, ion homeostasis, and stress-responsive metabolism. This review synthesizes current knowledge of GABA metabolism, transport, developmental functions, signaling crosstalk, and stress adaptation. To connect these areas without overstating causality, we propose a three-layer GABA-centered working framework comprising upstream regulation of GABA homeostasis, GABA-dependent metabolic and transport processes, and downstream hormonal and physiological reprogramming. We also identify major unresolved questions concerning GABA perception beyond ALMTs, subcellular compartmentalization, direct molecular targets, context-dependent responses, and translation to field applications.
items.authors: Liu S, Zhou M, Sun C, Liu Y, Zhu F, Rhaman MS, Xie Y.

items.title: Physiological Responses and Transcriptome Analysis of 'Hanfu' Apple Plants Under PEG-Simulated Drought Stress.
items.abstract: Drought stress constitutes a major constraint on apple growth, development, and yield. Although drought responses have been extensively studied in apple, the early physiological and transcriptomic responses of 'Hanfu', a cultivar widely cultivated in the cool regions of northern China and reported to possess drought resistance, remain insufficiently characterized. Therefore, this study integrated physiological measurements and transcriptome analysis to characterize the short-term drought responses of 'Hanfu' apple. One-year-old grafted 'Hanfu' apple seedlings were grown hydroponically and then treated with 5%, 10%, and 15% PEG-6000 for 6, 12, 24, and 48 h to impose PEG-induced osmotic stress as a simulation of drought-related water deficit. Leaf water potential, photosynthetic pigments, superoxide anion (O2·-), hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), malondialdehyde (MDA), and antioxidant enzyme activities were measured. RNA sequencing identified differentially expressed genes (DEGs), enriched pathways, and drought-responsive transcription factor families. The results showed that PEG-simulated drought stress aggravated leaf water deficit, reduced photosynthetic pigments, and downregulated photosynthetic-related genes expression (CAB, CP24, PSA, and PNSL2). ROS and MDA levels were increased, activities of SOD and POD were enhanced, and antioxidant-related genes (PPO, APX, PK1, and PER) were upregulated. Genes involved in plant hormone signal transduction showed marked differential expression, particularly those associated with the IAA and ABA signaling pathways. Related genes such as ARF5, GH3.1, SAUR32, ARG7, PP2C, ABI, and HAB1 could play important roles in responding to PEG-simulated drought stress. Also, MYB, WRKY, bZIP, AP2, bHLH, Dof, NAC, and ARF may be the major transcription factor families involved. Overall, 'Hanfu' apple leaves may coordinate photosynthesis, antioxidant defense, IAA and ABA signaling, and transcriptional regulation to respond to drought stress. These findings provide a physiological and molecular basis for further functional validation of drought-responsive genes and may contribute to future breeding for drought resistance and drought management in apple.
items.authors: Chen X, Zhou T, Lyu D, Li L, Qin S.

items.title: Physiological Responses and Time-Course Transcriptomic Analysis of Morchella sextelata Strain Mel-21 During NaCl Exposure.
items.abstract: Salt stress limits fungal growth and distribution, but the mechanisms underlying salt tolerance in Morchella remain unclear. Here, we combined physiological measurements, transcriptomic analysis, weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA), and heterologous expression assays to characterize salt-stress responses in Morchella sextelata. Among 24 preselected isolates representing four Morchella species, M. sextelata Mel-21 obtained the highest composite screening score under 1 mol·L-1 NaCl and was selected for detailed analysis. A concentration of 300 mmol·L-1 NaCl was subsequently selected as the representative stress condition. Salt stress increased electrical conductivity, osmotic pressure, Na+ accumulation, antioxidant enzyme activities, and proline content, while decreasing the K+/Na+ and Ca2+/Na+ ratios. Intracellular and extracellular polysaccharides showed distinct time-dependent accumulation patterns, and the corresponding crude extracts exhibited increased radical-scavenging activities under NaCl stress. Relative to the common 0 h baseline, RNA-seq identified 3654, 3843, 4289, 3566, and 2494 differentially expressed genes after 3, 6, 12, 24, and 48 h of NaCl exposure, respectively. These genes were enriched in pathways related to ribosomes, oxidative phosphorylation, protein processing in the endoplasmic reticulum, carbohydrate metabolism, and ABC transporters. Gene05935, encoding a predicted multi-pass transmembrane protein, showed consistently higher transcript abundance during NaCl exposure than at the common 0 h baseline. Heterologous expression of Gene05935 in Saccharomyces cerevisiae was associated with higher mean endpoint OD600 values under the tested high-salinity conditions, while the Arabidopsis thaliana assay provided preliminary qualitative observations of seedling appearance during NaCl exposure. Because time-matched untreated controls were not included, the transcriptomic differences cannot be attributed specifically to NaCl. Together, the physiological measurements and temporal expression profiles identify Gene05935 as a candidate for further functional characterization and may inform future cultivation-oriented evaluation of Morchella under saline conditions.
