items.authors: Qiang S, Yang SD, Huang ZC, Zhao QM, Sun J, Yang T, Zhao XQ, Li ZY, Zhang JY, Liu Y, Wang JR.

items.title: CRISPR/Cas genome editing strategies to enhance abiotic stress tolerance in sugar crops.
items.abstract: Sugar crops including sugarcane, sugar beets, and sweet sorghum, are fundamental for global sucrose supply and crucial feedstocks for bioethanol production and industrial bioproducts. However, yield and sucrose accumulation are significantly influenced by abiotic stresses, including drought, salinity/alkalinity, heat, chilling/freezing, and heavy metal toxicity. The polygenic complexity of stress tolerance, particularly in sugarcane with its large, polyploid, and haplotype-diverse genome, presents significant challenges for conventional breeding, rendering it slow and imprecise. This review combines advances in genome-editing technologies, including CRISPR/Cas systems (Cas9 and Cas12a), along with transcriptional techniques (CRISPRa/i), base editors, and prime editors. These tools, combined with the progress in reference genomes, haplotype-resolved assemblies, and pangenomes, have facilitated precise gene discovery, genomic selection, and targeted editing. CRISPR-based approaches offer promising avenues for enhancing key stress-responsive pathways governing oxidative homeostasis, membrane integrity, osmotic regulation, hormone signaling, and ion-homeostasis in sugar crops. Prominent candidate targets include transcription factors (TF), signaling components, raffinose biosynthesis genes implicated in freezing tolerance, regulators of salt and alkaline stress, and determinants of heavy metal tolerance and sequestration. Translational challenges, such as off-target effects, low transformation efficiencies, and editing multiple homologues or haplotypes, are being addressed such as DNA-free ribonucleoprotein (RNP) delivery, high-throughput screening, haplotype-specific target design, and haplotype-aware guide RNA engineering based on unique genetic variation sites across different gene haplotypes. Collectively, the integration of advanced CRISPR toolkits with enhanced genomic information resources and phenotyping capabilities holds significant potential for accelerating the development of precision-bred, multi-stress-resilient sugar crops that sustain yield, quality, and industrial value under abiotic stress conditions.
items.authors: Liu HB, Kumar T, Abu-Ellail FFB, Lin XQ, Li CJ, Xu CH, Arif M, Khan W, Ismail M, Zhao LP, Sakr EAE, Haq NU, Lu X.

items.title: Helium Enhances Brassica napus Cadmium Tolerance by Reducing Cadmium Uptake/Translocation and Modulating Redox Balance.
items.abstract: Helium, a traditionally inert gas, has garnered interest in medicine, yet its role in plant heavy metal responses is still elusive. Here, we investigated whether or how helium orchestrates rapeseed cadmium (Cd) tolerance. Hydroponic experimental results demonstrated that helium-enriched solution markedly alleviated Cd-induced inhibition of root growth. Importantly, helium-inhibited Cd uptake was evidenced by non-invasive micro-test technology (NMT). By using grafting experiments, we clearly observed differential responses in Cd accumulation. Since shoot tissues had relatively lower Cd contents, the inhibited root-to-shoot Cd translocation might be used to explain the low Cd accumulation achieved by helium. Further analysis indicated that helium enhanced Cd sequestration in root cell walls. Remarkably, Cd-triggered oxidative damage was effectively eliminated via stimulating the antioxidant system. Collectively, these findings suggest that restricted Cd uptake and inhibition in translocation, as well as antioxidant capacity stimulation, might be important mechanisms for helium-orchestrated Cd tolerance, thus providing a potential approach for sustainable agriculture and food security.
items.authors: Cheng P, Xue P, Li W, Wang J, Cai C, Guan R, Shen W.

items.title: Blue light optimizes photosynthetic physiology and photoprotective molecular mechanisms of Hydrangea quercifolia seedlings.
items.abstract: IntroductionHydrangea quercifolia is a rare ornamental shrub whose natural populations have declined due to habitat loss, necessitating efficient artificial propagation techniques. Light quality is a critical environmental factor regulating seedling growth and physiological quality; however, the molecular mechanisms by which different LED light spectra modulate photosynthetic physiology and hormone signaling in H. quercifolia remain poorly understood.MethodsWe investigated the regulatory mechanisms of four LED light qualities-white (W), blue (B), red (R), and red:blue = 3:1 (R3B1)-on the growth, photosynthetic performance, chloroplast ultrastructure, hormone metabolism, and transcriptomic profiles of H. quercifolia 'Harmony' seedlings. Physiological parameters were measured on days 7, 14, and 21, and RNA sequencing was performed to identify differentially expressed genes and associated signaling pathways.ResultsBlue (B) light significantly increased chlorophyll, anthocyanin, and cytokinin (CTK) contents, promoted chloroplast proliferation and grana thylakoid development, and enhanced photosynthetic efficiency. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that B light upregulated genes encoding photosystem I (PSI) and photosystem II (PSII) reaction center proteins (especially PsbS, Photosystem II S subunit), strengthened non-photochemical quenching (NPQ) and photoprotective capacity, and reduced brassinosteroid (BR) biosynthesis by suppressing BRI1 (Brassinosteroid Insensitive 1) and BSK (Brassinosteroid-Signaling Kinase) expression. In contrast, R3B1 and red (R) light induced chloroplast shrinkage, reduced chloroplast number, and triggered starch accumulation. R3B1 light inhibited PSII oxygen evolution and electron transport, downregulating chloroplast-related genes; while R light suppressed cytokinin biosynthesis by downregulating CRE1 (Cytokinin Response 1) and activated BAK1 (BRI1-Associated Receptor Kinase 1)-mediated BR signaling.DiscussionThese findings demonstrate that blue light plays a pivotal role in promoting the high-quality development of hydrangea seedlings by optimizing photosynthetic apparatus assembly, enhancing photoprotection, and repressing BR-mediated growth inhibition. The differential molecular responses to distinct light spectra provide a theoretical basis for designing optimized artificial light environments and improving the efficiency of horticultural seedling production.
items.authors: Su P, Wang D, Gao Y, Chen X, Hou J, Wu L.

items.title: The ecological adaptability of pinewood nematode populations: survival strategies, mechanisms and co-evolution.
items.abstract: BackgroundBursaphelenchus xylophilus (pinewood nematode, PWN) is the causal agent of pine wilt disease and ranks among the most destructive invasive pests threatening global forest ecosystems. Since its introduction to China, this nematode has triggered massive ecological and economic losses, while its distribution range continues to expand northward. The association between the widespread dispersal of B. xylophilus in invaded areas and the ecological adaptability of its populations has drawn considerable attention.ResultsThis review systematically synthesizes recent research advances regarding the ecological adaptability of PWN populations, elaborating on molecular mechanisms and ecological strategies that enable the nematode to colonize novel environments. In terms of thermal adaptation, differentially expressed genes, small heat shock protein families and the accumulation of key metabolites collectively shape adaptive pathways to resist extreme high and low temperature stress. For host adaptation, PWN displays polyphagous feeding habits and relies on diverse arboreal fungi as nutritional resources when pines were weakened or died. Detoxification enzyme cascades and effector proteins enable the nematode to counteract host defensive metabolites. Specifically, effectors suppress host peroxidase activity, thereby quenching reactive oxygen species bursts and disrupting plant hormone regulatory pathways to attenuate pine immune responses. Co-evolutionary interactions between PWN and vector beetles manifest across multiple dimensions, including synchronized life cycles, specialized dispersal-stage juveniles, and infochemical-mediated interspecies communication. PWN also forms intricate interaction networks with associated fungi and bacteria, which exert vital functions in nutrient acquisition, pathogenicity enhancement and terpenoid degradation. Notably, ascaroside pheromones serve as central signaling molecules that modulate interspecific competition and reproductive phenotypic plasticity. Population genetic analyses have uncovered shifts in genetic diversity, regulatory pathways governing population structure and reproductive efficiency, as well as synergistic evolutionary correlations between invasive population genetics and pathogenicity. Multi-omics analytical frameworks provide novel perspectives for dissecting the adaptive evolution of PWN.ConclusionThe invasive success and widespread dispersal of B. xylophilus are fundamentally driven by its strong population ecological adaptability. Finally, this review summarizes the existing research gaps and proposes future research priorities alongside targeted pest management strategies. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry.
items.authors: Ying CX, Wen TY, Ding XL, Wu XQ.

items.title: Integrative multi-omics reveal the impact of different light spectra on lateral branching and growth of medicinal plant Artemisia argyi.
items.abstract: Light quality is a decisive environmental regulator of growth and secondary metabolism in medicinal plants, yet the spectral requirements of Artemisia argyi, a species prized for bioactive metabolites such as artemisinin, eupatilin, and jaceosidin, remain poorly defined. This study integrated physiological, transcriptomic, and metabolomic analyses to evaluate the response of A. argyi to 4 weeks of supplemental light-emitting diode (LED) lighting of three spectral compositions: blue-red (BR, 3:1), red-blue (RB, 3:1), and white (control), with three biological replicates per treatment. Physiologically, BR light produced the tallest stems, the largest and densest foliage, and the greatest stem diameter, shoot fresh and dry weight, and number of lateral branches; relative to RB and white light, plant height increased by 109%, 100%, 78%, and 8.6% and leaf number by 51.61%, 58.33%, 37.20%, and 4.2% across weeks 1-4, accompanied by higher antioxidant enzyme activity and reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels. RNA sequencing yielded 44.18-50.75 million raw reads per sample with a mapping ratio of 83.47%-87.06% and Q30 > 94%. Pairwise analysis identified 2,025 differentially expressed genes (DEGs; 1,173 upregulated and 852 downregulated) for BR vs. RB, 974 (652 upregulated and 322 downregulated) for BR vs. white, and 601 (141 upregulated and 460 downregulated) for RB vs. white, enriched in light-responsive, photosystem, chlorophyll- and proline-metabolism and circadian pathways. Key regulators included the two-component response regulator-like APRR1 (a CheY-like phosphoacceptor), proline dehydrogenase (ProDH), the chlorophyll b reductase NOL, and terpenoid-backbone (isoprene) genes. Metabolomic profiling detected 174, 129, and 81 differentially accumulated metabolites in BR vs. RB, BR vs. white, and RB vs. white, respectively, with 486 metabolites up- and 459 downregulated in BR vs. RB and pronounced enrichment of amino acid, carbohydrate, lipid, and secondary-metabolite (flavonoid, terpenoid, and alkaloid) biosynthesis. Collectively, these results demonstrate that BR supplemental light coordinately enhances growth, lateral branching, and bioactive-compound biosynthesis, offering a practical basis for the precision cultivation of A. argyi and the targeted production of its medicinal compounds.
items.authors: Mehmood A, Yipeng Z, Song J, Yang Z, Wu Y.

items.title: Physiological and Transcriptomic Insights into Melatonin-Mediated Alleviation of Cadmium Stress in the Endangered Plant Plantago fengdouensis.
items.abstract: Plantago fengdouensis is an endangered species threatened by habitat loss, population fragmentation, and cadmium (Cd) contamination. This study evaluated the effects of exogenous melatonin (MT) on Cd tolerance from seed germination to the seedling stage. In Petri-dish assays, 50-100 mg L-1 Cd markedly inhibited germination; 50 mg L-1 was selected as the lowest concentration producing severe inhibition while retaining sufficient germination for mitigation testing, and 100 μM MT provided the strongest alleviation. In pot experiments, MT promoted seedling growth, shoot and root biomass accumulation, and root and leaf development while reducing Cd accumulation and root-to-shoot translocation. Physiological analyses showed that 200-250 μM MT most effectively alleviated Cd-associated damage by maintaining photosynthesis, enhancing antioxidant and osmotic-adjustment responses, and modulating endogenous hormones. Transcriptome analysis identified 4871 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between C50M200 and C50M0, with prominent enrichment in plant hormone signaling, cell-wall/plasma-membrane functions, secondary metabolism, and photosynthesis. Exploratory weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) further identified treatment-associated modules and candidate hub genes. Overall, the data support coordinated MT-associated responses involving stronger antioxidant defense, reduced Cd accumulation/translocation, and hormone-signaling remodeling. Because transcriptomes were obtained from leaves and WGCNA included nine samples, the inferred molecular mechanisms should be regarded as candidate pathways pending targeted expression and functional validation.
items.authors: Peng Y, Wang BR, Zhang JB, Zuo YW, Liang X, Zhou SM, You SQ, Deng HP.

items.title: Welwitschia leaf senescence is orchestrated via ERF113-ERF115-mediated antagonism between hormone signaling pathways.
items.abstract: Phytohormone crosstalk is fundamental to plant development and adaptation. While the coordinated actions of different hormones are well recognized, the underlying molecular mechanisms in specific biological processes remain largely elusive. Here, we identified the WmERF113-WmERF115 module as a central hub that mediated jasmonic acid (JA)/abscisic acid (ABA)-gibberellins (GA) antagonism to regulate leaf senescence in Welwitschia, a desert plant with only two leaves that grow continuously over an exceptionally long lifespan. We revealed that the JA/ABA-inducible transcription factor (TF) WmERF113 directly activated senescence-associated genes (SAGs), promoting senescence and chlorophyll degradation, whereas the GA-responsive WmERF115 repressed the same targets to mitigate senescence. Notably, WmERF113 and WmERF115 physically interacted to form a heterodimer, mutually inhibiting each other's binding to target promoters. Furthermore, these two TFs acted as reciprocal trans-acting factors, repressing each other's expression through promoter cross-binding. This multiple-layer regulatory circuit ensured that leaf senescence of Welwitschia progressed in a temporally and spatially restricted manner. Our study provided an important conceptual framework in which phytohormone crosstalk was translated into TF antagonism for fine-tuning senescence, offering new insights into the adaptive strategies that enable plant survival in extreme environments.
items.authors: Xu H, Song Q, Mamo W, Tolosa LN, Zhang J, Aboushanab AGMF, Wang Q, Wan T.

items.title: Elucidating the Stem of Crassulaceae: A Structural Chemical-Anatomical Analysis.
items.abstract: Crassulaceae comprises succulent species characterized by extensive water-storage tissues and considerable anatomical diversity, yet comparative information on the chemical composition and structural organization of their stem cell walls remains limited. This study characterized stem cell-wall composition and anatomy in 33 Crassulaceae species using sequential extraction, lignocellulosic fractionation, Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), epifluorescence microscopy, and multivariate analyses. Significant interspecific differences were detected in extractives, lignin, cellulose, hemicellulose, the semiquantitative FTIR-derived syringyl-to-guaiacyl spectral index (S/G index), and cellulose structural indices. Principal component analysis revealed complementary gradients associated mainly with the hemicellulose-cellulose balance, lignin content, and cellulose organization, whereas PERMANOVA indicated significant multivariate differentiation among genera. Partial least squares discriminant analysis showed moderate genus-level discrimination and identified the total crystallinity index (TCI), lateral order index (LOI), and FTIR-derived S/G index as the variables contributing most consistently to genus differentiation. Anatomically, cell-wall components were heterogeneously distributed among tissues, with lignified secondary walls primarily associated with xylem vessels, fibers, and lignified parenchyma when present, whereas nonlignified cellulosic walls predominated in cortical and pith parenchyma. Differences were also observed in periderm organization and in the distribution of phenolic-rich cellular contents. Together, these results demonstrate substantial chemical, spectroscopic, and anatomical diversity in Crassulaceae stems and indicate that variation in cell-wall traits is partially structured among genera. This comparative framework provides a basis for future studies evaluating the functional, ecological, evolutionary, and applied significance of stem cell-wall diversity in succulent plants.
items.authors: Maceda A, Andrés-Hernández AR, Reyes-Santiago J, Soto-Hernández M, Terrazas T.

items.title: Beyond Mycorrhizae: A Multi-Kingdom Community in Epiphytic Orchid Roots Reveals Cyanobacteria Intracellular and a Velamen Microbial Refuge.
items.abstract: Orchid biology has long been dominated by the paradigm of mycorrhizal dependency; however, the nutrient acquisition strategies of epiphytic orchids in canopy niches remain poorly understood. Using an integrated approach of multilocus metabarcoding (16S, ITS, 18S) and advanced microscopy (SEM, TEM, CLSM), we characterised the root microbial community of the threatened epiphytic orchid Cattleya purpurata. We report the discovery of intracellular Nostoc-like cyanobacteria within cortical cells, coexisting with the mycorrhizal fungus Tulasnella at a root colonisation rate of 18%. Furthermore, we identified: (1) a diverse velamen-associated microbiome hosting plant growth-promoting bacteria (e.g., the Burkholderia-Caballeronia-Paraburkholderia complex), nematodes and microalgae; and (2) a vast unknown fungal diversity, with over 39 genera and numerous ASVs unmatched in databases. We demonstrate that C. purpurata roots sustain a complex multi-kingdom community. We propose that the root velamen acts as a multi-kingdom microbial refuge, expanding the concept of symbiosis in orchids beyond fungi. Based on the intracellular presence of Nostoc-like cyanobacteria and their known diazotrophic capacity in other plant symbioses, we hypothesise a previously little-known nitrogen pathway mediated by cyanobacteria in a canopy environment, to be functionally tested in future studies.
items.authors: de Medeiros Oliveira E, Meyer E, Lovato PE, Guerra MP, Gris T, de Almeida AFN, Mayer JLS.

items.title: Exogenous Brassinosteroid Promotes Vegetative Growth in the World's Smallest Water Lily (Nymphaea thermarum).
items.abstract: Nymphaea thermarum, the world's smallest water lily, provides a useful system for investigating hormonal regulation of vegetative growth. This study investigated vegetative growth, hormone immunoreactive estimates, and tissue-specific transcriptional responses to exogenous 24-epibrassinolide (EBL) in N. thermarum. Plants were subjected to a concentration gradient of 24-epibrassinolide (EBL; 0, 200, 400, 600, 800, and 1000 nM) under soil-based pot culture with EBL treatment solutions, and morphological, hormonal, and transcriptomic analyses were performed. Growth responses were non-monotonic, with BR400 producing the highest mean longitudinal leaf radius, petiole length, and leaf area, while transverse leaf radius was comparable to that under BR200; all four traits under BR400 were significantly greater than in the control. Hormone immunoreactive estimates varied across treatments, with the highest mean gibberellin (GA)- and brassinosteroid (BR)-immunoreactive estimates observed under BR400; however, neither differed significantly from CK. The highest mean indole-3-acetic acid (IAA)-immunoreactive estimate occurred under BR600. Transcriptomic analysis identified 1053 DEGs in leaves and 2028 in petioles under BR400 treatment compared with the control. GO and KEGG analyses revealed enrichment of cell-wall-organization- and phenylpropanoid biosynthesis-related categories among DEGs. Photosynthesis-related genes were down-regulated in leaves, accompanied by lower chlorophyll a and total chlorophyll concentrations under BR400. These findings characterize EBL-associated vegetative growth and transcriptional responses in N. thermarum and identify candidate genes and processes for future functional studies of water lily architecture.
items.authors: Li BY, Xie JS, Wang YJ, Jin QJ, Xiao D, Yang ZJ, Xu YC.

items.title: NLR Immune Receptors Can Exhibit Tissue-specific Expression Patterns Across Legume Species.
items.abstract: Pathogen pressure threatens legume crop productivity worldwide. Nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat (NLR) immune receptors serve as crucial plant resistance genes, recognizing pathogens and triggering immunity. However, the extent and patterns of NLR expression in different tissues and organs, notably across evolutionary time, remain largely uncharacterized. To investigate tissue specificity of NLR expression in the Fabaceae (legumes), we conducted comparative analyses integrating phylogenomics and transcriptomics in root and leaf tissues across different legume species. The NLR repertoires of 28 legumes were grouped into 5 monophyletic clades: coiled-coil NLR (CC-NLR), Toll/interleukin-1 receptor NLR (TIR-NLR), G10-subclade CC NLR (CCG10-NLR), RESISTANCE TO POWDERY MILDEW 8-like CC NLR (CCR-NLR), and TIR-NB-ARC-like β-propeller WD40/tetratricopeptide repeats (TNPs). Most legume NLRs belonged to CC-NLR and TIR-NLR clades, followed by CCG10-NLR, CCR-NLR, and TNP clades. In 7 of these species, comparative analysis of NLR expression in leaves versus roots revealed that over half (∼57%) of expressed NLR genes showed predominant expression in one tissue: 34% in roots (451/1336), and 23% in leaves (311/1336). We identified 324 root-specific NLRs, 171 leaf-specific NLRs, and 841 nonspecific NLRs, with an average tissue specificity per species of 32%. The closely related species grass pea (Lathyrus sativus) and pea (Pisum sativum) were an exception, showing higher levels of leaf-specific rather than root-specific NLR expression. We also identified conserved tissue expression patterns across legume species, resulting in a comprehensive resource describing tissue expression bias, enrichment, and specificity for 113 phylogenetic NLR subclasses. These legume NLR repertoires will support comparative studies between species and inform precision-breeding programs considering tissue expression patterns.
items.authors: Marques RM, Santos C, Pai H, Vaz Patto MC, Kamoun S, Kourelis J.

items.title: Genome-wide characterization of the PLATZ transcription factor family in chickpea reveals evolutionary diversification and genotype-dependent responses to drought and salinity
items.abstract: Abstract Plant A/T-rich sequence- and zinc-binding (PLATZ) proteins are plant-specific, zinc-dependent DNA-binding transcription factors that regulate plant growth, development, and stress responses, yet this family remains poorly characterized in chickpea (Cicer arietinum L.). Here, ten non-redundant CaPLATZ genes were identified using three complementary approaches—keyword-based retrieval, BLASTP homology searching, and HMMER-based conserved-domain screening—and characterized through structural, evolutionary, regulatory, developmental, and stress-responsive expression analyses. items.authors: Barua A, Sampatirao D, Kanth DR, Amara Y, Yadava YK, Kalwan G, Tomar R, Senthil K, Kumar A, Sreevathsa R, Gaikwad K, Jain PK.

items.title: Fast structural remodeling of Jatropha curcas thylakoids upon recovery underpins chloroplast resilience to drought.
items.abstract: Jatropha curcas is a moderate stem-succulent oil crop renowned for its drought tolerance. While the photosynthetic activity of drought-stressed and rewatered Jatropha curcas has been investigated, little is known about the effects of drought and rewatering on chloroplast integrity and thylakoid architecture, critical determinants of photosynthetic performance under stress. Here, we exposed J. curcas seedlings to 19 days of water withdrawal followed by rewatering. Leaf relative water content remained unchanged throughout, indicating efficient water retention. Leaf anatomy was largely preserved, but chloroplasts became slightly smaller. Small-angle neutron scattering and transmission electron microscopy revealed a 2-4 nm decrease in granum repeat distance under drought. Electron microscopy further showed that this decrease was stronger in palisade than in spongy parenchyma chloroplasts. In thylakoids, the photosynthetic complexes were adjusted differently under drought: photosystem (PS) I and light harvesting complex (LHC) II remained unchanged, whereas PSII complexes decreased, increasing the PSI/PSII and LHCII/PSII ratios. Among the remaining PSII, larger supercomplexes were proportionally enriched, suggesting their higher drought stability. These changes coincided with a moderate decrease in PSII activity (Fv/Fm) and increased non-photochemical quenching. After rewatering, granum repeat distances recovered within hours (0.5-1 h in spongy and 5 h in palisade chloroplasts), revealing the involvement of rapidly reversible membrane remodeling under drought, while full recovery of photosynthetic performance and thylakoid protein composition was slower, requiring days. The high plasticity and rapid recovery of the thylakoid architecture is proposed to enable Jatropha curcas to restore its drought-affected photosynthetic apparatus and resume photosynthesis once water becomes available.
items.authors: Hembrom R, Sapeta H, Zsiros O, Markó M, Nagy G, Sárvári É, Solti Á, Oliveira MM, Garab G, Solymosi K.

items.title: Adaptation Begins at the Wall: Hormonal Control of Cell-Wall Plasticity Under Abiotic Stresses.
items.abstract: The plant cell wall functions as both a mechanical framework and a dynamic environmental sensor, with its remodeling tightly coordinated by phytohormone signaling and cell-wall integrity (CWI) surveillance. This review synthesizes how hormonal networks regulate wall processes including cellulose deposition, pectin modification, and lignification translating extracellular perturbations via receptor kinases and second messengers into adaptive growth responses. We argue that abiotic stress resilience does not stem from uniformly reinforced walls, but from the capacity to dynamically tune wall mechanics in a spatiotemporally precise manner. Evaluating emerging tools like spatial multi-omics and precision genome editing, we propose a translational roadmap to engineer context-dependent wall plasticity. Integrating causal genetics with field-level phenotyping will be essential for developing climate-resilient crops that maintain yield stability under fluctuating environments.
items.authors: Amin N, Jiao J, Ma G, Liu L, Ahmad N, Wei J.

items.title: Genome-wide identification of the BES1 gene family and functional study of VcBES1.3 under salt stress in blueberry (Vaccinium corymbosum).
items.abstract: BES1 (BRI1-EMS-SUPPRESSOR 1) transcription factors mediate brassinosteroid signaling and regulate plant growth, development, and stress responses. The BES1 family has not been characterized in blueberry (Vaccinium corymbosum L.). We identified 16 VcBES1 family members and classified them into four groups based on phylogenetic analysis. Promoters of the BES1 genes mainly contain cis-elements associated with abiotic stress and phytohormone signaling. Tissue-specific expression analysis showed that the VcBES1 family is expressed predominantly in roots and stems. All members except VcBES1.8 and VcBES1.9 responded positively to salt stress. Among them, VcBES1.3 displayed the strongest salt induction. The protein accumulated in the nucleus. Overexpression and RNA interference (RNAi) experiments established that VcBES1.3 enhances salt tolerance. This study characterizes the VcBES1 family, defines its tissue-specific and stress-responsive expression patterns, and demonstrate that VcBES1.3 as a positive regulator of salt tolerance in blueberry.
items.authors: Zhang B, Liu X, Huang J, Su H, Luo X, Sun Y, Zhao F, Lu X, Lin S, Wang D, Huang G, Zhou W.

items.title: Development of PEG-Mediated Genetic Transformation for Pine-Inhabiting Fungus Pestalotiopsis disseminata.
items.abstract: Pestalotiopsis disseminata widely inhabits pines, but the lack of an efficient genetic transformation system has limited its functional genomic studies. Here, we optimized protoplast preparation and established a PEG-mediated transformation and GFP-labeling platform for strain ZXD579. The selected conditions used mycelia cultured for 24 h and digested for 3 h at 28 °C with 1% lysing enzyme, 0.1% driselase, and 1% lysozyme in 0.6 M KCl supplemented with 50 mM CaCl2. The protoplast yield reached (1.51 ± 0.15) × 107 protoplasts/mL, and the regeneration rate exceeded 90%. Hygromycin B at 130 μg/mL completely inhibited wild-type growth and was suitable for transformant selection. The pCT74-eGFP plasmid carrying the reporter gene and hygromycin B phosphotransferase gene (hph) was introduced into protoplasts using PEG. Putative transformants were examined by PCR and fluorescence microscopy; GFP fluorescence was detected in hyphae and conidia. Transformation efficiency was 4.2 ± 0.6 transformants per μg plasmid DNA, and 60% of 15 randomly selected hygromycin-resistant transformants were PCR-positive. GFP-labeled transformants showed no significant difference in vegetative growth and exhibited comparable preliminary pathogenicity phenotypes relative to the wild-type strain. This protocol provides a foundation for gene manipulation in P. disseminata.
items.authors: Zhan Z, Wang Q, Wang H, Terhonen E, Zhou L, Kulinich OA, Xu H, Zhou X.

items.title: Deep Learning Based Cell Segmentation of 3D Confocal Images of Wood for Enzymatic Hydrolysis Applications
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Plant cell walls are an abundant renewable resource for biobased products, but their recalcitrance limits enzymatic hydrolysis efficiency. Cell and tissue morphological parameters provide reliable biomarkers for predicting enzymatic hydrolysis efficiency. Accurate cell segmentation in 3D microscopy images is essential for quantifying these parameters. Although deep learning has achieved high performance in biological image segmentation, confocal microscopy’s limited penetration depth leaves elongated wood cells partially imaged, creating open-ended structures that challenge existing segmentation methods. Based on an artificial longitudinal domain restriction, an adapted framework is presented here for the training of a 3D U-net model for the cell segmentation of wood images. Quantitative evaluation on a dedicated benchmark dataset identified a model configuration that reduced segmentation errors and produced more robust predictions during early enzymatic hydrolysis. These results support the use of the framework to quantify morphological parameters relevant to assessing and predicting biomass conversion efficiency.
items.authors: Faraj, A., Hossein Khani, S., Paës, G., Refahi, Y.

items.title: A spatially deployable iron redox rheostat tunes root growth under nutritional stress.
items.abstract: Root growth must continuously adjust to fluctuating nutrient availability, yet the mechanisms that quantitatively integrate environmental signals into developmental responses remain poorly understood. Distinct nutrient stresses, including ammonium toxicity and phosphate deficiency, inhibit primary root growth through iron-dependent processes, suggesting that iron acts as a central regulatory node. Here, we show that plants use an antagonistic module composed of CYBDOM ferrireductases and LPR ferroxidases to regulate apoplastic iron homeostasis and control root growth in a graded manner. Genetic perturbation of this module demonstrates that root growth inhibition scales quantitatively with iron accumulation, supporting a proportional control mechanism rather than a binary response. Loss of CYBDOM function causes excessive iron accumulation, elevated reactive oxygen species, and impaired meristem activity, whereas increased CYBDOM activity buffers iron deposition and confers resistance to stress. Mechanistically, iron-induced oxidative stress promotes HYP1 expression, which in turn limits further iron accumulation. Transcriptomic analyses distinguish ammonium-specific responses from Fe-associated transcriptional changes enriched in redox buffering and cell-wall remodeling. Finally, we show that this regulatory module is redeployed in distinct tissues under phosphate deficiency, indicating that plants reuse a conserved iron-based mechanism to coordinate growth across environmental contexts. Together, our findings establish genetically controlled Fe accumulation as a key determinant of developmental plasticity under nutrient stress.
items.authors: Clúa J, Berbel A, Urbez C, Madueño F, Poirier Y, Blázquez MA.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
also: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Ecophysiological and Transcriptomic Responses of Mangrove Seedlings to Environmentally Relevant Cu-Pb-Cd Combined-Metal Stress.
items.abstract: Mangrove wetlands are important coastal blue-carbon ecosystems that are increasingly exposed to combined-metal stress by copper (Cu), lead (Pb), and cadmium (Cd). However, how mangrove seedlings coordinate metal exclusion, redox regulation, and photosynthetic adjustment under environmentally relevant metal mixtures remains insufficiently resolved. In this study, five dominant mangrove species, Bruguiera gymnorrhiza, Rhizophora stylosa, Kandelia obovata, Aegiceras corniculatum, and Avicennia marina, were exposed to a gradient of Cu-Pb-Cd combined stress under hydroponic and soil-culture systems for 30 days. We measured tissue metal accumulation, growth, leaf hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), chlorophyll content and fluorescence, and examined root and leaf transcriptomic patterns. Roots generally accumulated more Cu, Pb, and Cd than leaves, while seedlings grown in soil accumulated less metal than those in solution. At higher mixture concentrations, A. corniculatum and K. obovata showed greater visible injury, H2O2 accumulation, and reductions in chlorophyll and PSII-related fluorescence parameters. B. gymnorrhiza and A. marina showed comparatively smaller changes. Root- and leaf-associated transcriptomic patterns suggested possible involvement of transport-related and photosynthesis-related pathways, although these associations do not establish causal mechanisms. These findings indicate that mangrove tolerance to Cu-Pb-Cd combined-metal stress is jointly regulated by root metal exclusion, H2O2-mediated redox changes, and photoprotective adjustment, thereby clarifying plant-level mechanisms of abiotic stress tolerance under combined metal exposure. The results identify B. gymnorrhiza and A. marina as preliminary candidates for further evaluation under field conditions.
items.authors: Zhou Y, Huang G, Zhao Y, Yu Y.

items.title: Inhalable Plant Exosome-like Nanoparticles from Houttuynia cordata Ameliorate Acute Lung Injury via Redox Modulation and Immune Reprogramming.
items.abstract: Background: Acute lung injury (ALI) features oxidative stress, macrophage dysfunction, and barrier disruption, with limited safe therapies. Plant-derived exosome-like nanovesicles (PENs) delivered noninvasively to the lung are promising but understudied. Methods: In vitro, HELNs were evaluated for their ability to scavenge ROS, restore mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP) modulate M1/M2 polarization, and suppress pro-inflammatory cytokines. RNA-seq was also used to evaluate the TNF/NOD-like pathway and mitochondrial-related gene expression. In vivo, the evaluated parameters included biodistribution, therapeutic outcomes (lung wet/dry weight ratio, BALF protein concentration, MPO and MDA levels, histology), immune cell profiles, and cytokines. Biosafety was assessed via hematology, serum biochemistry, and histology. Results: In vitro, HELNs acted dose-dependently by scavenging ROS, recovering MMP, promoting M2 and suppressing M1 polarization, and reducing TNF-α, IL-6 release. Additionally, RNA-seq confirmed downregulation of TNF/NOD-like signals and regulated mitochondrial gene expression. In vivo, nebulized HELNs preferentially accumulated in inflamed lungs, with significantly higher pulmonary retention than intravenous delivery. HELNs reduced lung wet/dry weight ratio, BALF protein, MPO and MDA levels, and histological injury scores; decreased neutrophils and CD4+/CD8+ T cells; increased alveolar macrophages and Tregs; and lowered TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6. No significant systemic toxicity was observed. Conclusions: Nebulized HELNs offer a safe, effective, noninvasive ALI therapy by disrupting the oxidative stress-inflammation vicious cycles, reprogramming pulmonary immunity, and restoring barrier integrity, with strong translational potential.
items.authors: Yin T, Hu J, Xu L, Huang S, Zhang B, Qiu L, Liu Y, Cui D, Zhou Z, Zeng J, Zha M.

items.title: Riboflavin Primes Pepper Resistance to Ralstonia solanacearum Through Coordinated Antioxidant Responses and Lignin Deposition.
items.abstract: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are pivotal regulators of plant-pathogen interactions. Comparative transcriptomic analysis of a bacterial wilt-susceptible pepper cultivar (HS03) and a resistant cultivar (HR01) revealed impaired riboflavin biosynthesis in HS03. Exogenous riboflavin application compensated for this deficiency and conferred significant protection against Ralstonia solanacearum. Physiological and transcriptomic analyses further demonstrated that riboflavin functions as both an inducer of ROS signaling and a modulator of defense-associated metabolism. Riboflavin treatment elicited a biphasic defense response characterized by an early H2O2 burst accompanied by dynamic changes in antioxidant enzyme activities. In particular, the activities of superoxide dismutase (SOD), catalase (CAT), and peroxidase (POD) increased markedly at 6 h after riboflavin application compared with control. Following R. solanacearum inoculation, riboflavin-pretreated plants exhibited higher POD, ascorbate peroxidase (APX), and CAT activities at 6 h post-inoculation compared with control. This early antioxidant response induced by riboflavin was followed by increased lignin accumulation and the transcriptional activation of genes associated with cutin, suberin, and wax biosynthesis, galactose metabolism, and tyrosine metabolism at 12 h post-inoculation. Riboflavin pretreatment also enhanced the expression of genes encoding nonexpressor of pathogenesis-related genes 1 (NPR1) and calmodulin (CALM), implicating hormone signaling and calcium-mediated pathogen recognition in riboflavin-induced resistance. Collectively, these results suggest that riboflavin primes pepper defense against R. solanacearum by coordinating early ROS-associated antioxidant responses and subsequent cell-wall reinforcement. Riboflavin may therefore represent a promising environmentally compatible agent for the sustainable management of bacterial wilt in pepper.
items.authors: He F, Geng Y, Li H, Jia X, Wang P, Guo Z, Guo X, Deng X, Li Z.

items.title: Salinity-Modulated Germination and Metabolic Reprogramming in Quinoa Seedlings: Genotype-Dependent Effects on Nutritional and Bioactive Compounds and Prospects for Microgreen Valorization.
items.abstract: Germination is highly sensitive to abiotic stresses such as salinity, which can impair seedling establishment and seed reserve mobilization. Quinoa is a promising crop due to its salinity tolerance and high nutritional value. This study evaluated the effects of NaCl-induced salinity on germination performance, metabolic responses, and nutritional quality of three quinoa seed lots representing two varieties, Regalona (Q1) and Amarilla sacaca (Q2, Q3). Salinity significantly reduced germination rate and kinetics, as well as radicle and shoot growth, with the strongest effects at 500 mM NaCl. During the germination process, starch and protein contents decreased, reflecting reserve mobilization, while vitamin E increased under moderate salinity, particularly in Q1 and Q2, but declined under severe stress. Secondary metabolites, including phenolics, flavonoids, tannins, and saponins, exhibited strong genotype- and stress-dependent variation. HPLC-DAD identified gallic, syringic, vanillic, caffeic, and protocatechuic acids, as well as rutin, quercetin, and kaempferol, with marked differences between raw seeds and seedlings. At moderate salinity (300 mM NaCl), TFC increased by 22% and 42% in Q1 and Q2, respectively, relative to RS, whereas Q3 showed a 45% reduction. Under high salinity (500 mM NaCl), TFC decreased by 83% and 15% in Q1 and Q2, respectively, while Q3 exhibited a 35% increase relative to RS. These contrasting responses highlight genotype-dependent changes in flavonoid accumulation and reflect distinct metabolic plasticity among quinoa genotypes. Overall, these findings support quinoa as a promising functional microgreen crop for producing nutrient- and bioactive-rich foods under controlled conditions.
items.authors: Goussi R, Ben Youssef R, Ben Jouira H, Friji C, Selmi S, Khaled H, Manaa A.

items.title: CmABF3-CmTPP2/5 modulates trehalose-mediated hydrogen peroxide signaling and CBF-dependent pathway to enhance cold tolerance in melon seedlings.
items.abstract: Cold stress inhibits the growth and development of melon. Exogenous trehalose (Tre) has been reported to alleviate cold damage in melon seedlings; however, it remains unclear whether plants respond to cold stress by activating endogenous Tre synthesis and the associated upstream and downstream pathways. Here, the results show that cold stress markedly increases endogenous Tre levels in melon leaves. Transcriptome analysis identified two trehalose-6-phosphate phosphatase (key enzymes in Tre synthesis, TPP) genes, CmTPP2 and CmTPP5, which were strongly induced by cold stress. Silencing CmTPP2/5 significantly reduced Tre content, lowered the activities of superoxide dismutase, ascorbate peroxidase and glutathione reductase, and exacerbated cold-induced lipid peroxidation damage; meanwhile, it inhibited apoplastic H2O2 accumulation, restricted H2O2 transport into the cytoplasm, and downregulated the expression of C-repeat binding factor 1/2 (CmCBF1/2) under cold stress. Protein-DNA interaction assays demonstrated that the transcription factor CmABF3 binds to the ABRE motif in the CmTPP2/5 promoter to activate their transcription. Silencing CmABF3 gene significantly reduced CmCBF1/2 and CmTPP2/5 expression and reduced Tre accumulation. Inhibition of trehalase activity by validamycin A elevated Tre content, enhanced antioxidant capacity under cold stress, promoted apoplastic H2O2 production and transport, and upregulated CmCBF1/2 expression. Silencing CmCBF1/2 also inhibited the production and transport of apoplastic H₂O₂ and reduced melon cold tolerance. These findings reveal that cold stress triggers CmABF3-mediated activation of CmTPP2/5, leading to Tre accumulation, which then enhanced antioxidant defenses via regulation of apoplastic H2O2 production and transport, and coordination with the CBF-dependent pathway to improve cold tolerance in melon seedlings.
items.authors: Liu T, Zhang H, Lu K, Tian J, Han Y, Li H, Zhang Y, Dong L, Ye X, Qi H.

items.title: PlMYB51 and PlMYB1R1 switch PlABI5-PlCesA6 function to regulate seed dormancy and germination in Paeonia lactiflora.
items.abstract: Seed dormancy is a key strategy for plants to adapt to fluctuating environments and ensure population propagation. Paeonia lactiflora seeds exhibit typical double dormancy, characterized by a prolonged germination cycle and low emergence rate that severely restrict their large-scale propagation. Although ABI5, the core transcription factor (TF) in the abscisic acid (ABA) signaling pathway, acts as a critical hub in maintaining seed dormancy, its upstream dynamic regulatory mechanism and downstream cell-wall-related target genes remain largely unknown. In this study, two upstream regulators of PlABI5, PlMYB51 and PlMYB1R1, were identified via yeast one-hybrid screening, and their regulatory mechanism was characterized. The results showed that both PlMYB51 and PlMYB1R1 belonged to the R2R3-MYB family. When acting alone, they directly bound to and activated the PlABI5 promoter, inhibiting seed germination. Upon forming a protein complex in the nucleus, their regulatory function was reversed and they repressed PlABI5 transcription to promote germination, supporting a proposed monomer activation-complex inhibition switch model. Furthermore, PlABI5 specifically targeted the PlCesA6 promoter and inhibited its expression without affecting the homolog PlCesA3. PlCesA6 positively regulated seed germination by promoting hypocotyl cell elongation, and its overexpression rescued the inhibition caused by PlMYB51/PlMYB1R1 overexpression. Collectively, this study proposes a working model for the PlMYB51/PlMYB1R1-PlABI5-PlCesA6 cascade in controlling seed dormancy and germination, and identifies a putative functional switching mode of MYB TFs mediated by protein-protein interactions. These findings provide key gene resources and a theoretical basis for artificial dormancy breaking and molecular breeding in P. lactiflora.
items.authors: Xin R, Zhou X, Guan S, Kang X, Song W, Wang Y, Wang S, Sun X.

items.title: Light-induced phyB-NPR1 interaction activates systemic acquired resistance.
items.abstract: Light perception by phytochromes controls different aspects of plant-environment interactions including plant immunity; however, the underpinning molecular mechanisms are less well-understood. Upon localized attack on leaves by avirulent pathogens, the systemic accumulation of salicylic acid (SA) is required for the establishment of systemic acquired resistance (SAR) throughout the plant to curtail pathogen spread. We demonstrate that light-mediated Small Ubiquitin-like Modifier 1 (SUMO) conjugation to phytochrome B (phyB) is critical for increasing cellular SA levels to orchestrate SAR upon avirulent bacterial infection. SA promotes SUMOylation of phyB, which enables it to interact with the SA receptor, Nonexpressor of Pathogenesis-Related 1 (NPR1) via its SUMO1-interacting motif. SUMOylation of phyB is enhanced by the accumulation of SUMO-Conjugating Enzyme (E2) (SCE1) and the degradation of SUMO protease Overly Tolerant to Salt 1 (OTS1) in SAR-induced systemic tissues. Using confocal imaging, we show that SUMOylated phyB undergoes liquid-liquid phase separation together with NPR1 in nuclear bodies. We further validated through immunoprecipitation, ChIP and RNA-seq analysis that SUMOylated phyB associates with NPR1 and TGA transcription factors in nuclear photobodies to induce the expression of PR1 gene. We reveal a post-translational modification mechanism in which light-induced SUMOylation of photoreceptors promotes SAR by regulating NPR1 function.
items.authors: Ghosh S, Ghosh S, Long X, Mansi M, Clark L, Srivastava AK, Kakkunnath S, Orosa B, Bhagat PK, Bailey M, Gough C, Zhang C, de Lucas M, Sadanandom A.

items.title: The MsSCL28.5-MdMYB87 module enhances drought tolerance by promoting adventitious root development in apple rootstocks.
items.abstract: Drought stress severely limits apple cultivation. Malus sieversii, a wild ancestor of domesticated apple, provides a valuable genetic resource for improving drought tolerance in cultivated apple rootstocks. Although plant-specific GRAS [GIBBERELLIC-ACID INSENSITIVE (GAI), REPRESSOR of GAI, and SCARECROW] transcription factors (TFs) are known to regulate development and stress responses, their precise functions and mechanisms in apple remain largely unexplored. Here, we demonstrated that overexpression of MsSCL28.5, a GRAS TF from M. sieversii, substantially enhances drought tolerance of rootstock 'M26' (Malus domestica). Transgenic plants exhibited increased adventitious root (AR) growth and improved reactive oxygen species scavenging capacity. MsSCL28.5 directly binds to the promoters of MdLBD16a and MdLBD21b, key genes regulating AR growth. We further identified the TF MdMYB87 as an interacting partner of MsSCL28.5. The resulting MsSCL28.5-MdMYB87 complex synergistically activates the transcription of MdLBD16a/21b. Additionally, grafting experiments confirmed that MsSCL28.5-overexpressing rootstocks systemically enhance the drought resistance of non-transgenic scions. Furthermore, we discovered that comprising reduced methylation of the SCL28.5 promoter coupled with a TATA-box insertion in the MYB87 promoter collectively contributes to the superior drought tolerance observed in M. sieversii. Our findings present molecular insights into how transcriptional regulation of SCL28.5-MYB87 module are integrated into drought response of different apple rootstocks.
items.authors: Turupu M, Du B, Zhang X, Wen Z, Wang H, Wang S, Chen Y, Quan F, Ru C, Zhang D, Li T.

items.title: In Vitro Inhibition of Phytophthora nicotianae by Berberine and Associated Physiological and Transcriptomic Responses.
items.abstract: Phytophthora nicotianae is a destructive plant-pathogenic oomycete. This study evaluated the in vitro inhibitory activity of berberine against strain ACCC 39210 and examined associated physiological and transcriptomic responses. Berberine inhibited mycelial growth, with an estimated EC50 of 42.1 μg/mL (95% CI: 7.66-76.55 μg/mL). Exposure to 42 and 200 μg/mL increased malondialdehyde (MDA) content and superoxide dismutase activity, while decreasing peroxidase activity, ATPase activity, and ATP content. Catalase activity only decreased significantly at 200 μg/mL. Conductivity measurements, propidium iodide staining, and microscopy provided evidence of cellular-envelope injury. Exploratory RNA-sequencing analysis using unadjusted p 1 identified 1255 and 1417 candidate differentially expressed genes at 42 and 200 μg/mL, respectively. Functional annotations suggested changes in metabolism, transport, and stress responses. Quantitative reverse-transcription PCR showed concordant expression directions for eight selected genes, using the same biological samples and a single reference gene; this comparison did not provide independent biological validation. These findings associate berberine-mediated growth inhibition with cellular-envelope injury, altered antioxidant enzyme activities, reduced ATP availability, and transcriptional responses in one isolate. Causal mechanisms, efficacy in planta, crop safety, and sensitivity across isolates require further investigation.
items.authors: Xu Z, Tan Z, Hu Q, Li Y.

items.title: Root saprotropism: A tropism guided by environmental pH sensing.
items.abstract: In saprotropism, roots perceive fungal-derived acidic pH gradients via the RGF-RGFR module to trigger asymmetric abscisic acid signaling, reorient microtubules, and drive root bending away from decay. Extracellular pH is a key convergence mode that mediates diverse plant-microbe interactions.
items.authors: Wang K, Liu L.

items.title: Author Correction: Cell-based CRISPRa screen identifies a papillae-specific receptor kinase mediating broad-spectrum fungal resistance in rice.
items.authors: Wang FZ, Bao Y, Qiu J, Chen MX, Jiang H, Li Z, Xiong X, Jiang X, Kou Y, Li JF.

items.title: Transcriptome insights into root adaptation of Erigeron canadensis to combined cadmium and lead stress.
items.abstract: The invasive plant species, Erigeron canadensis L., exhibits a propensity to colonize heavy metal-contaminated areas. However, its molecular adaptation mechanisms to heavy metals remain poorly understood. This study explored its adaptive mechanisms under combined cadmium (Cd) and lead (Pb) stress by investigating growth performance, heavy metal accumulation, and root molecular responses. Aboveground growth of E. canadensis was unaffected by any treatment, whereas root biomass was reduced only under high-concentration combined Cd and Pb stress. Cd and Pb were predominantly accumulated in roots instead of aboveground tissues. Notably, a translocation factor (TF) > 1 for Cd implied that E. canadensis actively accumulated Cd in roots and translocated it to aerial parts. However, a TF < 1 for Pb suggested that this species employed an exclusion strategy to mitigate Pb stress. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in E. canadensis roots were primarily involved in transport, signal transduction, antioxidant defence, transcription regulation, and ribosome function under heavy metal stress. Zinc transporter ZntB was verified to mediate Cd uptake and tolerance, while natural resistance-associated macrophage protein 3 and cyclic nucleotide-gated ion channel 2 were shown to mediate Cd and Pb uptake and tolerance by heterologous expression in yeast. Up-regulated amino acid, sugar, and auxin transporters together with ribosomal proteins may contribute to the maintenance of nutrient supply, auxin homeostasis, and protein synthesis for normal root growth. High-level metal stress triggered more extensive down-regulation of ROS-associated genes in E. canadensis roots. These findings provide root-specific molecular insights into the E. canadensis adaptation to heavy metal stress.
items.authors: Zhang H, Qi S, Shi Y, Dai Z, Ren G, Du D, Ji Z, Deng Y.

items.title: Cigarette Smoke Extract Impairs Regeneration and Tissue Homeostasis in the Planarian Dugesia japonica and May Be Associated with Changes in MAPK-Related Signaling.
items.abstract: Cigarette smoke extract (CSE) is used to assess tobacco toxicity, but its effects on freshwater planarian regeneration remain incompletely characterized. We investigated CSE toxicity in Dugesia japonica using acute toxicity tests, phenotypic observation, biochemical assays, immunofluorescence, TUNEL staining, and transcriptomic and proteomic analyses. The 96 h median lethal concentration (LC50) was 8.55% under the study-specific CSE definition. Exposure to 1% and 5% CSE impaired regeneration, with mortality and morphological abnormalities in the 5% group. CSE exposure also altered antioxidant and cholinergic enzyme activities, increased reactive oxygen species (ROS)-related fluorescence and malondialdehyde (MDA) content, and delayed neural remodeling. Fewer H3P-positive mitotic cells and more TUNEL-positive cells were observed, together with changes in proliferation- and apoptosis-related transcripts. Transcriptomic and proteomic analyses identified molecular responses involving stress, metabolism, and cellular homeostasis, although their overall concordance was low. Selected expression changes suggested mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK)-related signaling as a candidate response, but pathway activation and causal involvement were not established. These findings characterize regeneration impairment and associated cellular and molecular responses under laboratory CSE exposure conditions. They do not establish ecological risk at environmental exposure levels.
items.authors: Zhao Z, Wang E, Yang K, Zhang C, Song L, Xu Z.

items.title: A Review of the Roles of Calcium Signaling and Homeostasis in Nicotine Addiction: A Mechanistic Hypothesis Involving ATP2B2/PMCA2 and α7-Nicotinic Acetylcholine Receptors.
items.abstract: Calcium (Ca²⁺) signaling is essential for neurotransmitter release, synaptic plasticity, gene expression, and neuronal excitability. Nicotine, the addictive component of tobacco, activates nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs), including alpha4ß2- and a7-containing receptor subtypes, thereby altering neuronal Ca²⁺ entry. ATP2B2 encodes plasma membrane calcium-transporting ATPase 2 (PMCA2), a neuronal high-affinity Ca²⁺ extrusion pump that helps shape local Ca²⁺ microdomains. Published work has shown that PMCA2 functionally associates with a7-nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (alpha7-nAChRs) through postsynaptic density protein 95 (PSD-95) and can influence a7-nAChR surface expression. Genetic and transcriptomic studies have also linked ATP2B2-related pathways to substance use phenotypes, but there is no direct evidence that chronic nicotine alters PMCA2 expression. This narrative review distinguishes established findings from indirect evidence and untested predictions. We propose a mechanistic hypothesis in which chronic nicotine exposure may establish a new calcium-homeostatic equilibrium characterized by alpha7-nAChR downregulation and compensatory PMCA2 upregulation. We also hypothesize that, during early withdrawal, persistently elevated PMCA2 activity could contribute to excessive Ca²⁺ extrusion, reduced presynaptic glutamate release, cognitive impairment, and relapse vulnerability. These predicted effects require direct testing in nicotine exposure and withdrawal models. This review aims to examine the roles of calcium signaling and homeostasis in nicotine addiction, with particular emphasis on ATP2B2, which encodes the calcium ion pump PMCA2, and alpha7-nAChR.
items.authors: Wang T, Liang X, Xiang B, Gao L, Liu K.
items.journal: Medical science monitor : international medical journal of experimental and clinical research

items.title: Physiological and Transcriptomic Analyses Reveal Divergent Responses of Vegetative Growth and Inflorescence Development to Temperature in Chrysanthemum × morifolium.
items.abstract: Temperature strongly affects chrysanthemum flowering, but its stage-specific effects on vegetative and reproductive development remain unclear. Here, the obligate short-day chrysanthemum cultivar Chrysanthemum × morifolium 'Zijiao' was grown under three different day/night temperature regimes. We anatomically identified eight stages of floral induction and differentiation by observing the shoot apical meristem. The 25/16 °C treatment promoted coordinated inflorescence development, with floral bud differentiation completed within 42 days, the greatest number of florets, and the largest floral buds among the treatments. In contrast, the 30/18 °C regime enhanced plant height and internode elongation but delayed late floral bud differentiation. Photosynthetic pigment levels were generally maintained under the two warmer treatments relative to 20/13 °C, whereas carbohydrates, soluble proteins, superoxide dismutase, and peroxidase showed temperature- and stage-dependent changes. Leaf transcriptome profiling after 10 days revealed the differential regulation of hormone signaling, primary metabolism, antioxidant responses, and peroxisome-related pathways. The developmental expression of heat shock transcription factors A (CmHSFA4), CmWRKY40, CmMYB, and CmGATA8 further indicated stage-specific transcriptional responses. T2 and T3 showed significant positive relationships with CmMYB and CmWRKY40 expression, respectively. Thus, under the conditions tested, intermediate temperature favored reproductive development, whereas warmer conditions sustained vegetative growth and acclimation but compromised late floral organogenesis. These findings provide a physiological and transcriptional basis for cultivar-specific temperature management in chrysanthemum production.
items.authors: Zhang Q, Zhao SY, Jiang H, Nie M, Yang ZY, Lv JH.

items.title: Auxin-mediated RcARF8-RcWRKY29-RcERF98 module protects the rose petals against the Botrytis cinerea by modulating ascorbic acid biosynthesis and reactive oxygen species scavenging.
items.abstract: As one of the world's most important ornamental crops, rose (Rosa sp.) is highly susceptible to grey mold disease caused by Botrytis cinerea. Outbreaks of this disease during long-distance transportation often lead to substantial economic losses. This study identifies the WRKY transcription factor RcWRKY29 as a key regulator in the defense response against B. cinerea. Integrated RNA sequencing and DNA affinity purification sequencing analyses revealed RcERF98 as a direct target of RcWRKY29. Knockdown or overexpression RcWRKY29 correspondingly altered RcERF98 transcript levels, which in turn modulated ascorbic acid (AsA) accumulation and reactive oxygen species (ROS) scavenging in petals. Furthermore, exogenous application of naphthalene acetic acid significantly enhanced disease resistance and concurrently upregulated RcWRKY29 expression. We demonstrated that the auxin response factor RcARF8, but not RcARF1, binds to the RcWRKY29 promoter and activates its transcription. Moreover, knocking down or overexpression of RcARF8 affected the expression of both RcWRKY29 and RcERF98, thereby regulating AsA biosynthesis and ROS homeostasis, and ultimately determining disease susceptibility. Collectively, our findings reveal a signaling module in which the auxin-mediated transcription cascade involving RcARF8-RcWRKY29-RcERF98 confers resistance to B. cinerea by coordinating AsA-dependent ROS scavenging in rose petals.
items.authors: Wu J, Jing M, Yang S, Li Q, Li D, Fu Q, Ma X, Wang D, Li J, Jian H, Yan H, Tang K, Zhang H, Qiu X, Jing W.

items.title: Characterization of Ca2+-Dependent SOS-like Pathway Components Involved in the Salt Stress Response of an Intertidal Macroalga, Pyropia haitanensis.
items.abstract: Intertidal red algae show much stronger tolerance to hypersaline stress than terrestrial plants. However, the characteristics of Ca2+ signaling and the SOS-related ion regulatory mechanisms involved in their hypersaline stress responses remain unclear. In this study, the representative intertidal red alga Pyropia haitanensis was used to characterize Ca2+ signal transduction under hypersaline stress and to identify key components of the SOS pathway. Hypersaline stress rapidly induced a Ca2+ signal mainly driven by extracellular Ca2+ influx, which peaked at 15 min. Inhibition of Ca2+ influx significantly suppressed Na+ efflux, whereas inhibition of SOS1-mediated Na+ efflux enhanced Ca2+ influx. These results suggest that SOS1-associated Na+ efflux is Ca2+-dependent and closely associated with Ca2+ signaling during the hypersaline stress response. Based on the reference genome, 14 SOS-related candidate genes were identified. Most of these genes were significantly upregulated at approximately 10 min after hypersaline treatment, showing a rapid response pattern. Among them, PhSOS1-4 responded significantly at the transcriptional, protein abundance, and phosphorylation levels. PhSOS1-4 interacted with PhSOS3L-5 and PhSOS2L-2, respectively, whereas no direct interaction was detected between PhSOS3L-5 and PhSOS2L-2. These results suggest a possible SOS-like regulatory mode in P. haitanensis that is distinct from the classical SOS pathway in higher plants. In this pathway, PhSOS3L-5 may directly interact with PhSOS1-4 and potentially participate in the rapid regulation of Na+ efflux. Heterologous expression showed that both PhSOS1-4 and PhSOS3L-5 enhanced the hypersaline tolerance of Chlamydomonas reinhardtii. These findings provide new insights into the strong Na+ efflux capacity of intertidal red algae.
items.authors: Wen J, Si H, Li J, Xu K, Xu Y, Ji D, Wang J, Xian W, Xie C, Wang W.

items.title: Oral nicotine pouch extracts disrupt osteogenic differentiation in human embryonic stem cells.
items.abstract: Oral nicotine pouch (ONP) use has increased in recent years due to the perception that these products are a safer alternative to combustible tobacco products. However, little is known about the potential developmental toxicity of ONPs, particularly during bone formation. In this study, we evaluated the effects of ONP extracts from multiple ZYN flavors and nicotine concentrations on osteogenic differentiation using a human embryonic stem cell (hESC) model. H9 hESCs were differentiated toward the osteogenic lineage and continuously exposed to ONP extracts throughout differentiation. Cellular metabolic activity was assessed using the MTT assay, while ATP content, total protein content, alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activity, glutathione peroxidase (GPx) activity, and calcium deposition were evaluated using biochemical assays and Alizarin Red S staining. Gene expression was assessed using RT-qPCR and single-cell RNA sequencing, followed by pseudotime trajectory and transcriptomic point of departure (tPOD) analyses. ONP exposure caused concentration-dependent reductions in MTT activity, ATP content, total protein content, ALP activity, GPx activity, and calcium deposition. Expression of the osteogenic marker RUNX2 was generally decreased following ONP exposure, while TWIST1, SOX10, and TBX5 expression were increased in several treatment groups. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis demonstrated significant alterations in cell cluster distribution and pseudotime trajectory following ONP exposure, suggesting disrupted osteogenic lineage progression. Transcriptomic analysis further identified widespread perturbation of bone development-related genes across treatments. Wintergreen 6 mg had among the greatest transcriptomic potency metrics. Together, these findings reveal that ONP extracts disrupt osteogenic differentiation in hESCs and alter developmental lineage progression. This study provides mechanistic evidence that oral nicotine pouch extracts perturb early osteogenic differentiation in a human stem cell model and supports further evaluation of their developmental toxicity.
items.authors: Bertotto LB, Iwobi N, Meletz RM, Zepeda M, Khanal K, Vera-Colon M, Sparks NRL.

items.title: Schizophyllum commune Enhances Dendrobine Accumulation in Dendrobium nobile in Association with Induced Fungal Cellulolytic Activity and Host Jasmonate Biosynthesis.
items.abstract: ObjectiveTo explore the mechanism by which Schizophyllum commune elevates dendrobine accumulation in Dendrobium nobile, and verify whether cellulase derived from this fungus triggers jasmonate biosynthesis to mediate the regulation of alkaloid production.MethodsEndophytic fungi were isolated from D. nobile stems via tissue block isolation and identified by ITS sequencing. A plant-fungus symbiotic system was established with axenic plantlets. Dual RNA seq transcriptomic analysis, RT qPCR, pharmacological interventions with methyl jasmonate (MeJA) and the JA biosynthesis inhibitor salicylhydroxamic acid (SHAM) and Extracellular cellulase activities assays was performed.ResultsIn this study, none of 29 endophytic fungal strains from D. nobile stems produced dendrobine independently. Symbiotic screening subsequently identified Schizophyllum commune CY01 1H (SC) as the best strain that significantly increased dendrobine accumulation in D. nobile plantlets. Dual RNA seq revealed that SC colonization substantially activated jasmonic acid (JA) biosynthesis, accompanied by marked upregulation of the key biosynthetic gene DnLOX2. In contrast, downstream JA-signaling components exhibited an atypical transcriptional pattern, DnJAR was downregulated, whereas DnJAZ was upregulated. These results suggest that SC colonization induces a reconfiguration of JA signaling that may contribute to the maintenance of symbiotic homeostasis. In the fungus, cellulase-encoding genes were significantly induced. Experimental verification that MeJA promoted dendrobine accumulation, whereas SHAM suppressed it, and SC symbiosis partially mitigated this suppression. Stem section assays showed dynamic increases in extracellular cellulase activities (endoglucanase, cellobiohydrolase, β glucosidase), peaking at day 19, with endoglucanase being the highest.ConclusionsThese findings support a cross-regulatory model in which S. commune CY01-1H induces cellulolytic enzyme production during colonization, coinciding with host JA-biosynthetic activation and JA-signaling reprogramming, ultimately enhancing dendrobine accumulation. This study provides integrated evidence from fungal and host transcriptomes and enzymatic assays, expanding our understanding of endophyte-mediated regulation of medicinal plant metabolism. S. commune CY01 1H represents a promising biostimulant for sustainable improvement of dendrobine yield in cultivated D. nobile.
items.authors: Zhao Y, Ouyang Y, Xiong N, Ji X, Jia Q, Qin L, Xie J, He Y.

items.title: [Microbial Reduction Modified Biochar Mediated the Generation of Reactive Oxygen Species in Water and its Removal of Tetracycline].
items.abstract: With the growing application of biochar （BC） in environmental remediation， the role of BC in mediating reactive oxygen species （ROS） generation in the environment and its subsequent impact on pollutant degradation has become a research focus. Accordingly， this study selected rice straw-derived BC as the target material and Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 as representative microorganisms in aqueous-terrestrial media to investigate the reductive modification of BC by microorganisms under anaerobic conditions， while further exploring the capacity of microbial reduced biochar （RBC） to mediate the generation of ROS （·OH， H2O2， and O2-·） in aqueous environments and the corresponding performance and mechanism for tetracycline （TC） removal. The main results are as follows： ① Microbial reductive modification induced significant changes in the physicochemical properties of BC. Compared to the original BC， RBC exhibited higher hydrophilicity and polarity， lower aromatization， higher surface roughness， a 54%-63% increase in specific surface area， notable enhancements in the number of oxygen-containing functional groups （OFGs） and the degree of carbon defects， a 79%-92% rise in electron-accepting capacity， and a 20%-425% increase in the content of persistent free radicals （PFRs）. ② Microbial reductive modification also remarkably improved the capacity of BC to mediate ROS generation. As for BC prepared at 500℃ and 700℃， microbial reduction led to an 87%-95% increase in ·OH concentration and a 68%-126% increase in H2O2 concentration mediated by RBC （relative to the original BC）， with O2-· concentration notably rising from undetectable levels by the original BC to 1.47-5.25 μmol·L-1 by RBC， and this enhanced ROS-mediating capacity of RBC was closely associated with its increased PFRs， OFGs content， lattice carbon defects， and electron-accepting capacity. ③ In terms of TC removal， RBC outperformed the original BC by 139%-157% in removal efficiency， with its TC adsorption capacity increasing by 35%-161% and TC degradation capacity by 154%-495%. The total removal of TC by RBC was mainly through degradation. ④ A significant positive correlation （P<0.05） was observed between TC removal capacity of BC and the generation amounts of the three typical ROS it mediated， which indicated that all ROS may be involved in the degradation of TC in BC suspensions. TC was gradually degraded through reactions such as dehydroxylation， demethylation， deamidation， ring opening cracking， deamination， and dehydration in biochar suspensions.
items.authors: Tang SM, Liu LL, Fang J, Yang HQ, Yao JY, Jia HZ.
items.journal: Huan jing ke xue= Huanjing kexue

items.title: Effects of seed priming using cold argon plasma on enhancement of guar (Cyamopsis tetragonoloba) seed germination and growth under salt stress conditions.
items.abstract: BackgroundSalinity stress is a significant abiotic factor that severely hinders seed germination and early seedling establishment in numerous crop species. This study investigated the effectiveness of cold atmospheric argon plasma as an eco-friendly seed priming strategy to enhance salinity tolerance in guar (Cyamopsis tetragonoloba L.).ResultsAn atmospheric-pressure dielectric barrier discharge (DBD) system was used for the treatment. Seeds were exposed to argon plasma at four different discharge power levels: 1.2 W (0.40 A, 3 V), 2.04 W (0.51 A, 4 V), 3.05 W (0.61 A, 5 V), and 4.26 W (0.71 A, 6 V) for one minute, while untreated seeds served as the control. Both plasma-treated and control seeds were placed in Petri dishes under three different salinity levels (0, 50, and 100 mM NaCl), with each treatment replicated three times. The effects of plasma treatment were evaluated by assessing germination performance, seedling growth traits (including fresh and dry biomass, and shoot and root length), oxidative stress markers (such as malondialdehyde and other aldehydes), photosynthetic pigments (chlorophyll a, chlorophyll b, total chlorophyll, and carotenoids), and ion homeostasis (the contents of Na⁺ and K⁺). The results showed that argon plasma treatment significantly improved seed germination and seedling growth in a power-dependent manner under saline conditions. Moderate discharge power levels (2.04 W and 3.05 W) produced the highest germination percentages and the greatest root and shoot elongation. Additionally, plasma-treated seedlings exhibited reduced lipid peroxidation, a lower Na⁺/K⁺ ratio, and enhanced accumulation of photosynthetic pigments, indicating better regulation of oxidative stress and improved ionic balance under salinity stress.ConclusionsCold atmospheric argon plasma priming at optimal discharge power levels effectively enhances early-stage salinity tolerance in guar. This method represents a promising, sustainable, and non-chemical approach for improving crop establishment in saline environments.
items.authors: Firouzkoohi F, Nasibi F, Noori H.

items.title: Release of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) from spent granular activated carbon: Importance of the long-term releasable PFAS pool and suppression by calcium ions.
items.abstract: Release of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) from spent granular activated carbon (GAC) remains a critical yet poorly quantified process under variable water quality. In particular, the magnitude and controls of PFAS release flux from spent GAC are not well understood. In this study, spent GAC from a full-scale drinking water treatment plant was repacked into a series of columns to quantify the release flux of nine targeted PFAS that had accumulated during full-scale operation. When PFAS-free water was introduced, PFAS concentrations increased along the flow direction and approached plateau levels over time, indicating sustained release within the bed. PFAS release was lower under Ca2+-containing conditions than under Na+-dominated conditions, with stronger effects observed for more hydrophobic PFAS and little response for perfluorobutanoic acid (PFBA). Release fluxes varied among PFAS. PFAS release fluxes were only partially related to PFAS chain length and showed no clear relationship with total PFAS loading. Instead, greater release fluxes were generally associated with larger long-term releasable PFAS pools, quantified as the desorption potential in long-term batch desorption tests. These results indicate that PFAS release can occur during GAC operation when the carbon is exposed to water with lower PFAS concentrations than those encountered during GAC loading, and that Ca2+-containing conditions can suppress the release of more hydrophobic PFAS.

items.title: Ameliorative Mechanisms of ZnO Nanoparticles in Salinity-Stressed Basil Callus: From Redox Defense to Metabolomic Normalization.
items.abstract: Salinity is a major abiotic stressor inducing osmotic imbalance, ion toxicity, and oxidative damage in plant cells. This study investigates the ameliorative effects of 100 mg L-1 zinc oxide nanoparticles (ZnO NPs) on Ocimum basilicum L. callus cultures under salinity stress (0-90 mM NaCl) through an integrated enzymatic and GC-MS metabolomic approach. Exposure to 90 mM NaCl significantly suppressed biomass and increased oxidative stress markers (H2O2 and MDA). Notably, ZnO NP supplementation exhibited a selective modulatory role, preferentially stimulating the ascorbate-glutathione cycle, with ascorbate peroxidase activity reaching a peak of 1.16 U mg-1 protein. While ZnO NPs alone caused a slight increase in oxidative stress indicators, they significantly mitigated severe stress by reducing H2O2 levels and stabilizing protein content. Metabolomic profiling revealed that salinity triggered a shift toward sesquiterpene hydrocarbons (79.71%), whereas ZnO NP application reprogrammed secondary metabolism toward ester compounds (40.50%) and oxygenated metabolites, effectively normalizing salt-perturbed metabolite pools. Principal component analysis explained 72.5% of total variation, clearly distinguishing nanoparticle-driven recovery from stress-driven damage. These findings demonstrate that ZnO NPs enhance stress tolerance by reinforcing metabolic bridges between antioxidant defense and biomass preservation, offering a robust strategy for nano-enabled resilience.
items.authors: Tabay Sümbül D, Turan Büyükdinç D, Özcan Aykutlu A.

items.title: Growth, Heavy Metal Accumulation, and Translocation in Chamomile (Matricaria recutita L.) and Safflower (Carthamus tinctorius L.) Under Severe Cd and Pb Contamination in an Alkaline Soil.
items.abstract: Severe cadmium (Cd) and lead (Pb) contamination can compromise the productive and safe use of agricultural and degraded soils, yet plant tolerance, metal partitioning, and removal efficiency under alkaline soil conditions remain insufficiently resolved. This study aimed to evaluate growth responses, Cd and Pb accumulation, root-to-shoot translocation, and phytoremediation traits in chamomile (Matricaria recutita L.) and safflower (Carthamus tinctorius L.) under severe Cd and Pb contamination in an alkaline soil. A 4-month greenhouse experiment used 120 independent 5-L pots containing alkaline soil amended with 0, 50, or 100 mg Cd kg-1 and 0, 1500, or 3000 mg Pb kg-1. Chamomile accumulated 138.6 mg Cd kg-1 DW in shoots at Cd50, with a Bioconcentration Factor (BCF) value of 3.04 and a Translocation Factor (TF) of 1.56, whereas 100 mg Cd kg-1 caused severe biomass suppression and reduced translocation. Safflower showed significant growth stimulation at Pb1500, with shoot dry and fresh weight increasing by 17% and 44%, respectively, while Pb remained predominantly belowground (TF < 1); growth was strongly inhibited at Pb3000. Aboveground removal remained low, representing approximately 0.18% of the measured post-harvest soil Cd pool for chamomile at Cd50 and 0.008% of the soil Pb pool for safflower at Pb1500. Chamomile therefore warrants repeated-harvest evaluation for Cd phytoextraction, whereas safflower warrants long-term assessment for Pb phytostabilization-oriented management. Field and multi-season studies are needed to verify remediation efficiency, metal mobility, and safe biomass management.
