items.title: Capillin, a Polyacetylene from Argyranthemum frutescens, a Promising Hit Compound for Antikinetoplastid Drug Discovery.
items.abstract: Chagas disease and leishmaniasis, caused by the protozoan Trypanosoma cruzi and different Leishmania species, respectively, remain public health problems in developing regions due to high prevalence and the limited efficacy and safety of current treatments. Plant-derived natural products are emerging as a promising source of safer antikinetoplastid agents. The present work explores Argyranthemum frutescens as a source of antiparasitic compounds to identify new therapeutic candidates. To address this aim, a bioassay-guided fractionation of the ethanolic root extract from cultivated A. frutescens was carried out against kinetoplastids, including T. cruzi, L. amazonensis, and L. donovani. Polyacetylenes with leishmanicidal and trypanocidal activity were identified using this approach. Among them, compound 1 showed greater activity than the reference drug miltefosine against L. amazonensis and T. cruzi. Compound 1 showed activity against the amastigote stages of both parasites, surpassing the activity of the leishmanicidal reference drug. Notably, compound 1 showed a good selectivity index against the mammalian cell line. The findings indicated that the nature of the chemical group present at the propargyl-benzyl position plays a role in compound bioactivity. Subsequent assays revealed that this compound induces programmed cell death-related processes in T. cruzi and L. amazonensis, including ATP depletion, chromatin condensation, plasma membrane damage, accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), and alterations in mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm). Collectively, these findings highlight the potential of polyacetylenes as promising antikinetoplastid lead compounds and identify A. frutescens as a valuable natural source for the development of therapeutic agents against Chagas disease and leishmaniasis.

items.title: Harnessing large-scale genomics-based screening for the identification of expansin genes responsive to abiotic stress in Peucedanum praeruptorum.
items.abstract: IntroductionExpansins are crucial for cell wall relaxation and significantly impact plant growth and development. However, the expansin gene family in Peucedanum praeruptorum remains to be systematically characterized.MethodsHere, we systematically identified expansin genes in P. praeruptorum and analysed their molecular characteristics, evolutionary patterns, and expression profiles in response to methyl jasmonate (MeJA). Subcellular localization prediction, gene structure analysis, chromosomal localization, collinearity analysis, and cis-acting element analysis were performed. Based on cis-element screening, PpdEXPA01, PpdEXPA10, PpdEXPA13, PpdEXPB1, and PpdEXPB2 were selected to validate their expression under exogenous MeJA stress.ResultsA total of 39 PpdEXP genes were identified and classified into four subfamilies: EXPA (24 genes), EXPB (9 genes), EXPLA (2 genes), and EXPLB (4 genes). Subcellular localization predictions indicated that all members are localized in the cell wall, and all expansin proteins are hydrophilic. Gene structural analysis showed that the number of introns ranged from one to four and that all genes contained two conserved domains: DPBB_EXPA_N and Expansin_C. Chromosomal localization analysis showed that the 39 PpdEXP genes were distributed across 11 chromosomes, with tandem duplication events occurring on chromosomes 3, 4, and 7. Collinearity analysis indicated that segmental and whole-genome duplication were the main driving forces behind the expansion of the expansin gene family. Analysis of cis-acting elements revealed 1,237 elements in total, which were primarily classified into three categories: hormone response, light response, and stress response. Expression profiling revealed that PpdEXP genes exhibit significant tissue specificity. The five selected genes had significant tissue- and time-specific expression patterns in roots, stems, and leaves under exogenous MeJA stress.DiscussionThis study systematically elucidated the molecular basis and expression regulation patterns of the P. praeruptorum expansin family, providing a foundation for further functional characterization of PpdEXP genes and their potential roles in growth, development, and stress responses.
items.authors: He C, Qi M, Li X, Dai J, Song C.

items.title: Spatial Gene Expression in Fungi: mRNA Localization, Condensates, and Beyond.
items.abstract: Polarized growth and cellular asymmetry are broadly conserved properties of fungal life, from transient bud-site selection in unicellular yeasts to sustained hyphal extension in filamentous and coenocytic species. While vesicle trafficking, cytoskeletal organization, and cell-wall remodeling are well-established contributors to these processes, the role of mRNA localization is only beginning to be fully appreciated. In this review, we examine how the spatial regulation of mRNAs and their translation contributes to fungal polarity, morphogenesis, and environmental adaptation. We discuss current knowledge around three interconnected layers contributing to mRNA localization: active cytoskeletal transport-actin-based in compact yeasts and microtubule-based in long hyphae; partitioning into biomolecular condensates such as P-bodies and Whi3-mRNA assemblies; and cytoplasmic-scale architectural features including bulk flow, nuclear positioning, and nuclear heterogeneity that become increasingly important in multinucleate and coenocytic systems such as arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi. Together, these mechanisms establish spatial gene expression as an integral component of fungal polarity, with implications for fungal development, host-pathogen interactions, and ecological adaptation, and for our broader understanding of polarized growth in eukaryotic cell organization.
items.authors: Otterdijk SV, Wang Z, Arends R, Tutucci E.

items.title: Statistical inference of keystone taxa reshaping the assembly rules of forest root microbiomes.
items.abstract: Root-associated fungi and bacteria play pivotal roles in terrestrial ecosystem processes. However, identifying keystone taxa driving below-ground microbial assembly remains a major challenge. Here, we present a statistical framework for identifying microbes that reorganize microbiome assembly. Using 1,270 root samples collected from a cool-temperate forest in Japan, we reconstruct assembly landscapes describing the probabilistic structure of community states. We then find that several endophytic fungi (e.g., Phialocephala and Oidiodendron) are strongly associated with the reorganization of assembly landscape topography along abundance gradients, coinciding with shifts in mycorrhizal symbiosis. Independent datasets from Europe confirm that the highlighted genera are significantly associated with changes in mycorrhizal colonization patterns. Prokaryotic communities exhibit transitions among states characterized by core taxa, Pseudomonadota, or Actinomycetota, strongly associated with abundance gradients of Candidatus Udaeobacter and several endophytic fungi. These findings provide a scalable framework for prioritizing candidate keystone taxa and linking microbiome assembly to ecosystem-scale processes.

items.title: Time-ordered co-expression network analysis reveals b-locus-mediated transcriptional cascades underlying sugarcane resistance to smut fungus (Sporisorium scitamineum).
items.abstract: Sugarcane smut, caused by the biotrophic fungus Sporisorium scitamineum, causes serious yield and sugar losses. Growing resistant varieties is the main control method. The fungal b mating-type locus (b-locus) is required for filamentous growth and virulence, but how it shapes the host response is not well understood. Here, we compared a resistant cultivar (GT29) and a susceptible cultivar (GT11-80) after inoculation with a wild-type (WT) strain or a b-locus deletion mutant, with sampling from 0 to 7 days postinoculation (dpi). We measured bE gene copy number by quantitative PCR (qPCR), assayed defense enzymes and phytohormones, and performed RNA sequencing followed by time-ordered gene co-expression network (TO-GCN) analysis. The WT strain proliferated rapidly in GT11-80 but was strongly restricted in GT29, and the b-locus mutant reached much lower levels than the WT strain in GT11-80 by 7 dpi. GT29 showed a stronger and more sustained oxidative burst (O2- and H2O2) than GT11-80 and maintained higher antioxidant enzyme activities. For hormones, WT infection induced more jasmonic acid (JA) and 1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylic acid (ACC; the ethylene precursor) than the mutant, with the highest levels in GT29 at 5 dpi, whereas salicylic acid (SA) accumulated late (7 dpi) in GT11-80; abscisic acid (ABA) stayed high under WT infection but dropped under the mutant. TO-GCN analysis identified a WT-specific, time-ordered transcription factor (TF) cascade in GT11-80 that was lost under mutant infection, whereas the GT29 network kept its temporal order under both conditions. In the jasmonic acid/ethylene (JA/ET) subnetwork, ERF1 was a central hub in GT11-80, while in GT29 ERF1 was much less connected and EIN3 was the main hub. Overall, the b-locus is required for the time-ordered transcriptional response during infection, and the resistant and susceptible cultivars differ in their hormone dynamics and JA/ET network structure. These findings provide candidate genes and network features for breeding smut-resistant sugarcane.
items.authors: Song XP, Zhang XQ, Lu BQ, Huang DM, Liang YJ, Zhang BQ, Deng YC, Li DM, Li YR, Liang Q, Verma KK, Yan MX.

items.title: Multi-Omics Analysis Reveals Hormonal, miRNA-Associated, and NLR-Linked Aphid Defense in Lycium barbarum.
items.abstract: Aphid infestation constrains goji berry production, yet its defense architecture remains poorly resolved. We integrated comparative transcriptomics, phytohormone profiling, small RNA sequencing, and genome-wide nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat (NLR) analysis to dissect aphid defense in Lycium barbarum (cv. Ningqi-10)and susceptible L. chinense. Aphid bioassays confirmed that L. barbarum imposes a significant fitness cost on aphids, reducing survival, longevity, and fecundity. Transcriptomic comparison revealed fewer but more defense-enriched differentially expressed genes in the resistant accession. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) identified a stress-associated turquoise module (288 genes, r = 0.981) receptor-like kinases and mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) components, bridging extracellular signals sensing and hormone signaling. Phytohormone profiling showed that salicylic acid (SA) accumulated to 72 h, whereas jasmonic acid (JA) peaked transiently at 24 h, producing an increased SA/JA ratio suggesting a shift to SA-dominated signaling. MiR398a-3p and miR319-3p dynamics coincided with this SA/JA shift, suggesting a possible link to hormone-coordinated regulation and candidate targets for validation. NLR analysis identified 151 candidate genes, including 18 L. barbarum-biased NLRs up-regulation under SA-dominated signaling, implying a link to SA signaling. Collectively, these findings support a multi-layered framework integrating SA signaling, transcriptional reprogramming, and coupled miRNA and NLR responses in aphid defense.
items.authors: Yan T, Zhou ZK, Shi PF, Yue JY, Sang H, Shi RR, Chang SJ, Hai L.

items.title: Biochar-mediated modulation of drought tolerance and antioxidant defense in Desi and Kabuli chickpea (Cicer arietinum L.).
items.abstract: BackgroundDrought stress severely impairs chickpea productivity through osmotic imbalance and oxidative damage. This study evaluated the efficacy of soil-applied biochar (0%, 1.5%, and 3% v/v) in enhancing the drought tolerance of two contrasting chickpea genotypes (Desi and Kabuli) subjected to varying moisture regimes (100%, 75%, 50%, and 25% field capacity).ResultsThe 1.5% biochar application provided the most effective physiological and biochemical balance under severe water deficit. It sustained osmotic adjustment by improving leaf relative water content (up to 12%) and modulating proline accumulation. Furthermore, biochar activated reactive oxygen species (ROS) scavenging mechanisms, upregulating key antioxidant enzymes (CAT, SOD, APX, GR) and modifying specific isoenzyme profiles. This coordinated response reduced lipid peroxidation (malondialdehyde) by ~ 36% under extreme stress. Genotypically, Desi exhibited strong inherent structural resilience, whereas Kabuli demonstrated high enzymatic plasticity.ConclusionsBiochar appears to function as a biochemical modulator enhancing drought tolerance in chickpea via coordinated osmotic adjustment and targeted ROS scavenging. Integrating appropriate biochar doses shows strong potential as a sustainable agronomic strategy to support crop resilience in vulnerable semi-arid agroecosystems.

Zinc and Iron Homeostatic Interactions in a Mutant Lacking Nicotianamine Vacuolar Storage and Citrate Xylem Loading
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Metal homeostasis in plants relies on coordinated uptake, chelation and transport mechanisms involving, but not limited to, citrate and nicotianamine (NA). In Arabidopsis ( Arabidopsis thaliana ), disruption of the citrate exporter FRD3 (FERRIC REDUCTASE DEFECTIVE 3) causes constitutive iron (Fe) deficiency responses, altered Fe, manganese (Mn) and zinc (Zn) distribution, with Fe accumulation in the root cell wall. This ultimately results in oxidative and biotic stress responses, and impaired root development, phenotypes that are partially alleviated by Zn excess. In this study, we investigated the consequences of impairing both citrate loading into xylem vessels and NA partitioning within cells. The frd3 zif1 double mutant exhibits enhanced sensitivity to Zn excess, severe defects in root system architecture and meristem maintenance, persistent oxidative stress and compromised reproductive development. These phenotypes correlate with sustained activation of Fe deficiency signalling and marked defects in root‐to‐shoot metal translocation. Our findings reveal that coordinated citrate export and NA compartmentation form an integrated buffering strategy required to maintain metal homeostasis and partitioning, as well as redox balance and proper development, including root plasticity and seed yield, under fluctuating metal availability.
items.authors: Fanara S, Scheepers M, Latour C, Boulanger M, Schloesser M, Bosman B, Carnol M, Fratamico A, Sarthou M, Tocquin P, Hanikenne M

items.title: PpPKp1 Coordinates Growth and Cold Tolerance by Integrating Energy‐Cytokinin Signalling via Pyruvate Metabolism in Poa pratensis
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Plastidial pyruvate kinase (PKp; EC 2.7.1.40), as a core enzyme regulating plant carbon metabolism, has been confirmed to be a key component in plant stress response. However, the specific regulatory network in cold response and the molecular mechanism mediating cold tolerance remain elusive. This study reveals that the expression of PpPKp1 , a chloroplast‐localized plastid pyruvate kinase gene from Poa pratensis var. anceps cv. Qinghai, is significantly induced by low temperature and drought stress. Overexpression of PpPKp1 in Arabidopsis thaliana and Poa pratensis enhanced pyruvate kinase activity and pyruvate content, thereby improving tillering capacity and biomass accumulation under cold conditions, while also promoting root elongation, shoot growth, and maintaining the relative stability of ROS. Conversely, RNAi ‐mediated suppression of PpPKp1 in P. pratensis elicited contrasting phenotypes and physiological responses. Mechanistic investigations demonstrated that under cold stress, PpPKp1 facilitates energy supply by enhancing glycolytic/TCA cycle flux and simultaneously coordinates arginine biosynthesis with cytokinin signalling transduction. This integrated mechanism of ‘energy provision‐metabolite synthesis‐signal regulation’ is closely associated with the maintenance of plant growth and development under cold conditions, balancing resource allocation between stress resistance and growth. Ultimately, it leads to significantly enhanced cold tolerance. Our work unveils for the first time the molecular mechanism by which PpPKp1 regulates plant cold responses through coupling central carbon metabolism and hormone signalling. It provides novel insights into the synergistic network of ‘plastid metabolism‐systemic stress resistance’ in plants, and offers candidate genes and a theoretical basis for the genetic improvement of cold tolerance in crops.
items.authors: Zhang Y, Dong W, Ma H, Zhao C, Shi X, Zhang Y, Ma F, Nai G

items.title: Synthetic tools to redirect the ubiquitin E3 ligase activity of a plant-specific N-recognin
items.abstract: Abstract The Arg/N-degron pathway regulates important agronomic traits. In plants, the PROTEOLYSIS 1 (PRT1) protein binds to aromatic amino-terminal residues and recruits ubiquitin (Ub) conjugating enzymes to ubiquitinate substrate proteins. Here, we demonstrate that PRT1 recruits the UBC35-UEV1A complex via RING1 of PRT1. This stimulates UBC35 to produce K63-linked Ub chains. To afford chemical control over Ub signalling, we construct a synthetic substrate of PRT1 with an N-terminal calmodulin-binding peptide (CBP). The addition of the CBP sequence to the substrate creates an off switch for PRT1-dependent ubiquitination that is regulated by calcium and calmodulin. Finally, we produce a set of nanobodies that are recognised by PRT1 and induce the ubiquitination of a reporter protein. Altogether, we introduce and biochemically validate several tools to both redirect and chemically control the Arg/N-degron pathway.
items.authors: Oldham KEA, Yee S, Chan KX, Mabbitt PD
